#6376. The Ice Giants' Magnetic Fields are Very Strange Compared to Earth's

Most planets appear to have magnetic fields, even if they're only weak, remnant fields. Earth has a strong field generated by its internal geodynamo. The other rocky planets have magnetic fields of varying strengths, with the possible exception of Venus. The outer gas planets, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, all have strong dynamos.

But the magnetic fields generated by the ice giants Uranus and Neptune have some strange properties.

Earth's molten core and internal convection generate its magnetic fields. But the ice giants' magnetic fields are likely generated by fluids that are electrically conductive. These are water, ammonia, and methane ices under extreme pressure and temperatures that alter them and turn them into ionic and superionic phases. Not only is their electrical conductivity at play, but so is convection and the planets' rotations.

But beyond what generates them, they also have other differences. Earth's magnetic field has well-defined north and south poles that drift a little over time, and even flip every couple of hundred thousand years or so. But Voyager 2 showed us how different Uranus and Neptune are. Their fields are in disarray compared to Earth's. They're tilted and multi-peaked.

Uranus' magnetic field doesn't originate in its center, and is tilted almost 60 degrees from its axis of rotation. It's overall geometry is strange, and the magnetic field across its surface is asymmetrical in strength.

Neptune's magnetic field is similarly strange, but weaker. Like Uranus' it's tilted from its rotational axis, by about 47 degrees. It's also offset from the planet's physical center like Uranus'.

The most critical difference between the magnetic fields of Earth and those of Uranus and Neptune is that the fields around the ice giants experience shorter-term variability. In short, they're a weird mess.

While planetary scientists know that these fields are generated inside the planets, they've had to make some guesses as to why they're so strange. New research in Nature Communications Physics has made some progress understanding the pair of ice giants and their strange magnetic fields. It's titled "Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune," and the lead author is Chi Yan. Yan is a research associate at the University of Texax Jackson School of Geosciences.

"Uranus and Neptune exhibit magnetic fields that are non-dipolar and non-axisymmetric, unlike those of any other known planet," the researchers write. "These fields are generated by fluid motions in electrically conducting planetary interiors via dynamo action, offering a window into otherwise inaccessible deep processes."

As we often say at Universe Today, understanding the oddballs and outliers in a group of objects sheds light on how processes operate across the broader group they're a part of. This is true of the ice giants and their magnetic fields. "Understanding why Uranus and Neptune have such unusual magnetic fields provides critical insight into dynamo processes across planets and stars," the authors explain.

This work is based on modelled dynamos that are controlled by interior composition and temperature. They assumed that electrical conductivity increases with depth. The authors say they "produce large-scale magnetic features consistent with the observed fields of Uranus and Neptune..."

This schematic shows the different interior layouts used in the models. a through c show radially variable electrical conductivity profiles for dynamo models with convective shell geometries. d through f show the associated shell geometry for each of a through c. Image Credit: Yan, C., Soderlund, K.M., Aurnou, J.M. et al. Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune. Commun Phys 9, 336 (2026).

âDeep inside Uranus and Neptune, pressures and temperatures become extremely high,â lead author Yan said in a press release. âUnder these conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth.â

Voyager 2 gave us our only good close-up look at Uranus and Neptune. It likely caught those fields in a snapshot in time, and the model shows both planets' magnetic fields could shift and change markedly in only decades. The fields are most likely configured much differently than when Voyager 2 visited. This is much different than on Earth, where the magnetic north pole drifts between about 5 and 60 km per year, or about one degree every few decades.

"These non-dipolar dynamos exhibit substantial temporal variation, although the rate fluctuates and can be transiently slow," the authors write. They explain that changes in both intensity and orientation are a possibility in the decades since Voyager 2 flew past Uranus and Neptune, "though the extent of any such variation remains poorly constrained observationally as each planet has been measured in situ only once."

âEarthâs magnetic tilt drifts by only a degree or so over 50 years,â said Yan. âOur models show the ice giants can behave very differently. In some stretches the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades. In others it shifts only slightly over the same span.â

This figure compares observations of Uranus' and Neptune's surface magnetic fields with the fields from models. The figure "demonstrates that the most Uranus-like snapshot from Model 6 (panel c) and the most Neptune-like snapshot from Model 11 (panel d) can change substantially on decadal timescales, with their close morphological resemblance to the respective observed fields (panels a and b) deteriorating markedly after 32 years (panels e and f)," the authors explain. Image Credit: Yan, C., Soderlund, K.M., Aurnou, J.M. et al. Electrical conductivity structure drives anomalous and potentially time-varying magnetic fields at Uranus and Neptune. Commun Phys 9, 336 (2026).

"We demonstrate that dynamo models incorporating an electrical conductivity that increases with depth can promote non-dipolar, non-axisymmetric magnetic fields," the authors write, including the M1 peak observed at Uranus and Neptune.

The M1 peak is an important, maybe the most important part, of Voyager 2's magnetic field observations. M=1 represents the lop-sided parts of a magnetic field. On Earth and other planets like Jupiter and Saturn, the magnetic field's power is dominated by symmetric or M=0 components. So for those planets, the M-1 components are at least an order of magnitude weaker than their M-0 components.

But that's not true on Uranus and Neptune. They show a stark contrast. They both have a very strong M-1 peak, the part that represents asymmetric fields. This means that they have dipoles, quadrupoles, and octupoles that are messy and skewed from the axis of rotation.

"Despite current observational and computational limitations, our results indicate that ice-giant-like dynamos can, in some intervals, undergo substantial magnetic field variations on decadal timescales that, if confirmed by future in situ or auroral measurements, could have significant impacts on the surrounding planetary magnetospheres," the authors write.

The JWST has observed the ice giant aurorae and the charged particles involved. These particles respond to the magnetic fields, and those observations could confirm if the magnetic fields have indeed shifted since Voyager 2 visited. Researchers are still working on those observations.

The image on the left is an enhanced-color image of Neptune from NASAâs Hubble Space Telescope. On the right, that image is combined with data from NASAâs James Webb Space Telescope. The cyan splotches are auroral activity captured with the JWST's Near-Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec). Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, Heidi Hammel (AURA), Henrik Melin (Northumbria University), Leigh Fletcher (University of Leicester), Stefanie Milam (NASA-GSFC)

âWe are busy working on whatâs contained within these observations, but the shape and structure of the aurora, as well as other weird patterns in the ionosphere promises to provide us with a way of understanding how the magnetic fields have changed, an important stepping stone,â said Tom Stallard, a professor at Northumbria University who led the JWST observation campaign.

The researchers will combine the JWST data with their models and data from Voyager 2 and take their results as far as they can to try to determine the state of the magnetic fields today. But they're up against some limitations, limitations that can only be lifted by another mission to the ice giants.

There are no firm plans for a mission to the ice giants, but there are concepts. One is NASA's Uranus Orbiter & Probe that would study the planet and its moons, and even send a probe into Uranus' atmosphere. The Neptune Odyssey is another NASA concept. It would also consist of an orbiter and an atmospheric probe. The science community has recognized the importance of these missions, but they're just concepts at this point.

This research may extend to the issue of habitability, though probably only tangentially. Uranus' four major moons could all potentially have subsurface oceans under icy covers, though this is far from confirmed. If they do, then Uranus' magnetic field and related radiation belts could affect these bodies of water, their longevity, and their potential habitability.

#6375. Food contains thousands of overlooked chemicals. This physicist is mapping them

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Tina Hesman Saey, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Computational physicist Giulia Menichetti is looking for “dark matter” in our food. In addition to known macronutrients, vitamins and minerals, the things we eat contain a whole world of natural chemicals we have no idea about. And those chemicals may affect our health.

“They have the ability to interact, to bind to human proteins, to modulate our microbiome,” says Menichetti of Harvard Medical School. “We want to leverage this to talk more and more about the role of food and nutrition in human health.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Menichetti leads Foodome, a project to map our food’s full chemical complexity. Her team uses AI to mine scientific papers for every chemical compound that has ever been linked to a food. She singles out ones that haven’t been tracked by epidemiological studies — the “nutritional dark matter.” So far, her team has cataloged about 140,000 molecules.

When one hears about chemicals in food, they might initially think of artificial additives. Her team addresses those, but she’s also interested in naturally occurring chemicals. Take garlic, for example. Foodome has cataloged almost 7,000 different molecules in raw garlic alone. Some of these compounds have been investigated for health effects, but some are entirely new.

Foodome is still mining the scientific literature for these molecules and building out databases. Eventually, Menichetti would like AI to be able to predict how all these food molecules interact together and in the human body.

“There is a legacy of chemical complexity that comes from organisms that are all around us,” she says. “Food is part of that. It is actually our way to interact with our environment. We need to study it better.”

#6374. The 2026 Best New Bakeries in America

Precision pastries are sweeping the nation. These bakers are leading the charge.

If there’s one thing we’ve noticed over the past several years, it’s how much bakeries have stepped up their game.

Some embody a personal expression of a baker’s identity, while others push the envelope beyond expected flavor combinations; all excel at a time when “little treat” culture is at its peak. — Missy Frederick, editorial director

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

If one new place in Chicago needs no further hype, it is Bad Butter. You’ll know you’re there when you spot the line cascading out of the whitewashed storefront along West Cortland Street, a queue that doesn’t let up until the pastry case is empty. Formerly a head baker at Soho House Chicago, Dan Koester was stuck at home like the rest of us in 2020, handing off excess home-baked sourdough loaves to friends and family and making some available for free pickup. After he was officially laid off that summer, he launched his own online bakery business, earning a massive following along the way.

One residency at the Emily Hotel later, Koester debuted his Bucktown bakery, demonstrating the full range of his skill. Still warm, charred, and dimpled flats of focaccia showered with scallion furikake rest on its shelves. Impossibly crisp and exquisitely laminated twice-baked almond croissants burst with subtle, aromatic almond paste. A spicy harissa monkey bread with a cloudlike texture is cooled by a pool of creamy labneh drizzled with silky olive oil.

The bakery’s menu has breadth and also manages to arc with the season. Customers snake along the floor waiting their turn to claim a towering cruffin, dusted in fine grains of sugar and piped full of ginger plum jam, or a seasonal tart piled with plump, lacquered blueberries. A pastry box filled with these confections is well worth the wait. — Brenna Houck, dining editorial manager

Born as an underground dinner party operated out of Karla Subero Pittol’s Echo Park garage, Chainsaw finally got its own digs in November 2025 in the form of a lively cafe in Melrose Hill, an unquestionably gentrifying neighborhood that has become home to some of Los Angeles’s best independent restaurants. At the cafe, Subero Pittol channels her Venezuelan heritage through a menu of arepas plump with beans, limey guasacaca, and cheese; a Venezuelan hot dog (“perro caliente”) buoyed by an acidic slaw; and her bracingly tart passionfruit-lime icebox pie, which commands a cult following all its own.

Stepping into Chainsaw feels like you could be in Subero Pittol’s own kitchen as she greets regulars and newcomers as if they are old friends. Customers study a handwritten menu that changes daily — it doesn’t help to come in too attached to any one dish (save the ever-present icebox pie) when you may get tempted by another. The cafe’s impact on Los Angeles feels clear in the near-constant crowds that hover outside, reading their newspapers over an espresso or tucking into the latest of Subero Pittol’s ideas, such as a full English breakfast served for a single day. In a city lacking in untamed Venezuelan cooking, Chainsaw offers a home for Subero Pittol to celebrate the cuisine in a way that feels distinctly Los Angeles. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest

With both Afghan and Latin American influences, Diljān gives New Yorkers a bakery with a point of view and innumerable reasons to become a regular. Ali Zaman and Mohamed Ghiasi, owners of Astoria’s Little Flower Cafe, teamed up with Bryan Ford, Honduran American baker and cookbook author, to conceptualize the bakery, now perched on a corner near Atlantic Avenue in Brooklyn Heights.

Their combined talent makes for some of the city’s most compelling baked goods. For the Saffron Shah, laminated pastry holds delicate saffron cream in the shape of a crescent, an important Islamic symbol. Halwa tops the sticky bun, while a swirl of samosa pastry wraps halal lamb under a dusting of powdered sugar. Don’t miss the enormous Afghan flatbread crowned by toppings such as halal beef bacon with scallions or sour cherry cream cheese. The team has also branched into pizzas topped with cheese and Afghan cumin, kofta kebabs, or beef pepperoni. Look for specials like the flan with cardamom-poached apricots and conchas stuffed with firni, a rice pudding. — Nadia Chaudhury, deputy editor, Eater New York

San Francisco’s pastry game is stronger and more competitive than ever before, and Parachute Bakery steps to the forefront of a crowded field with a mix of patisserie standards and seasonal standouts. At his Ferry Building bakery, pastry chef Nasir Armar marries his fine dining training, honed at Michelin-starred Sorrel and Saison, with flavors that make everyone sit up and take notice (and snap a food photo or two for their socials).

Vegetables and savory complements are given their own footing on the menu. Stalks of grilled asparagus shine in a baton-shaped croissant shell, with fennel jam, sheep’s milk ricotta, and ramp pesto alongside them; one brief, bordering-on-gimmicky croissant got piped with clam chowder, a reference to the soup in a bread bowl famously served on the city’s wharf. Even potato-laden samosas and bright tomato shakshuka get interpreted into pastry form. Parachute succeeds with its experimental vision, a hype well-earned that leaves fans clamoring for what they’ll come up with next. — Dianne de Guzman, editor, Eater SF

#6373. Scientists Trap a Single Antimatter Particle for Months in Quest To Solve the Universe’s Biggest Mystery

A single particle of antimatter, suspended for months in a laboratory trap, could help physicists unravel why matter survived to build the universe around us.

Northwestern University physicists have brought a positron, the electron’s antimatter counterpart, into a precisely controlled quantum state for the first time. After capturing the energetic particle from radioactive decay, they cooled it to nearly absolute zero and suspended it in a near-perfect vacuum.

Their achievement, described in Physical Review Letters, creates a “one-positron quantum cyclotron.” Like an artificial atom, the trapped positron has distinct quantum energy levels that researchers can manipulate and observe.

That control opens a path toward an exceptionally precise comparison of matter and antimatter. By measuring the positron’s magnetic properties and comparing them with an electron’s, the team hopes to test a fundamental prediction of particle physics and search for signs that current theory is missing something.

The Standard Model describes fundamental particles and three of nature’s four fundamental forces (electromagnetic, strong nuclear, and weak nuclear forces). Although experiments have repeatedly confirmed its predictions with extraordinary precision, it cannot explain why the observable universe contains overwhelmingly more matter than antimatter.

“Antimatter gets its popular charm from science fiction,” said study leader Gerald Gabrielse. “If you take an electron and an anti-electron (or positron) and collide them together, they both disappear. We describe that as annihilation, a concept that fuels science fiction writers’ imaginations. The big mystery of the universe is the Big Bang should have created equal amounts of matter and antimatter. But, if that were true, it would annihilate, and we’d be left with nothing. There’s clearly something wrong with that theory, and that’s what we’re trying to figure out.”

The unresolved question is how matter escaped annihilation to build stars, planets, and people.

“We know the Standard Model has to be wrong somewhere—or at least incomplete,” Gabrielse said. “For example, it cannot predict why the universe exists, so that’s a pretty big loophole. We’re very precisely examining the most fundamental and simple systems to find where the theory breaks down. We hope to find an unambiguous answer.”

Nearly everything on Earth consists of electrons, protons, and neutrons. An antimatter world could instead contain positrons, antiprotons, and antineutrons. Gabrielse says that if everything here were made of antimatter, the difference would be extraordinarily difficult to recognize. The trouble begins when matter and antimatter meet, which makes an ordinary container unsuitable for holding a positron.

“If we want to study antimatter, we must handle it carefully,” Gabrielse said. “To be clear, it’s not dangerous. We don’t have enough antimatter to make an explosion.”

The Northwestern team used specialized electric and magnetic fields to suspend the particle away from the walls of an advanced trap. A near-perfect vacuum minimizes encounters with ordinary matter, allowing the positron to remain confined for months.

Capturing it required first overcoming its enormous initial energy. The researchers obtained positrons from the radioactive decay of sodium-22, a rare isotope of sodium, then slowed a particle dramatically and guided it into the trap.

Inside the trap, the temperature is about 300 millikelvins, just 0.3 degrees Celsius (0.54 degrees Fahrenheit) above absolute zero. Cooling allows the researchers to bring the positron’s cyclotron motion, its circling movement in the magnetic field, into its lowest quantum energy state.

“We cool it down so much that it’s in its quantum ground state,” Gabrielse said. “We actually coaxed this very fast positron to sit there and behave for months at a time.”

The team then used carefully tuned microwaves to deliver tiny amounts of energy and detected the positron’s transitions between individual quantum states. Being able to both trigger and observe those changes provides the control needed for a highly precise magnetic measurement.

The experiment combines two strands of Gabrielse’s career. His group previously developed techniques to isolate electrons and measure their magnetic properties, while his pioneering work on slowing, capturing, and cooling antiprotons helped establish low-energy antimatter research. The new study extends the quantum control achieved with electrons to a single antimatter particle.

In earlier work, Gabrielse’s team used a one-electron quantum cyclotron to measure the electron’s magnetic moment to about one part in 10 trillion, among the most precise measurements ever made of an elementary particle. The magnetic moment describes how strongly a particle interacts with a magnetic field.

The next goal is to make a comparable measurement of the positron. Electrons and positrons have opposite electric charges, and theory predicts magnetic moments equal in magnitude but opposite in direction. An unexpected mismatch would challenge the Standard Model and could offer clues to the universe’s imbalance between matter and antimatter.

“Current theories suggest that there will be no difference in the two measurements,” Gabrielse said. “If it turns out they are not equal, that would be the biggest discovery in physics in the last century.”

Reference: “One-Positron Quantum Cyclotron” by T. G. Myers, L. Soucy, B. A. D. Sukra, B. Sinha and G. Gabrielse, August 20, 2026, arXiv. DOI: 10.1103/gbkc-6nlj

This study was funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation.

#6372. Astrophysicists Want to Forecast When a Black Hole Launches Its Jets

Black holes are not just objects. Some astrophysicists prefer to call them locations. From this vantage point, they're locations where the Universe's laws of physics are pushed to their extreme limits.

Black holes are gravitational gluttons that draw everything in their vicinity towards them. When another star strays too close, the black hole can strip its gas away. The gas doesn't necessarily disappear over the event horizon and leave our observable Universe. It first gathers in a rapidly rotating accretion disk, where its temperature is raised to extreme levels. Some of this superheated material is ejected in a pair of collimated jets from the black hole's axis of rotation.

These jets are streams of plasma and particles that can reach relativistic speeds. They can have an enormous reach; the largest ones come from supermassive black holes and can extend for millions of parsecs into space. Though astrophysicists have witnessed many of these jets, their exact causes remain uncertain. The extreme gravity, magnetic fields, and temperatures around black holes is all a part of it.

Astrophysical jets shape their surroundings by heating star forming gas and moving it around on a massive scale. Stars form from cool gas, and the energy from jets works directly against that. The jets can also inflate bubbles where gas is too diffuse to collapse and form stars.

This JWST NIRCam image shows the jets coming from Messier 87, one of the most massive galaxies in the local Universe. These jets aren't from an x-ray binary, they're from its central SMBH that has billions of solar masses. It's an example of extreme astrophysical jets and an indicator of the extreme physics at black holes. Image Credit: Jan RÃ¶der, Maciek Wielgus et al., Astronomy & Astrophysics (2025)

Astrophysicists want to be able to predict when these jets are triggered so they can quickly gather follow-up observations, and new research in The Astrophysical Journal has made some progress. It's titled "Jet Forecast: Timing of Discrete Jet Ejections of Stellar-mass Black Holes Anticipated via X-Ray Properties," and the authors are Toshihiro Kawaguchi and Kazutaka Yamaoka. Kawaguchi is from the Graduate School of Science and Engineering at the University of Toyama, and Yamaoka is from the Institute for Space-Earth Environmental Research (ISEE) at Nagoya University.

The pair of researchers have been working on this problem for a while. In a 2025 study, they examined an x-ray binary consisting of a black hole and a donor star and found a link between the parameters of the inner accretion disk and jet activity. That research suggested that as the accretion disk's inner edge shrank towards its innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO), the black hole launched its jets. "This fact suggests that the jet materials originate from accreting matter from the innermost part of the disk," the authors wrote.

That was progress, but in that paper the researchers pointed out that more observations were needed. "Both X-ray spectral and timing observations are very important to understand the accretion disk states which can change very rapidly. Dense, simultaneous coverage with radio observations are also crucial to understand diskâjet interactions," the authors wrote in the conclusion to their 2025 paper.

This illustration is representative of XTE J1859+226, the system the authors studied in their 2025 paper. It shows a black hole not only drawing material away from the donor star, but also stretching the star into a distorted shape. Image Credit: J. M. Corral-Santana/Corral-Santana et al. 2011 MNRAS

Their 2025 paper was based on observations of a single black hole x-ray binary gathered during an outburst in 1999â2000. This work is based on observations of four black hole binary systems: one from the 2025 paper and three new ones.

There seem to be changes in an x-ray binary's (XRB) x-ray emissions prior to jets being launched. The spectrum is altered, and variability decreases. Astrophysicists have interpreted these changes as a signal that jets are about to be emitted. But the signals haven't been clear and reliable enough, so astrophysicists haven't been able to use them to time their follow-up observations. The researchers' previous work showed that as an accretion disk's inner edge shrank down to its ISCO, jets were launched. This could be the reliable signal astrophysicists are searching for.

This work expands their observations to more XRBs to see if this holds true. The researchers hope to develop a forecasting model for XRB jet launching so that more complete observations can be obtained.

The results show that the rapidly decreasing radius of the inner disk, called Rin, combined with a decrease in x-ray emission variability (indicated by rms), are a reliable predictor of jet launching. "All the four sources turned out to show the precursors of jet ejections (drops in Rin and rms) 1â10 days before radio activities," the authors write.

This artistâs depiction of a jet ejection shows how the jet from the black hole turns on when the inner radius of the accretion disk shrinks down to the ISCO fast enough. Image Credit: Professor Toshihiro Kawaguchi from University of Toyama, Japan and Dr. Kazutaka Yamaoka from Nagoya University, Japan.

They also found that there are no reliably detected increases in the amount of mass accreted prior to the launching of jets. "They show no huge jumps in M prior to each jet ejection," the researchers explain.

In at least one of the XRBs, that rate actually decayed in the 30 days leading up to jet launching. "We examined the time evolution of the accretion rate M of XTE J1859. It turned out to be exponentially decaying during the outburst (with an e-folding timescale of â¼30 days), and shows no huge jumps around the jet ejections," they write.

But XTE J1859 did show a tantalizing hint of enhancement. "There is a hint of â¼20% enhancement in M just before the jet productions," the authors write.

But that's just a hint, and better observations are needed to support it. "Such fine structures in the time evolution of M will be examined by the better data via the âjet forecastâ in the future," the researchers write.

Another notable finding concerns the Eddington limit. It's a theoretical threshold balanced between the inward force of gravity and the outward force of radiation. In two of the four systems, jets formed below this threshold. Some models of jet ejection say that super-Eddington accretion beyond this limit is necessary to launch jets, but these results say otherwise.

âMonitoring of Rin seems to be suitable for predicting the timing of jet ejections,â said Prof. Kawaguchi. âThe development of a âjet forecastâ would enable us to concentrate observing facilities on the expected timing of jet ejections, thereby accelerating our understanding of jet physics.â

Their jet forecasting model would be based on shrinking Rin and X-ray variability, and when both are detected, alerts would be sent out to other telescopes for more complete observations. Those observation would hopefully reveal some more of the extreme physics that dominate and define black holes.

"When both Rin and rms continuously decrease and when Rin is about to reach the ISCO, alerts can be circulated as a âjet forecastâ for triggering ToO (Target of Opportunity) observations," the authors write.

This is more than just purely academic. Earth has been subjected to bombardment by high-energy particles throughout its history. The Earth's protective magnetic shield deflects most of them, but some get through and trigger showers of secondary particles. Convincing evidence is thin, but some researchers still consider them a factor in the course of life on Earth.

âJet ejections in the Universe produce high-energy photons and particles, such as neutrinos, and such cosmic rays have long influenced the evolution of living creatures on Earth, including human beings,â concluded Prof. Kawaguchi.

The new Peerium architecture aims to power hyper-efficient computers capable of training AI models with up to 40 trillion parameters.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Engineers in China have built a new computer architecture they say can one day make up to a million artificial intelligence (AI) chips work as one. For comparison, Elon Musk's AI company, SpaceXAI (soon to be SpaceXSI), describes its Colossus cluster as the world's most powerful AI training system, comprising 200,000 interconnected chips.

Traditionally, the AI chips used to train foundation models are housed in separate servers and communicate over a network to share data and divide workloads. But the new architecture, Peerium, uses a high-speed interconnect system designed to maintain efficient communication between chips across multiple racks, even as the number of chips scales into the hundreds of thousands.

Huawei unveiled the new architecture Sept. 17 at the company's annual CONNECT conference.

Representatives from Huawei said in a statement that computers powered by Peerium could train models with up to 40 trillion parameters. For comparison, competing hardware, like GB200 NVL72 from NVIDIA and CS-3 from Cerebras, have reported training at the trillion-parameter scale, rather than the tens-of-trillions.

"Over the next two years, there will be roughly 6 or 7 frontier AI labs in China, and all will aim at training foundation language models of sizes ranging from 10 to 40 trillion parameters," Liao Heng, chief scientist for Huawei's chip design arm HiSilicon, told the Associated Press. "So you need such a scale of infrastructure to train these models."

Peerium's performance relies on three elements: nested parallelism, unified memory addressing, and peer-to-peer interconnects, Huawei representatives said in the statement.

Nested parallelism allows workloads to be broken into smaller tasks and organized across hierarchical groups of chips that work in parallel. It's similar to how a company breaks down work into departments and then smaller teams, all of which coordinate their efforts toward a common goal. Unified memory addressing allows processors to access memory across other servers, as opposed to only that attached to the processor's own server. Peer-to-peer interconnects allow components to communicate more directly with one another, rather than relying on an intermediary.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

All three principles are designed to make more efficient use of computing resources so that a single system can coordinate larger numbers of chips to handle demanding AI workloads.

According to Huawei, existing interconnect technologies — which link processors and servers to enable them to communicate — cannot support the Peerium architecture at the scale it envisages. For instance, NVIDIA uses NVLink for communication within racks and InfiniBand for communication between racks. The inter-rack communication bandwidth in this setup is 200GB per second, Eric Xu, Huawei's rotating chairman, told the AP.

"With such a low inter-rack communications bandwidth, there is no way you can make one million processors work as one computer," he said.

Huawei instead developed its own interconnect technology, UnifiedBus, which the company says delivers inter-rack communications bandwidth of up to 800GB per second.

"When one million processors work as one computer, this lays the foundation for better and more efficient AI training and inference," Xu added. "Therefore, I see UnifiedBus as the path for the future AI era. I believe, in the years to come, other players would certainly follow suit."

Alongside Peerium, Huawei also announced the Atlas 950 SuperPoD, a computing system built on Peerium and powered by more than 8,000 Huawei Ascend 950DT AI accelerator chips.

Xu said testing for AI training is underway on these SuperPoDs and that results show that they use their available computing power for AI training more efficiently than AI computing clusters that aren’t based on Peerium and UnifiedBus.

Huawei expects to begin supplying the SuperPoDs by early next year, at the latest, before its SuperClusters, which link multiple SuperPoDs to form a larger AI computing system, based on Peerium, eventually come online. Representatives said that one SuperCluster with 256,000 computing cards — hardware modules that add processing capacity — is currently being deployed and tested.

Models with large numbers of parameters demand greater computing resources and infrastructure, which isn't always desirable as it increases costs. In the summer, researchers used an IBM quantum computer to reduce the perplexity of Meta's Llama 3.1 8B language model — a measure of how well it predicts the next word or token — while keeping the number of parameters almost unchanged.

Fiona Jackson is a freelance writer and editor primarily covering science and technology. She has worked as a reporter on the science desk at MailOnline, and also covered enterprise tech news for TechRepublic, eWEEK, and TechHQ.

Fiona cut her teeth writing human interest stories for global news outlets at the press agency SWNS. She has a Master's degree in Chemistry, an NCTJ Diploma and a cocker spaniel named Sully, who she lives with in Bristol, UK.

#6370. Solving the Space Junk Crisis Isn't Just About Counting Trash—It’s About Control and Economics

If people ever think about cleaning up space debris, they typically think of something equivalent to a giant garbage truck in the sky, collecting lost astronaut tools and dead satellites then hauling them back down to Earth to be deposited in a landfill. But dealing with space debris doesnât work that way, and a new paper, available in pre-print on arXiv from Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASAâs Jet Propulsion Laboratory, who we typically cover for his work on the Solar Gravitational Lens idea, makes a good argument as to why.

Dr. Turyshev has turned his attention to orbital debris at a critical juncture. According to the filings made to the FCC, SpaceX, the company that runs the largest satellite megaconstellation, had their Starlink satellites perform 144,404 collision avoidance maneuvers in the six months from December 2024 through May 2025. Even accounting for the fact that there are more Starlink satellites in orbit now than ever, that means, on average, each one is having to dodge a potential crash every week.

Fortunately, Starlinks themselves arenât exactly in the âdanger zoneâ of orbit. They typically orbit around 500-600 kilometers, along with other megaconstellations such as Amazonâs Kuiper and Chinaâs Qianfan. In the paper, Dr. Turyshev separates this orbit from those higher up. At 500-600, there is enough atmosphere left that the area is semi self-cleaning - dead satellites and debris in these orbits will burn up in a few years.

Fraser talks about the oribtal dance that keeps satellites from crashing into one another.

Higher up, though, there are bigger problems, both literally and figuratively. At around 850 kilometers, giant rocket stages from launches past lurk with no control, and little to no atmosphere to drag them down in a reasonable time frame. They could stay in orbit for decades or centuries and donât have any means of avoiding one another. When they inevitably collide, they will spray debris both into their own orbit but also into higher and lower ones, potentially causing even greater problems for the lower orbiting communications megaconstellations.

According to European Space Agency Data cited in the paper, about 96 percent of the long-term collision risk comes from these dead objects. And Dr. Turyshev further proves that, even if we stop launching rockets tomorrow, the amount of debris already up there would collide and shatter faster than nature can clear it.

This isnât a surprise to anyone who has been paying attention to the problem of space debris for any length of time. That orbital cascade, commonly known as Kessler Syndrome, has been a long-standing problem orbital dynamicists have been grappling with for decades. According to Dr. Turyshev, controlling it comes down to three separate levers.

Fraser talks about some techniques to remove space debris from orbit.

First, regulators have to ensure that satellites are designed to intentionally deorbit quickly once their missions end. Luckily, they are already moving in that direction, with the FCC recently introducing a rule requiring satellites to clear out within five years of retirement, rather than the twenty-five years that had held sway for the last few decades. According to the paper, if the reliability of disposal rises from 90 to 99 percent and a satelliteâs allowable afterlife is cut to five years, it decreases the environmental hazard by a factor of 50.

A second lever is better vision. Space Situational Awareness (SSA) systems are great at tracking large bulky objects, but terrible at smaller objects the size of a bullet. But even for larger ones, thereâs still a level of âfuzzinessâ that analysts have to deal with, which means they know a general box where an object is in space, but not its exact position. When that box is large, satellite operators waste precious fuel dodging objects that never really posed a threat in the first place.

Rather than trying to track every bolt and nut floating through space, Dr. Turyshev suggests that we need to concentrate on shrinking the uncertainty zone around potential high-risk close calls. That idea aligns directly with the real-world infrastructure upgrades that are happening through NOAAâs Traffic Coordination System for Space (TraCSS), which is expanding its pilot program to reach more commercial operators this year.

Fraser discusses whether there's a limit to how many satellites we can potentially launch.

The third lever is what to do with the semi-permanent debris thatâs already in space. Instead of launching expensive missions to deorbit and grab every single one of them, Dr. Turyshev suggests an alternative he calls Just-in-Time Collision avoidance. If two dead rocket upper stages are about to crash, operators could use ground-based lasers or small swarms of shepherd satellites to move a few meters out of the way just before impact. While not quite as much of a long-term solution (since it simply avoids the immediate problem), it does offer a much less expensive solution than attempting to deorbit everything.

Economic calculations will play a major role in any future space debris solution, and right now the market is broken, as Dr. Turyshev points out. Due to agreements in the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, a private cleanup company cannot simply fly up to an abandoned Soviet rocket booster and deorbit it. Technically that rocket booster is still owned by the government that launched it (even if, in this case, that government doesnât technically exist anymore). Also, orbital space suffers from the âtragedy of the commonsâ, as one firm removing a rocket booster benefits all of the other companies with equipment in orbit, despite the cost not being spread amongst them.

Dr. Turyshevâs solution is to create contracts that would pay for verifiable reductions in long-term risk - in other words, it would incentivize companies like Astroscale, which are intending to remove space debris, to remove the most dangerous pieces first. This would be financed by governments, using money from âdisposal bondsâ that pay back if the satellite successfully orbits without active intervention from Astroscale or one of its competitors.

Ultimately, this seems like a reasonable framework to build a long-term plan for space debris mitigation. But there are still some issues - like sheer scale. Even at a 99% successful deorbit rate, with potentially millions of satellites in orbit that would still leave tens of thousands of derelict ones at any given time. And thereâs definitely no clear path forward to a successor to the Outer Space Treaty. But the longer we as a space-faring civilization ignore these issues the worse the problem is going to get. Hopefully this paper helps provide part of the impetus to push towards a formal adopted solution framework. Or at the very least start a more comprehensive conversation about it.

S.G. Turyshev - Orbital Debris in Earth Orbit: Operations, Stability, Control, and Market Formation

UT - What Will It Take To Reach Zero Space Debris?

UT - A New Net-Membrane Could Clean Up Some Tricky Space Debris

#6369. The Best New Restaurants in America in 2026

The year’s top restaurant debuts give us infinite reasons to dine out right now

These are the 15 new restaurants that best captured the year in dining. Our team of editors and scouts traveled across the country, drawing on years of experience to build the 2026 winners list.

What we found remarkable: the quiet confidence of a chef who’s mastered Hungarian food in Pittsburgh; a fresh revamp of family-style Italian dining in Philadelphia grounded in the original restaurant’s 1950s roots; a cozy tribute to Southern cuisine in Denver that still manages to feel cool. What they have in common: a sincere commitment to making diners feel at home. — Missy Frederick, editorial director

Learn more about this year’s Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, and how editors selected them, here.

“You went to Kansas City for sushi?” I was asked more than once — with some derision — after returning from Missouri, so I can only imagine the uphill battle chef Peter Hoang faces at Akoya Omakase. Hoang isn’t easily daunted. He’s so committed to sourcing, he often personally drives to the airport to pick up the fish hand-selected by his two private buyers in Tokyo 26 hours after placing his order.

At Akoya, the fish quality is unassailable; the rice seasoned with precision. But Hoang consistently finds ways to complement Akoya’s sashimi and nigiri with unexpected accents. Smoky juvenile king mackerel gets a hit of acid and sweetness from pineapple chutney. Truffle, notorious for being overwhelming on just about anything, manifests in pate form alongside dashi and kelp salt to highlight delicate hirame. The miso-butter-accented crab nigiri (a steal at $6) calls to mind decadently dipping crab legs in drawn butter. While affordable for omakase, $165 is still a commitment: Akoya diners have the option to test the waters with a la carte offerings and lunch specials in a warm and unpretentious restaurant. Befitting the Midwestern stereotype, the personable chefs, who chat freely with those seated across the bar, are eager to answer questions. Even tables in the dining room chime in.

Hoang, who worked in his father’s mid-2000s sushi restaurant before heading to bigger markets like New York and Chicago, is excited to be part of his hometown’s emerging Japanese dining scene — one that’s increasingly drawing national attention thanks to ambitious restaurants like Anjin izakaya and promising newcomers like day-to-night Tian Tea House/Moon Bar. Kansas City just might develop a reputation for cuisine beyond barbecue. — MF

Assuming new ownership of beloved, old restaurants can be a risk, but South Philly local Joey Baldino has the formula down: Keep the trappings, dial in the food. After taking over his family’s private Palizzi Social Club and retaining its members-only allure, Baldino bought Bomb Bomb Bar, which first opened in 1951, and reopened it last year. The bar’s lore precedes it: A rival business bombed it twice, immortalized by the large neon sign of two cartoonish bombs. Some reboots feel ironic, but not this one; the payphone by the door, the swordfish on the wall, and even the endearingly gruff servers feel like they’ve been there forever. It’s proof that classic Philly and modern culinary destination Philly can coexist.

In the front room, locals analyze Eagles games, and you might hear children playing in the street. In the back dining room, the procession of seafood here, priced at $65 per person, feels like a steal in this era of rising prices. The meat for the lobster Française has been removed from its shell, battered and fried, placed onto a buttery sauce, and then crowned with its shell once more. The crispy calamari gets enlivened with twangy cherry peppers. But it’s the overall dining experience that’s unbeatable: The restaurant hasn’t reinvented the wheel, but as the Beach Boys play and you sip a pepperoncini martini while watching your server pour hot fudge onto a sundae, you remember (perhaps while still wearing a bib) that complete novelty isn’t always necessary. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

Cassis is big in every sense. The nearly 200-seat dining room of the Milwaukee restaurant is an immaculately designed jewel box of gleaming tile, cozy banquettes, and antique mirrors, and even on a Wednesday night, it’s packed and roaring, with a towering, glowing bar at the center of the action. The latest project from Kyle and Meghan Knall, the couple behind nearby acclaimed bistro Birch, channels the conviviality and polish of a classic, old-world French brasserie while remaining distinctly Midwestern in spirit. It’s an all-day restaurant with both heart and panache.

Kyle Knall’s cooking roots itself in French tradition without feeling stodgy or like Parisian cosplay. Instead, it takes cues from his farm-to-table approach at Birch: Classical technique provides a framework for showing off Wisconsin ingredients with playfulness, vividness, and attention to detail. Oeuf mayo gets a jolt from intensely herbaceous, bright green aioli; ravioli Dauphiné pairs almost sugary-sweet summer corn with buttery Wisconsin-made Pleasant Ridge Reserve cheese; and an understated, frill-free but deeply umami foie gras eclair transforms one of French cuisine’s richest ingredients into an almost weightless bite.

At a moment when ambitious dining often means intimate tasting-menu counters and an air of exclusivity, Cassis makes a case that dinner can still feel like a real night out on the town. The cooking has an eagerness to please that succeeds. Within its walls, you’re offered an increasingly rare pleasure: a space where you’re invited to settle in, linger, order another bottle of wine, and maybe even have a friendly chat with the table next to you. Cassis could exist — and surely thrive — in New York or Las Vegas, but it’s more exciting in Milwaukee, where its scale and ambition feel like a vote of confidence in the city itself. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor, Eater

In 2026, the Midwest has proven a formidable destination for dining, with restaurants from Cleveland to Milwaukee leaning into what makes the region’s food special. Creepies in Chicago embodies this movement: A nonsensical (if memorable) name belies a thoughtful restaurant destination from chefs David and Anna Posey. The refreshing space feels contemporary, but with cottage-esque touches — geometric patterns dot the furniture, cartoonish artwork shares space with kitchenware tchotchkes, and mini curtains hang from open shelving.

Chef de cuisine Tayler Ploshehanski embeds French technique into dishes fiercely grounded in Chicago’s identity. Steamed mussels get kissed with classic Pernod and a fennel giardiniera that honors the city’s iconic Italian beef sandwiches. An Alsatian-leaning tarte flambe comes “tavern-style,” a nod to the square-cut pizza beloved by locals. Not every dish invokes the Great Lakes; the generous portion of gougeres may be Midwest-appropriate, but here the French classic takes a decadent turn as warm Brie seeps from the center of each choux pastry. A textbook roast chicken’s umami-laden sauce gains extra depth from liver; drag one of the restaurant’s hefty, yet impossibly crispy fries through its drippings for the best bite of the night. Save room for Anna Posey’s desserts: The savory soft-serve trend manifests as a baguette-infused concoction topped with chocolate and buttery breadcrumbs. In a year when a diner can grow weary that Everything’s a Bistro these days, Creepies proves some still offer delights and surprises. — MF

I’ve always felt a connection to Cuban cuisine, having visited the island country in my youth and eaten many pan con lechons from LA’s Porto’s Bakery in iconic Glendale. But a July meal at Emelina, which snagged a Michelin star months after opening for its ambitious, $275 Cuban tasting menu, showed me the country’s cooking in an entirely new context.

I wasn’t the only one to find it a revelation. Several older Cubans fortunate enough to nab a reservation got emotional toward the end of the meal, moved to tears as they told me they’d never had Cuban food like this before.

Located in tony West Palm Beach, this striking restaurant from chefs Osmel González and Camila Salazar draws inspiration from the former’s family history and upbringing in Cuba. After working together at world-class restaurants like Disfrutar in Spain and SingleThread in California, they partnered with Alvaro Perez-Miranda to achieve their vision. Employing lush ingredients sourced from South Florida farms in Redland and Lake Worth, the meal starts with a tender knob of fried flounder topped with caviar — a winking nod to traditional pan con minuta, a fried fish sandwich slathered with tartar sauce. A mid-course of pristine tropical fruits including mamey, lychee, and mango, arranged over creamy ricotta and dotted with Benton’s country ham, conjures a bounty one might linger over on a Cuban beach. Rabo encendido, or braised oxtail with Koshihikari rice, takes the homestyle guisado to new heights.

Cuba has a long history of home restaurants called paladares, serving personalized versions of staple dishes like arroz con pollo. Emelina represents that same opportunity to delight and enlighten, casting attention on a cuisine and culture that could have been. In balmy West Palm Beach, it thrives. — Matthew Kang, correspondent

The winding walkway into Maroon is a portal into a new dimension, a leap from the beeps and bloops of the casino floor at the Sahara Las Vegas into a thrumming dining room, dimly lit and streaked with red-orange accents. Chef Kwame Onwuachi, who most recently earned acclaim at Tatiana in New York City and Dōgon in Washington, D.C., has become a beacon of African diasporic dishes in the middle of the Mojave Desert.

Onwuachi is building something approachable yet grounded in technique. The name Maroon comes from 17th- and 18th-century enslaved people who escaped and established mountain communities in Jamaica; the kitchen centers African and Caribbean flavors rooted in their foodways. Consider the artful array of bluefin tuna belly chunks, hamachi, and braised octopus, swimming in a tangy broth pool and best enjoyed spooned onto fried saltine crackers, that gets an intense but brief spice hit from Scotch bonnet peppers. Luxurious, palm-sized oxtail patties and jerk mushroom earn a dash of caviar and grated truffle, a maximalist garnish on the typically humble dish. Grilled butterflied shrimp brushed with achiote sofrito recall pescado zarandeado, while sweet white grape chow chow brings a puckery kick. The blackened jerk chicken, its juiciness sealed in with a crust of aromatic spices, might be the finest in the U.S.; oxtail fried rice could moonlight as Caribbean bibimbap, with saucy deboned beef and fork-tender stewed chicken on an assemblage of julienned peppers and peas. Yes, there is steak, but go for the seared, bone-in pork chop instead for its sweet glaze.

Maroon engages you with sensory brilliance and familiar yet indelible flavors, like a catchy song that gets better with each listen. In a different city, it might feel overwrought, but here in Las Vegas, it matches the city’s frenetic energy and lands like a satisfying opus. — MK

Maydan Market opened in 2025 as a collaborative restaurant space and marketplace home to a few different Los Angeles-born businesses; in essence, it functions as one super-incubator for some of the best food you can find in the city. Diners bounce around to try a pozole flight and pescadillas (sofrito-fried fish nested in supple blue corn tortillas) at Maléna, from the family behind the beloved Tamales Elena; a crisp, UFO-sized, asiento-painted tlayuda from Lugya’h, from Los Angeles legend Poncho’s Tlayudas; and chile-sauce-slicked gai tod from Golden Mountain Chicken (formerly Yhing Yhang), from the intrepid team behind Thai restaurant Holy Basil. They will certainly stop to perch at the rotating Club 104 stall, which has hosted Black-owned businesses such as Melnificent Wingz and Caribbean diasporic pop-up Rubie, as well as Palestinian home restaurant Mid East Eats. On their way out, they may circle the storefront simply named Sook to eye wines, spices, and woven goods sourced from the Levant.

This is not to mention the market’s anchor restaurants: the Lebanese-influenced Maydan and Compass Rose, respectable D.C. transplants from prolific restaurateur Rose Previte, who, alongside her team, curated the market with the knockout lineup of Indigenous vendors. Maydan Market feels boldly like one whole; people rarely come for a single hyped stall. The point, in effect, is the crawl. In a year marked by ongoing, unrelenting, nationwide ICE raids targeting Black and brown immigrants, the fact that the market centers Indigenous Mexican-owned businesses, allowing their owners the space and sovereignty to reach a wider stage and audience, speaks loudly. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager

Take the former location of Portland’s — if not North America’s — most famous Northern Thai restaurant, combine it with the city’s most prolific and highly decorated Thai chef and restaurateur in Akkapong “Earl” Ninsom, and pepper in an elite local bar manager — co-owner Eric Nelson. Mix it all together, and you get OK Chicken & Khao Soi. Those familiar with its predecessor, Pok Pok, will find the space uncannily similar: a covered patio and downstairs service at a small bar, upstairs seating at oilcloth-wrapped tables. Now customers order on paper tabs. It’s casual and intimate, with just the right level of noise to feel like you stumbled into a really good dinner party.

OK Chicken’s menu leans into the flavors of Chiang Mai, starting with crispy chicken wings and two styles of khao soi — one with chicken and another richly prepared with beef. Plates of smoky nam prik makheua (eggplant dip) come with crisp and waxy long beans, green cabbage leaves, and cucumber. A memorable dish of yum moo yang — tender grilled pork shoulder tossed with snappish chunks of celery stalk and leaves as well as sliced onion — relaxes in a funky fish sauce with Thai chiles that sneakily build in your system until your lips hum. An herbal tea slushie refreshes even when mixed with a shot of infused Scotch. Close the meal with longan sticky rice speckled with perilla seeds, showered with crispy coconut and bathed in salted coconut milk that balances the sweetness of the pale lychee fruit and tangy mango ice cream on top. Each bite or sip at OK Chicken is surprising and pleasurable in equal measure. — Brenna Houck, dining editorial manager

In kitchens across the country, chefs have been happily marrying Japanese and Mexican foodways: Both cuisines have a reverence for local grains, honor highly specific seafood preparations, and play on savory, acidic flavors. Ramen Del Barrio blossomed from this shared cultural language — a Japanese Mexican izakaya centering ramen.

Chef and owner Chris Krinsky deftly laces together these threads for dishes such as creamy carnitas tonkotsu with two types of pork, confit buche and belly, as well as a chewy tangle of fresh noodles — made in partnership with Austin chef Gary Wu — using flour from a local mill. A honeycomb tripe and hominy-studded pozole tonkotsu comes rojo- or verde-style, while the mole tsukemen gets paired with thick whole wheat noodles and carnitas for dipping into rich, hearty mole. Tuna tostada, served on top of a sheet of origami paper, packs a zesty punch thanks to a dried shrimp and morita chile aioli, chicharrones furikake, eel sauce, and salsa macha. The yaki-tacos — hefty yakitori skewers served on top of corn tortillas — use smoky pulpo and vegetarian-friendly mushrooms accented with pepitas.

This isn’t fusion for fusion’s sake. Krinsky was born in Maine, grew up in Mexico, and worked at Japanese restaurants throughout most of his career. He started his ramen journey cooking out of his garage and then opened a food court stand, for which he won an Eater Award in 2023. Somehow, his menu tastes better now that he has his own dedicated space where he hand-layered wood panels along the wall and lined the ceiling with sushi mats. A small television in the dining room blasts Spanish-dubbed anime. Ramen Del Barrio 2.0 feels wholly like a loving expression of his culinary fascinations and his commitment to honoring both traditions. — Nadia Chaudhury, deputy editor, Eater New York

In an unmarked space in San Francisco’s Nob Hill, chef Patrick Gabon and partner Celine Wuu quietly rewrote the playbook on fine dining with Restaurant Naides. Filipino food has not historically held a footing in the Bay Area’s higher-end echelons, but Naides’s dishes make a powerful claim that the cuisine deserves its place there. Gabon deploys the sour, salty, and sweet flavors of the Philippines with subtle tenacity: The saline funk of bagoong, or fermented salted shrimp, takes on new dimension in Gabon’s hands, where the condiment gets mellowed into a creamy sauce that acts as foil to tender slices of chayote, crisp duck cracklings, and the burst of caviar. His approach to the mouth-puckering sourness of sinigang invigorates the Philippines’ national dish by pouring dry-aged beef broth over meticulously sliced abalone and scallions. These plates manage to retain the soul of the food but in new forms; they don’t placate the audience, asking them instead to reconsider their fundamental notions of fine dining and how Filipino food presented in this way may upend them.

Wuu’s beverage program has become a force of its own. It’s not often that a nonalcoholic pairing manages to outshine a traditional wine program, but Wuu keenly matches the bold flavors of each dish. A drink mixing the flavors of green mango with rooibos and habañero cordial complements the salty punch of bagoong at one turn, while coconut water, osmanthus, and rose vinegar offer a gentle start with the opening snacks, composed of Gabon’s takes on lumpia, okoy, and puto. “As you age and you grow, you tend to go deeper in your roots: ‘How can I make something so traditional the best it can be?’” Wuu told me earlier this year. Naides has answered that question with every meal since. — Dianne de Guzman, editor, Eater SF

It’s tricky to pin down what exactly Rougarou is. It’s a restaurant, certainly, serving modern Southern food in the historic Five Points neighborhood in Denver. It also has a ripping bar program, late-night hours, live music on the patio, and a casual roguish charm. Inside an understated brick building on a flyby street, the dining room is full of personality, dim and moody, all hard surfaces that bounce around the fun clatter of spirited groups throughout the dinner hour.

The menu conveys the right balance of accessibility and intrigue: The ubiquitous tomato stone fruit salad gets a curry-inflected jolt of vinaigrette and a crunch of coconut benne granola. Charred zucchini is doused in smoked cheddar sauce and scattered with bits of country ham. Fried catfish sits on a pond of fermented hot and sour sauce, with pickled chiles that lash the tongue at first and Sichuan peppercorns that leave you gently tingling. And the signature Chicken on a Stick is a lovingly updated homage to a legendary gas station restaurant in Oxford, Mississippi.

While the food feels approachable, the cocktails are high-concept and assertive, leaning on tropical ingredients but pushing for wilder edges, like green banana, oversteeped oolong, and Haitian clairin, pungent and unctuous with fusel oils. A second visit, late at night, revealed a laid-back restaurant-industry hangout at the bar instead of the celebratory din I found earlier. Much like its namesake monster, Rougarou can shape-shift to host a group dinner, a date night, a jam session, or a beguiling nightcap. It’s the kind of restaurant that invites returns, and a great fit for this moment in restaurant culture. — Ben Mesirow, travel editor

D.C. hospitality veterans Jon Sybert and Jill Tyler took a risk when they converted Adams Morgan’s Michelin-starred favorite Tail Up Goat into Rye Bunny, a restaurant that straddles the line between upscale and casual. Appetizers start at $15 and entree prices go up to $40, and instead of table service, diners line up to order at a counter. In the end, both the owners and D.C. diners have seen a payoff. Sybert’s dishes are inventive yet comforting, with Aleppo honey-covered fried chicken served alongside delicately stacked anchovy and quince jam toasts built on thin slices of milk bread. Everything is still seasonal and sourced from nearby farms, but those high-grade ingredients are easier to afford now that the restaurant has been able to cut down on the number of staff by 20 percent. While D.C. diners are not crazy about queuing, the nightly line out the door has sustained for more than six months and become an unexpected way to meet neighbors. A server brings over a drink menu as you wait, so you can catch up with friends and sip on a Slovenian orange wine before you sit down.

Rye Bunny encompasses the simple joy of a neighborhood restaurant that’s an equally excellent destination for a weekday date night or a special occasion, and it represents a larger shift in our dining landscape that might save these mid-price-range restaurants as margins get thinner. — Emily Venezky, social media manager

When So. Fox opened in Atlanta’s Virginia-Highland neighborhood in July, chef Myles Moody and sommelier Rachael Pack had an instant hit, bringing new energy to that pocket of the city. But a successful restaurant often belies monumental effort behind the scenes. So. Fox’s signature dish — a whole roasted chicken — is only available to five lucky tables per night and regularly sells out before the second seating. Much like a great restaurant takes time to build, the simple bird takes days for its mustard brine to infuse, and the result is stunning: a glistening interior and exquisitely crispy skin.

So. Fox commands an insatiable demand for a table topped with that prized poultry, herby rabbit dumplings, and Carolina Gold rice. Snagging a spot at the welcoming bar or at the curved, floating table near the entry, which helps capture overflow crowds, is equally competitive. The space that formerly housed a burger joint (and before that, an auto repair shop) has been transformed into a bright, perennially packed dining room with grand windows, offering an optimal view of North Highland Avenue.

Short for Southern Fox, an American indigenous grape varietal, So. Fox showcases Pack’s longtime knowledge of natural, low-intervention, biodynamic, and Old World producers, many of whom she knows personally. Pack and Atlanta-born Moody first met while working at New York’s Michelin-starred Aska, and returned south to open Kinship Butcher & Sundry in 2021, which resides next door. This isn’t just farm-to-table; it’s produce from their own Ormewood Park farm, highlighted in grilled beef with Vidalia onions and braised leeks, and at the end of summer, in sugar snap peas with chives and farmer cheese.

It’s seasonal Southern fare that feels current and relevant, with a refreshingly casual approach — and people can’t help but show up for it. — Mona Holmes, editor, Eater LA

Somssi, from Ahris Kim and chef Daniel Gronert, is one of the clearest examples in New York of a restaurant that goes all-in on personal history, rather than focusing on the broader food culture of any one country or a region.

Korea-born Kim, who ran operations at Atomix, lived in Indonesia and the Philippines before moving to Wisconsin with her family. Gronert, who has German roots and spent time as a pitmaster in South Carolina, cooked across restaurants in Atomix’s parent company. Those influences show up in dishes like the caviar-crowned Potato Potato Potato, a crispy-soft tater tot simulacrum nested on miso hollandaise; ox tongue grilled and glazed with tare, a kaleidoscope of textures; and pork schnitzel presented like shrimp toast (it works).

With the team’s fine dining pedigree, Somssi sets a high bar for hospitality, yet it’s still casual: The room is designed to feel like a home, and the menu nods to places Kim and Gronert have lived.

The bar extends that expertise. Christian Gray’s cocktails include well-made minis, which the bartenders are game to explain to curious drinkers. Sommelier (and Punch contributor) Jenny Eagleton’s list of wines and sakes leans toward lesser-known areas. The duo and their staff reward handing your night over to them, whether you’re there with a group or alone with a Kindle.

Personal touches carry through the space in gloriously analog fashion. Lace curtains on the door spell out the restaurant’s name in embroidery, and handprints line the bathroom wall, left by the broader constellation of people who helped build Somssi into the singular restaurant it is today. — NC

Sunday is a very good night to be at Titusz. That’s Schnitzel Sonntag — when the Pittsburgh restaurant, clad in warm wood and gem-toned ceramic tile, offers an irresistible special at an even more irresistible price: a 4-ounce veal cutlet, breaded and fried in lard, for $13. The golden brown slab comes with a single lemon cheek on the plate and nothing else. It takes confidence to serve a dish so simply: Chef and owner Csilla Thackray gained hers in some of the city’s top restaurant kitchens. She named Titusz after her great-grandfather, and his portrait hangs by the first-floor bar. Her own name comes from her Budapest-born grandmother, who raised the chef on her cooking.

Call it grandmacore if you want to peg Titusz to a national trend, but the menu is modern, Austrian, Hungarian, and distinctly Thackray’s. Here, meggyleves, the Magyar sour-cherry soup, gets an electrifying swirl of paprika oil. The chef has made charring an art: You will want to pick up the bowl and drink every drop of charred leek and sauerkraut broth beneath her buoyant kaspressknödel (cheese dumplings). The Maillard reaction pays off again in the savory brown butter drizzled over a dessert of aranygaluska (think walnut monkey bread), served warm on a puddle of peach creme anglaise. Thackray’s husband — Sean Rosenkrans, another veteran of Pittsburgh’s restaurant scene — has built a stunning list of wines from Central Europe, as well as cocktails fluent in that idiom — a slug of herbal Unicum here, a toasty hint of caraway there. Everything makes profound and reassuring sense together. The decision to spend money at a restaurant might feel fraught right now; the choices at Titusz never do. — Beth Kracklauer, dining editorial manager

#6368. A Universe Without Dark Matter? Radical New Model Challenges Modern Cosmology

An older universe could give unexpectedly mature early galaxies billions more years to grow, according to a model that also reproduces galaxy rotation without dark matter.

To explain how galaxies rotate, the standard model of the universe relies on dark matter, an unseen source of gravity. A new paper published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society reports that an alternative model can reproduce the rotation curves of all 175 galaxies in the SPARC database without dark matter. These curves show how orbital speeds change with distance from a galaxy’s center, giving researchers a way to test the gravity their model predicts.

The galaxy study is part of a series of tests conducted during 2025 and 2026 by Rajendra Gupta, an adjunct professor in the University of Ottawa’s Department of Physics, and postdoctoral researcher Dr. Nikolaos Samaras. They compared important astronomical observations with predictions from CCC+TL, a model that puts the universe’s age at 26.7 billion years and proposes that neither dark matter nor dark energy is needed.

The standard cosmological model is called ΛCDM, short for lambda cold dark matter. Lambda, written as the Greek letter Λ, represents the cosmological constant associated with dark energy, which accounts for the universe’s accelerating expansion. “Cold” means that the dark matter moves slowly compared with light. Scientists have searched for dark matter and dark energy for decades, but neither has been directly detected.

CCC+TL stands for “covarying coupling constants plus tired light.” It combines the idea that fundamental quantities governing forces and particle interactions evolve together over time with the proposal that light loses energy as it travels. Under this framework, changing fundamental constants could produce effects usually attributed to dark matter and dark energy.

Putting that proposal to the test required more than adjusting the settings in existing cosmology software. CCC+TL changes the Einstein and Friedmann equations, which describe gravity and the universe’s expansion. For each test, Gupta and Samaras developed equations and computer code consistent with their model.

Beyond individual galaxies, the researchers examined the Bullet Cluster. There, the extra gravitational effect predicted by CCC+TL tracks the galaxies rather than the hot, X-ray-emitting gas. The team describes this result as an early proof of concept that needs further study.

“Observations attributed to dark matter and dark energy likely originate from covarying coupling constants,” says Gupta, whose paper on the origin of dark matter and dark energy explores this idea.

An older universe would also change how astronomers interpret the large, mature galaxies they keep finding early in cosmic history. Those observations have raised questions for ΛCDM because galaxies need time to grow. How much time they had depends on the model used to interpret their redshift, a measure of how much their light has shifted toward longer, redder wavelengths.

For observations during cosmic dawn that correspond to a universe about 300 million years old under the standard model, CCC+TL gives an age of about 4.6 billion years at the same observed redshift. That leaves much more time for galaxies to develop. In calculations reported in Galaxies 13, 115, early galaxies come out about 12 times larger in size and mass than the standard model predicts.

“Impossible early galaxies become predictable galaxies,” Gupta explains. “We predict that galaxies exist well beyond the distances the James Webb Space Telescope has reached.”

The James Webb Space Telescope’s GLIMPSE program plans to search for galaxies at redshifts that may exceed 50, potentially providing a test of that prediction. At those redshifts, the standard model may leave too little time for massive galaxies to form. CCC+TL does not impose the same time constraint.

The researchers also tested whether their framework could account for evidence from much earlier in cosmic history. Its predictions for the amounts of hydrogen, helium, and other light elements formed shortly after the Big Bang matched those of the standard model. It also agreed with cosmic-chronometer measurements, which use galaxy ages to estimate how quickly the universe has expanded over time.

A separate study of time dilation in supernova observations also supports CCC+TL, although that paper remains under review. Time dilation here refers to the stretching of the observed timescale of a stellar explosion. The team’s work also extends to the cosmic microwave background, the radiation left over from the early universe.

“Most emerging models explain only a limited set of observations,” Gupta says. “A new model must not conflict with the pillars of cosmology and astrophysics, and our findings meet that challenge, including the yet-to-be-published Cosmic Microwave Background challenge.”

“The success should encourage astronomers to take the new model seriously. It is challenging to understand and apply, but we believe it extends the physics of the Universe beyond ΛCDM limits,” concludes Gupta.

Reference: “A Big Bang Nucleosynthesis Consistency Test of the CCC+TL Cosmology” by Rajendra P. Gupta and Nikolaos Samaras, 25 June 2026, Universe. DOI: 10.3390/universe12070193

and all of this has been debunked utterly

Since there are no papers that are published in peer review (or even a prominent physicist publishing with that name), there is no challenge – it is online spam.

Hitchens razor is the spam filter here: “What can be asserted without evidence can also be dismissed without evidence.”

Well, the CCC+TL model seems to be a very promising way to eliminate Dark Matter and Dark Energy from our universe. I will be looking for more developments from testing this models claims.

That will be an infinite looking time, since it fails out of the gate. All astronomical objects agree, independently of cosmology, that the matter universe is no more than 14 billion years old. And standard cosmology agrees perfectly with that!

We regularly see articles challenging the existence of dark matter/energy, which many scientists have built their careers on .

What we need is a cage match, where one persuasion or the other wins.

Science sites presenting peer review published material in a neutral way is not the problem.

The cage fight is in professional publications and conferences. Ah yes, since we are into “spam physics” territory thanks to some comments: I notices that besides the current SpaceX mission that I watch in another window consistently doing trackable gravitationally guided orbits rejecting “flat Earth” notions it does something else. The spacecraft is sufficiently long that you can estimate the fish lens camera distortions (and of course there are proper ground photos showing straight cylinder shape). So independently of Earth observations you can estimate that effect and deduct it from the rotating Earth horizon *by eye*, effortlessly rejecting some common ‘physics’ spam.

I dunno what “no dark matter” spammers makes of neutrino experiments, since morally neutrino’s mass is 0.2 % of dark matter, just not the dominant massive (cold) dark matter we observe with other means.

This is why modifications to general relativity – especially Gupta’s old hobby horse – fails: They predict one thing well (usually rotation curves) but fail to give the correct upper limit on age that we get from stars, or as here size of galaxies which is observed by other means than rotation curves.

Props if they also get a second right (primordial nucleosynthesis, where total baryon density figures in). But dark matter alone has *tens of independent* observation types agreeing on its existence (Wikipedia), and LCDM has no rival as of yet.

I was going to leave it there but then I thought that it would be obvious that they somehow tried to duck the age question so I needed to do due diligence on that. But when I looked for a reference I noted that the article text implies that they may have not and I can stand by my assessment until someone proves me wrong. But more importantly, the article describe their model as a “tired light” model, which was rejected over a century ago on the grounds that images then would be more fuzzy. (And with today’s technology it should be even worse.)

Wikipedia: “Tired light is a class of hypothetical redshift mechanisms that was proposed as an alternative explanation for the redshift-distance relationship. These models have been proposed as alternatives to the models that involve the expansion of the universe. The concept was first proposed in 1929 by Fritz Zwicky, who suggested that if photons lost energy over time through collisions with other particles in a regular way, the more distant objects would appear redder than more nearby ones.

Zwicky acknowledged that any sort of scattering of light would blur the images of distant objects more than what is seen. Additionally, the surface brightness of galaxies evolving with time, time dilation of cosmological sources, and a thermal spectrum of the cosmic microwave background have been observed—these effects should not be present if the cosmological redshift was due to any tired light scattering mechanism.[1][2][3] Despite periodic re-examination of the concept, tired light has not been supported by observational tests and remains a fringe topic in astrophysics.[4]”
