#6367. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

D. Ancalle et al. Earwax as pest control. Soft Matter. 2026. https://doi.org/10.1039/d6sm00737f

#6366. Asteroid Bennu's Sample Delivers Another Surprise

One of the most interesting discoveries in recent years is that some of the molecules necessary for life are found on asteroids and comets. Sample return missions from asteroids have shown that these rocky bodies are far more than just rock. They host some of the fundamental building blocksâamino acidsâthat are used to construct proteins.

These discoveries are a collective a-ha! moment. It's becoming clear that some of the precursors for life could be widespread in the Solar System. And if they're widespread in ours, they could be widespread in others. The idea that life could appear elsewhere in the galaxy got a boost.

NASA's OSIRIS-REx was a big part of this when it returned a sample from asteroid Bennu in 2023. Examination of those samples revealed the presence of 14 of the 20 amino acids that make up proteins in Earth life, along with four of the essential building blocks for DNA and RNA.

Now, researchers have compared one of those molecules with the same molecule from another source, the Murchison meteorite, to see how they differ. The research is published in Nature Communications Earth and Environment, and is titled "Nitrogen and intramolecular carbon isotopic measurements of Î²-alanine in samples from asteroid Bennu and the Murchison meteorite." The lead author is OphÃ©lie Mcintosh, a former postdoctoral researcher in Penn Stateâs Department of Geosciences.

âI was genuinely gobsmacked by the enormous isotope difference between two neighboring atom positions within the same molecule. - Katherine Freeman, Professor of Geosciences at Penn State.

"Amino acids are central to prebiotic chemistry, and their abundances and isotopic compositions provide critical constraints on the synthetic mechanisms and environments in which they formed," the authors write. "Samples delivered to Earth from the carbonaceous asteroid (101955) Bennu by NASAâs OSIRIS-REx mission offer an opportunity to investigate amino acids preserved in pristine material unaffected by terrestrial contamination."

Î²-alanine (beta-alanine) isn't used by Earth organisms to build proteins, but it does play other roles in terrestrial life. Finding it in extraterrestrial rocks is interesting because that can provide some insight into pre-biotic chemistry and what conditions were like in the very early Solar System.

This research is focused on the different compositions of Î²-alanine found in Bennu and the Murchison meteorite. Since the Bennu sample was collected and preserved in a sterile capsule before being opened in laboratory conditions, it's especially valuable scientifically.

This sample of the Murchison meteorite sits in the National Museum of Natural History, Washington, D.C. Image Credit: By User:Basilicofresco - Derivative work from Image:Murchison meteorite.jpg, CC BY-SA 3.0, https://commons.wikimedia.org/w/index.php?curid=4301968

âAmino acids are the building blocks of proteins and peptides, but they are also found in carbon-rich meteorites and asteroid samples, so they can provide a direct link between space chemistry and the origins of life on Earth,â lead author Mcintosh said in a press release. âMost studies focus on the distribution and quantification of amino acids, so our question about how theyâre formed is quite new. We used very unique isotope instruments, including one that exists only at Penn State, to help answer those questions.â

A mission to collect an asteroid sample and return it to Earth is an extremely complicated endeavour. Scientists were hopeful that in the time that passed between planning and launching the mission and getting their hands on the sample, new laboratory techniques would be developed to investigate the sample as deeply and thoroughly as possible. That's what has happened in this case. The researchers were able to measure and compare the different isotopic compositions of Î²-alanine in the Bennu sample and in the Murchison meteorite sample.

They not only compared bulk compositions. In this work, they were actually able to measure and compare isotopic carbon differences in carbon atoms in the same molecule. This level of detail is new.

A device unique to Penn State allowed the measurement of isotopic averages in extremely small samples. It's called pico-CSIA, for Picomolar-scale compound-specific isotope analyses. A second device, a modified GC-Orbitrap (Gas Chromatography-Orbitrap Mass Spectrometer) measured specific compositions at specific locations in Î²-alanine molecules.

âIsotope ratios provide a measurable tag that can link molecules to specific reservoirs or processes,â said paper co-author Christopher House, professor of geosciences at Penn State. âFor our study, isotopes provided clues to an older history for specific atoms in a molecule.â

Looking at isotopic composition is a way to look further back in time for the Î²-alanine's formation history. Typically, researchers are looking at processes inside the asteroid body itself for clues to how it formed.

But examining isotopic composition from molecule to molecule is more fundamental, and carbon plays a critical role. It acts as scaffolding for organic moleculesâEarth life is carbon-based after allâand records isotopic differences between molecules and within molecules. "Intramolecular isotopic measurements, which capture the position-specific carbon isotopic distribution within a molecule, offer a particularly powerful approach as they can reveal reaction mechanisms, constrain precursor reservoirs, and reflect environmental conditions.

âThis intramolecular information provides a much more detailed isotopic fingerprint,â lead author Mcintosh said. âInstead of simply asking whether a molecule is enriched or depleted in a particular isotope, we can investigate how that isotope is distributed within the molecule and use this pattern to distinguish between possible formation pathways.â

This work takes isotopic composition to a whole other level. Especially when used on such a carefully handled sample as that from Bennu.

âBeing able to analyze the isotope values for each carbon and nitrogen within the beta-alanine molecule is a dream for geochemistry,â House said. âAnd here it is coupled to the ability to study a pristine asteroid sample returned to Earth by NASA.â

The isotope values from atom to atom within the same molecule were wildly different, which came as a surprise to the researchers. They may have formed before Earth did.

There was a lot of waiting and anticipation leading up to Bennu's successful sample collection maneuver. Once it was complete, there was more anticipation of the sample's arrival on Earth, and what we'd learn from it. That's partly what makes this research so interesting. Credit: NASA Goddard

âI was genuinely gobsmacked by the enormous isotope difference between two neighboring atom positions within the same molecule,â said project principal investigator Katherine Freeman, Professor of Geosciences at Penn State. âThe preservation of such startling differences is an indicator of the primordial nature of these molecules. We are working with molecules formed at the very dawn of the solar system, possibly even before the formation of Earth.â

The intramolecular isotope differences show that, while their formation pathways were the same, they took place in much different environments, or in different batches. It shows that the same chemical can form in different environments in the protoplanetary disk, and that the disk is spatially heterogeneous.

âOne of the main things we discovered, for both glycine and beta-alanine, is that they might have formed in different environments or places in the solar system,â Mcintosh said. âThis broadens our understanding of the type of environments where you can form those very important molecules for prebiotic chemistry.â

The figure below shows elevated 13C in the Bennu sample, and it's particularly important. "The substantially greater 13C enrichment of the carboxyl carbon in Bennu is consistent with the incorporation of carbon from isotopically distinct precursor reservoirs, potentially reflecting differences in the local chemical environments in which Î²-alanine or its precursors formed," the authors write.

This summary figure shows the carbon isotopic compositions across Solar System bodies, including Bennu (blue diamonds) and Murchison (grey squares). The figure presents bulk carbon values in different planetary bodies. Carbon is important because life is carbon-based, and it's like the structural scaffolding for organic molecules. Within a single molecule, carbon records isotopic differences in a way that other atoms like nitrogen and hydrogen don't. Notice the he greater 13C in carboxyl carbon (COOH) in Bennu, which is particularly important. Image Credit: Mcintosh, O.M., Baczynski, A.A., Rasmussen, C. et al. Nitrogen and intramolecular carbon isotopic measurements of Î²-alanine in samples from asteroid Bennu and the Murchison meteorite. Commun Earth Environ (2026).

âWhen you compare the Bennu and Murchison samples, the carbon isotope average is so close that when you factor in margin of error, theyâre basically the same,â Mcintosh said. âBut when you look at intramolecular carbon, theyâre completely different.â

"The samples display similar intramolecular isotope distributions, consistent with a common synthetic route, but differ markedly in their position-specific carbon and nitrogen isotope compositions," the authors explain.

That means the source materials were distinct isotopically. So they must have came from different locations and environments in the young Solar System. The authors say that the differences are hard to reconcile with any known processes taking place inside parent bodies. Instead, they reflect different chemical pathways in different parts of the protoplanetary disk.

An illustration of a protoplanetary disk. This work shows that the same organic molecules can form in different parts of the disk, though with different isotopic compositions. This suggests that prebiotic chemistry can form in a wider variety of conditions. Image Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/T. Pyle (SSC) - February, 2005

âBeta-alanine is a prominent example of the amazingly diverse collection of amino acid-like molecules found in space samples,â Freeman said. âIt can help us understand why there are so many different types of these compounds and where and how they were made. Ultimately, this helps us understand ways that space organics potentially shaped the unique chemistry in life.â

These results could also be helpful as missions to detect and study potential biosignatures elsewhere in the Solar System are launched. Missions to Jupiter's icy moons could benefit from these results, for example.

"Additionally, isotopic analyses of amino acids and other prebiotic molecules in Bennu samples and other pristine astromaterials provide a critical abiotic baseline for the search and identification of chemical biosignatures within our Solar System.

#6365. The Best Food Gifts Under $100 (That Are Just the Right Amount of Extra)

These luxe but affordable gifts feel sumptuous and whimsical, from eggnog petit fours to a glass ham ornament

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

I take my holiday gift shopping very seriously — if not for my giftee, for my own serotonin-seeking purposes. There’s nothing quite as satisfying as finding the right N/A cocktail bundle for your aunt, or a cake stand that doubles as a chip and dip bowl (the in-laws will love that one) for the avid entertainer.

We’re all on different budgets; some are on the hunt for tasty bargains and piggy-bank-friendly stocking stuffers, while others have a more robust chunk of change set aside for providing big-impact presents You might have already bookmarked Eater’s gift guides that are under-$25, which is full of all kinds of chic home and kitchen goods, but now [turns up gas] we’re shopping at the under-$100 range, which gives us even more wiggle room to sweep your giftees off their feet via a ham-themed ornament, a robust at-home chai kit, or a set of steak knives from Peter Luger.

We’re in prime gift guide season, folks. Fasten your aprons, and let’s shop for every kind of food-loving person on your holiday list.

No cocktail has been living, laughing, and loving harder than the ultra-dirty martini lately. This briny bundle from Big Night brings together the shoppy shop’s sleek olive-themed hors d’oeuvres picks with a jar of Quincy’s big, juicy Castelvetrano olives, Quincy cocktail onions, and bag of Filthy’s cult-fave olive brine.

For my money, a solid indicator of a fun household is whether or not there’s a wild cheese or cutting board in the mix. This psychedelic slab from Fredericks and Mae is both a beautiful serving board and functional chopping block for all of your kitchen needs, because it’s made out of a durable and non-toxic HDPE material.

Fredericks and Mae Red/Blue Cutting Board

The organic Los Angeles lifestyle brand Flamingo Estate has created the pasta-lover’s dream present: a chic trio of pomodoro rosso sauce, angel trumpet pasta, and a bottle of Flamingo Estate’s heritage EVOO. As with the rest of the Estate’s bundles, this set comes housed in one of its signature, ornate green boxes.

Imagine the flex of sawing through a Porterhouse at home with Peter Luger logo-stamped blades, which are made with stainless steel and wood handles that will transport their giftee back to the hallowed halls of the world-famous Brooklyn steakhouse. If you have a bit more room left in your gift budget, I suggest pairing it with some New York strip steaks from Snake River Farms.

Diaspora Spice Co. is one of Eater’s favorite places to buy spices online, because it’s home to dozens of single-origin heirloom spices from (mostly) India and Sri Lanka. As founder Sana Javeri Kadri explains on its site, a core tenant of Diaspora Spice Co.’s operations is rooted in undoing colonialist inequity in the spice trade; in her words: “We’re proud to pay our farm partners an average of 6x above the commodity price. In a system where fair trade is a mere 15 percent premium, we pay what we believe to be a living wage.” The equitable spice brand has partnered with the North Carolina-based pottery and lifestyle brand East Fork on this at-home chai bundle, which features the former’s brand new masala chai blend, Madhur jaggery, a stainless steel strainer, and a panna cotta colorway kuhlad from the indie pottery company.

Eater’s deputy brand director Nat Belkov introduced me to Craighill, a company that reimagines everyday carry and home essentials (think, scissors and carabiners) with a little more design flair. The Brooklyn-based studio redesigned the common wine key, and Belkov tells me that it mitigates all the annoying little things that can go wrong while using a wine opener. “I love the perfect angle on the foil cutter,” he says, “[and] I love that they tapped the knowledge of sommelier André Hueston Mack to make sure it worked well enough to be trusted by members of the industry. Seldom do I run into a product where I genuinely have a hard time choosing between different color variations like here, with the sleek matte black, pop of orange, or classy tortoise finish. But most of all, I love that this thing is guaranteed to work for life.”

MoMA Design Store Bodum Neon Nesting Mixing Bowls (Set of 4)

As a person who drinks coffee every day (and feels horrified when I run out), I would be thrilled to receive this American Girl doll-sized bag (weighing 4 pounds) of beans from the award-winning Joshua Tree Coffee. This year, the Big Bag — which is filled with the beans of your choice — even comes with a cute enamel mug.

Joshua Tree Coffee Big Bag & Bellied Enamel Mug Bundle

The Chitose is kind of like the Ferrari of kettles, because it boils water extremely fast and is made out of professional-grade, scratch-resistant 18-8 stainless steel. Plus, it cuts a cute silhouette and is compatible with induction top stoves.

Japanese Taste Chitose Induction Compatible Japanese Stainless Steel Kettle

These pastel eggnog petit fours come from the acclaimed Los Angeles-based confectionary Valerie Confections, and are made of a rich spiced buttercake, with bourbon ganache layers dipped in white chocolate and garnished with 23-karat gold leaf and chocolate biscuit pearls.

Ghia’s apéritif box is one of those drink-themed holiday gifts that sells out every year, because it pairs the brand’s signature amaro-esque N/A ambrosia with chic glassware from French-American glass artist and designer Sophie Lou Jacobsen. Whether you’re shopping for someone who doesn’t drink or is just trying to drink less alcohol in the new year, it’s a fashionable foot forward in the world of booze-free drinks.

Owning a double burner griddle is the culinary equivalent to flexing a California king size bed, because it can handle all of the pancakes, eggs, and grilled cheese orders from the family (without having to hop between skillets like a stove DJ). We love this one from Lodge, known for its excellent cast iron cookware.

Lodge Blacklock Triple Seasoned Cast Iron Double Burner Griddle

It’s likely that your giftee already owns cocktail glasses, but there’s also a non-zero chance that they’ve had a few stunners from their collection broken by jolly, wobbly party guests. Eater collaborated with heritage crystal glassware company Zwiesel Fortessa on a collection of timeless pieces, including this versatile set of six Nick and Nora-style glasses.

Eater x Zwiesel Fortessa Folly Crystal Glass, 6 Ounce Cocktail (Set of 6)

Sometimes the best present is one that contains even more presents: a giant box of Swedish candies, all curated by the cult-fave confectioners at BonBon. Dubbed the Holiday Connoisseur Box, this light pink coffret is filled with classic BonBon gummies (I spy Pippi Longstocking’s Gold Coins) and plenty of Swedish classics like Marabou Japp chocolate bars and Juleskum marshmallow candies.

Kudos to Emma Chamberlain on this postmodern-feeling French press. The YouTuber went viral yet again for her collaboration with West Elm, and this coffee press in particularly takes notes from its elders (Bodum and Alessi) with its sleek stainless steel design.

Emma Chamberlain x West Elm Stainless Steel Button French Press

John Derian is the Final Boss of curating swish food-themed holiday ornaments (I do also need this energy drink-themed ornament), so it’s hardly surprising that the New York-based designer plucked this boneless cooked ham ornament for this year’s batch of stunners.

A man's appendix had to be removed, but not for dangerous inflammation, as you might expect.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The symptoms: The man went to the emergency room because he had a sharp pain in his lower-right abdomen.

What happened next: When doctors examined the man, the type of pain and the location of his discomfort suggested that he might have appendicitis, or inflammation of the appendix.

Appendicitis can be dangerous because it can cause the appendix to burst and release bacteria from the bowels into the abdominal cavity, thereby infecting the cavity's lining. This infection, called peritonitis, can spread to the bloodstream and cause the life-threatening condition sepsis, which kicks the immune system into overdrive.

Even though the patient had acute pain in his lower-right abdomen, he did not show signs of peritonitis, such as fever, nausea, symptoms of dehydration and an elevated heart rate, according to a report of his case. His doctors then performed abdominal ultrasound scans and found that the man's abdominal organs, including the appendix, appeared normal, with no signs of inflammation.

The report's authors did not include details about the man's treatment after this examination. But eight months later, he was still in pain and returned to the hospital for further evaluation, they noted.

The diagnosis: This time, when medical personnel questioned the man, he recalled that approximately 15 years earlier, he had accidentally swallowed a piece of a long bone containing edible marrow. The report does not mention if the man sought treatment immediately after swallowing this bone.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

At this second visit, doctors performed an abdominal X-ray and found a round object near the upper right of the man's pelvis. It measured about an inch (2.5 centimeters) long and a little over an inch (3 cm) wide.

According to a subsequent CT scan, the object contained bone tissue and was near the appendix. When the doctors looked inside the patient's abdomen with a laparoscope — a long, flexible tool with a camera at one end — they saw that the appendix was enlarged.

The treatment: Surgeons performed a laparoscopic appendectomy, which uses small incisions in the abdomen to insert instruments for removing the appendix. Inside the appendix was a hardened mass of fecal matter, called a fecaloma, which surrounded a long bone.

The organ's muscular walls had been stretched out by the mass, but there were no signs of inflammation. No complications developed after the surgery, and the patient was discharged two days later. The report does not describe any follow-up visits or treatments.

The appendix (orange) is a small, thin pouch of tissue attached to the colon.

What makes the case unique: It's relatively uncommon for people to accidentally swallow something indigestible and then require a medical visit for it. In the United States annually, about 120,000 people — roughly 90% of whom are children — are treated for ingesting foreign objects, and most of the objects are swallowed accidentally. Most commonly, the adults requiring treatment have ingested jewelry, while children are more likely to swallow coins, toys and batteries.

Typically, small, swallowed items pass harmlessly through the intestines within 48 hours; less than 1% require surgical intervention. Some objects, however, need immediate attention. For example, sharp items can tear the esophagus or puncture digestive organs. Batteries are hazardous if swallowed, as they contain corrosive acid that can leak into the gut. And small magnets are a big risk, especially if two or more are involved, since they may stick together through intestinal walls, which can tear holes in tissues or cause blockages and contortions in the intestines.

Swallowed foreign bodies rarely affect the appendix. Whether they enter the organ depends on the size of the opening into the appendix where it connects to the colon (which can vary between individuals), the dimensions of the ingested object, and the appendix's position in the body at the time. These objects cause approximately 0.005% cases of appendicitis, according to the man's case report. Such items recovered by surgeons through appendectomies include pieces of coal, nails, bits of enamel and glass, shells, dental crowns and bullets.

When a foreign body migrates to the appendix, it typically generates appendicitis within a few months, at most. However, this is not always the case. One report described a man who had eaten pigeons as a child and discovered more than 30 years later that he had 27 lead shot pellets in his appendix. Despite containing these pellets from the birds' flesh, his appendix was not inflamed.

"It is therefore possible, although rare, that a foreign body in the appendix even after many years (in our case, 15 years) does not lead to an authentic appendicitis either histologically or clinically," the authors of the marrowbone case report wrote.

They added that their patient was the first record in the scientific literature of a sizable bone lingering inside an appendix for more than a decade without causing significant inflammation. His pain was likely caused by physical shifting of the hard mass. His experience presented "a unique clinical picture," the doctors wrote.

"This case could offer a possible diagnostic and therapeutic option for appropriately treating patients with foreign bodies within the appendix," they said.

For more intriguing medical cases, check out our Diagnostic Dilemma archives.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Antonacci, N., Labombarda, M., Ricci, C., Buscemi, S., Casadei, R., & Minni, F. (2013). A bizarre foreign body in the appendix: A case report. World Journal of Gastrointestinal Surgery, 5(6), 195–198. https://doi.org/10.4240/wjgs.v5.i6.195

#6363. Mars May Not Be Dead After All, New Discovery Suggests

Gas above a Martian volcano may come from hidden magma, offering clues to the planet’s remaining heat and its potential to support life underground.

Hydrogen chloride gas usually reaches its highest levels in Mars’s atmosphere during winter in the northern hemisphere, then mostly disappears in summer. Much of that seasonal pattern appears to follow the planet’s dust and water cycles. Above volcanic fissures on the flanks of Alba Mons, researchers found a recurring exception. Localized spikes of the gas appeared in the same place in early northern summer, raising the possibility of a source beneath the ground.

An international research team led by Alexander Trokhimovskiy suggests that the gas could be escaping from hot magma below the region. Its study, published November 4, 2026, in Science Advances, brings together atmospheric measurements and geological evidence to investigate a possible connection to dormant volcanism.

This artist’s impression shows hydrogen chloride gas rising from within Mars’ crust and venting to the atmosphere, where the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter detects it. The animation explains one scenario of how the timing of the hydrogen chloride detection is governed by seasonal water ice. Credit: ESA

The ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) first reported hydrogen chloride in the Martian atmosphere in 2021. On Earth, the gas commonly escapes from magmatic vents, making a volcanic source on Mars a possibility worth examining. Using infrared spectrometers in TGO’s Atmospheric Chemistry Suite, researchers detected a strongly localized concentration above Alba Mons just after winter frosts sublimated, turning directly from ice into vapor.

“Looking at the spatial distribution of the seeping, it became instantly obvious to me that there was something volcanic behind it, but it had to be demonstrated,” says Daniel Mège, a professor at the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences and co-lead author of the paper. “A huge part of the work consisted of examining all the possible chemical processes going on in the Martian atmosphere. We needed to be rigorous, critical, and creative to explain the presence of hydrogen chloride. The data were complex, but also excellent brain food.”

A closer look at Alba Mons with TGO’s CaSSIS camera revealed fresh, narrow fissures, some hundreds of meters long, associated with changes in surface color. Those features provided geological evidence to consider alongside the gas measurements.

The team proposes that a dormant magma chamber, an underground reservoir of molten rock, could supply gases that rise through the fissures. During winter, when temperatures fall as low as −120°C (−184°F), ice could block their escape. As the ice sublimates in early summer, the openings would allow the gases to reach the atmosphere. The fissures could therefore behave like fumaroles on Earth, vents that release volcanic gases. Deposits left by escaping gases could also explain the discoloration around them.

“The Trace Gas Orbiter was able to find the smoking gun. It was like looking for a needle in a haystack. It’s truly amazing that it spotted a handful of molecules from a perhaps intermittent source, whilst moving continuously along its orbit to monitor the whole Martian atmosphere,” Mège says.

Scientists still do not know how active Mars’s volcanoes are. The planet has the largest volcanoes in the solar system, and orbital images suggest that some were active within the last few million years. Seismometers have also detected marsquakes, the Martian equivalent of earthquakes. Both observations point to the possibility of continuing volcanic activity, although no new lava flows or eruptions have ever been observed.

“Our findings suggest that Mars has retained enough internal heat to support volcanic activity until recently, and possibly still does,” Mège says.

“These findings may prove to be TGO’s greatest success yet,” says Colin Wilson, ESA’s project scientist for the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter.

Magmatic gases such as hydrogen chloride could have been more abundant earlier in Mars’s history, contributing to a thicker atmosphere and a warmer climate that allowed liquid water to cover much of the surface. If molten rock rising through the crust encounters groundwater, it could also create warm niches potentially suitable for life.

“Looking for Martian life in the seeping fissures of the Alba Mons region would make a lot of sense. If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface,” Mège says.

Reference: “Enigmatic HCl detections as a potential signature of igneous activity on Mars” by Alexander Trokhimovskiy, Daniel Mège, Oleg Korablev, Kevin S. Olsen, Anna A. Fedorova, Benjamin Taysum, Pierre-Antoine Tesson, Mikhail Luginin, Franck Montmessin, Pavel Vlasov, Alexey Grigoriev, Juan Alday, Denis Belyaev, Nikolay Ignatiev, Andrey Patrakeev, Nikita Kokonkov, Yuriy Ivanov, Joanna Gurgurewicz, Antoine Pommerol, Gabriele Cremonese and Nicolas Thomas, 4 November 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeb9422

Funding: The ExoMars mission is a joint mission of the European Space Agency (ESA) and Roscosmos. The ACS experiment is led by the Space Research Institute (IKI) in Moscow, assisted by LATMOS in France. The science operations of ACS are funded by Roscosmos and ESA. #6362. A Brief-ish History of METI. Part III: The Legacy of Frank Drake & Carl Sagan

Welcome back to our continuing series on the Brief-ish History of METI, where we examine the rise, development, and possible implications of Messaging Extraterrestrial Intelligence (METI). In our first installment, we explored some of the foundational principles, how METI emerged as a possible answer to the "SETI Paradox," and the earliest experiments. In our second, we looked at the pioneering work of Cornell Professor Frank Drake, the "father of SETI," and how his efforts led to the first true experiment in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI): Project Ozma and the Arecibo Message.

We also touched on how these efforts led to his lifelong collaboration with fellow Cornell Professor and famed science communicator Carl Sagan. Today, we will see how this collaboration attracted the attention of NASA and led to the most ambitious projects to send messages to space, ones that might even be found by an extraterrestrial civilization (ETC) someday. These are none other than the Pioneer Plaques and the Voyager Golden Records, which are now in the outer Solar System or have entered interstellar space.

As noted in our last installment, Carl Sagan and Frank Drake first met in 1961, a year after Project Ozma took place. To build on the momentum the experiment created, Drake organized an informal symposium at the Green Bank Observatory (where Ozma was conducted) in 1961. To prepare for the event, Drake formulated an equation that summarized the challenges SETI researchers faced. This became known as the Drake Equation, which remains foundational to the fields of SETI and METI.

The equation states that the number of extraterrestrial civilizations in our galaxy that we could communicate with (N) depends on several variables. These include the annual rate of star formation in the galaxy (R*), the fraction of those stars with planets (fp), the number of planets with conditions suitable for life (ne), the fraction of planets that will develop intelligence (fi), the fraction of planets with intelligent life that will develop transmission technologies (fc), and the average length of time a civilization will be able to produce signals (L). Mathematically, the equation is expressed as:

As one of many prominent scientists attending the symposium, Sagan was impressed with Drake's theories and advocacy for using radio astronomy to search for possible ETCs. However, their interactions predated this meeting and included correspondence when both were young graduate astronomy students. Sagan became aware of Drake when he heard of his work measuring Venus's high temperature. After this meeting, the two became close colleagues and professors at Cornell University, where they went on to collaborate on several landmark projects.

In the early 1970s, the last Apollo mission successfully landed astronauts on the Moon (Eugene A. Cernan, Harrison H. Schmitt, and Ronald E. Evans). This historic accomplishment effectively ended the "Space Race," and NASA was busy contemplating its next moves. It was decided that the Pioneer program, which had sent nine probes to explore the Moon, Venus, Mars, and Mercury between 1958 and 1968, should shift focus to the outer Solar System, exploring the Main Asteroid Belt, Jupiter, Saturn, and the interstellar medium.

This made the probes especially significant, as they would be the first missions to achieve escape velocity from the Solar System. For this reason, journalist and science correspondent Eric Burgess (who was also the Pioneer program's chronicler) suggested that the probes carry a message, should an extraterrestrial species find them someday. Burgess approached Carl Sagan with the idea after hearing him lecture about communicating with extraterrestrial intelligence at a conference in Crimea.

Sagan was enthusiastic about the idea and approached Frank Drake to help design a message that could be interpreted by an ETC. NASA agreed to the plan and gave them three weeks to prepare it, and the two decided to create plaques that could be mounted on the Pioneer 10 and 11 missions. Linda Salzman Sagan, Carl Sagan's wife at the time, prepared the artwork, with additional contributions from space artist and science journalist Jon Lomberg, a long-time collaborator of Sagan's.

The result was the Pioneer Plaques, a pair of six-by-nine-inch (~23 cm by 15.25 cm) gold-anodized aluminum plates. Each contained an engraved pictorial message identifying the probes' place of origin, who sent them, and when they were sent. From top to bottom, left to right, the message included the following details:

A detailed view of the visual message on the Pioneer plaques, developed by Carl Sagan and Frank Drake. Credit: NASA Ames

The Pioneer 10 and Pioneer 11 probes launched on March 2nd, 1972, and April 5th, 1973 (respectively), becoming the first robotic missions to explore beyond Mars and the Main Asteroid Belt. The Pioneer Plaques have the distinction of being humanity's first interstellar message of greetings. But in a few years' time, Sagan and Drake would take things a step further, creating something that was meant to convey what life on Earth was like.

The success of the Pioneer 10 and 11 missions motivated NASA to contemplate an even more ambitious mission: dual probes to explore the planets of the outer Solar System. The twin Voyager 1 and 2 probes would launch in the summer of 1977 to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment of the outer planets. The mission would conduct close-up studies of Jupiter, Saturn, Saturn's rings, and larger moons. But as the mission progressed, NASA chose to use the alignment to include Uranus and Neptune - what came to be known as the "Grand Tour."

Since these missions would also achieve escape velocity from the Solar System, NASA decided to follow the precedent established with the Pioneer Plaques. This led Voyager project manager John R. Casani to suggest that the Voyager 1 and 2 probes also carry a "message in a bottle" containing information about humanity. He delegated the task to Carl Sagan, who was joined again by Frank Drake and Linda Salzman Sagan, and the three created a metal phonograph record containing information encoded in its grooves.

A record was chosen because it would outlast magnetic tape in the outer-space environment. This time, Sagan and crew were given six weeks to create the records and a budget of $1,500, the equivalent of about 8,780 USD today, though Sagan and his colleagues contributed money of their own. The fruits of their labors were the Voyager Golden Records, a series of 12-inch (30.5 cm) gold-plated copper disks containing sounds and images that portrayed the diversity of life and culture on Earth.

The outer cases were etched with pictograms (see above) similar to the Pioneer Plaques, showing where the probes came from. They also contained instructions for playing the record. In the upper left corner of the case, there is a drawing of the phonograph record and the stylus in the correct position for playing it. Around it, conveyed in binary arithmetic, are the time it takes for the record to complete one rotation (3.6 seconds), the total duration (1 hour), and how it should be played from the outside in.

The upper-right corner contains instructions for constructing pictures from the record. From top to bottom, these include a representation of the signal that indicates the start of a picture, how the signals must be grouped as a series of 512 vertical lines per picture, and what the first image looks like (a circle) to confirm the signals are being processed correctly. The drawing in the lower left-hand corner of the cover is the pulsar map (similar to the Pioneer Plaques) and a drawing of the hyperfine transition of neutral hydrogen.

The Voyager Golden Record (right) and its protective casing with instructions on how to play along with information about its origin (left). Credit: NASA

The record contains 115 encoded images that show human anatomy (a silhouette of a man and a pregnant woman), the structure of DNA, demonstrations of eating and drinking, major locations on Earth, sports and leisure, our planet's geography, and mathematical/scientific concepts. It also contains sound recordings of greetings in 55 languages, whale calls, and music from various cultures and eras (including Beethoven and Chuck Berry). Said then-President Jimmy Carter of the Records:

This is a present from a small, distant world, a token of our sounds, our science, our images, our music, our thoughts and our feelings. We are attempting to survive our time so we may live into yours.

The cover also features a "radioactive clock" in the form of an electroplated uranium-238 sample. Since this element has a half-life of 4.51 billion years, the recipients can calculate how long the probe has been in space. Unlike the Pioneer Plaques, the Voyager Golden Records had a dual purpose: as a message to any extraterrestrial civilization that intercepted them, or as a time capsule for future generations of human explorers should they find them first. As Sagan noted at the time:

The spacecraft will be encountered, and the record played only if there are advanced spacefaring civilizations in interstellar space, but the launching of this 'bottle' into the cosmic 'ocean' says something very hopeful about life on this planet.

Based on its current trajectory and velocity, Pioneer 10 will reach Aldebaran, a star roughly 65 light-years away in the Taurus constellation, in over two million years. Meanwhile, Pioneer 11 is headed for the Aquila constellation and will pass near one of its stars in about 4 million years. On August 25th, 2012, Voyager 1 made history by becoming the first probe to exit the heliosphere and enter interstellar space. Voyager 2 exited from a different location on November 5th, 2018, becoming the second.

They will be joined by Pioneer 10 and 11 probes around 2057, though this will be difficult to verify since both probes are unpowered and cannot send data back to Earth. These plaques and records are unique in that they remain humanity's first attempts to send physical messages into space intended for extraterrestrial recipients and/or future generations. They also established a legacy that continues to this day and is part of a larger debate surrounding the ethics of METI.

This illustration shows the positions of NASA's Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 probes outside the heliosphere, a protective bubble created by the Sun that extends well past Pluto's orbit. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

These missions have also inspired debate about what a modern message should be and have inspired some experiments. In a series of NASA-led studies that appeared in the AGU journal Earth and Space Science, an international team of scientists proposed what a modern Golden Record should contain. In the first study, titled "Message in a BottleâAn Update to the Golden Record: 1. Objectives and Key Content of the Message," the team summarized the importance of the "Message In A Bottle" (MIAB) and what should motivate future efforts:

These records not only offer a snapshot of Earth and human civilization but also represent our desire to establish contact with advanced alien civilizations. Our goal is to share our collective knowledge, emotions, innovations, and aspirations in a way that provides a universal, yet contextually relevant, understanding of human society, the evolution of life on Earth, and our hopes and concerns for the future. Through this time and space traveling capsule, we also strive to inspire and unify current and future generations to celebrate and safeguard our shared human experience.

Modern attempts to fashion a MIAB include the message attached to the Europa Clipper mission, currently en route to rendezvous with Jupiter and study its moon Europa. The message was unveiled in March 2024, about seven months before the mission launched, and consists of a triangular tantalum plaque - known as the Europa Clipper Vault Plate - measuring about 18 x 28 cm (about 7 x 11 inches) that features graphic elements on both sides. The inward-facing side features an engraving of U.S. Poet Laureate Ada LimÃ³n's handwritten "In Praise of Mystery: A Poem for Europa."

The outward-facing panel contains etchings of soundwaves that illustrate Earth's connection to Europa. Each etching is the word "water" spoken in one of 103 languages from around the world, which were converted into waveforms. Each waveform radiates outward from a symbol representing the sign for "water" in American Sign Language (ASL). Since the Europa Clipper is searching for possible evidence of life inside the icy moon, the Drake Equation is also etched into the plate.

Rather than being a message intended for extraterrestrials, this "Golden Record for Europa" honors the spirit of the original records, aiming to spark the imagination and offer a unifying vision. As Lori Glaze, director of the Planetary Science Division at NASA, said in a statement:

The content and design of Europa Clipper's vault plate are swimming with meaning. The plate combines the best humanity has to offer across the universe â science, technology, education, art, and math. The message of connection through water, essential for all forms of life as we know it, perfectly illustrates Earth's tie to this mysterious ocean world we are setting out to explore.

The "Message in a Bottle" plate attached to the Europa Clipper mission, currently en route to Jupiter. Credit: NASA

These messages highlight the major shift in consciousness that accompanied the Space Age. With humans now venturing out into space and exploring beyond Earth's orbit, a new awareness was taking root, one which saw humanity in cosmological terms. We were not only pondering the existence of extraterrestrial intelligence and civilizations. We were also considering how we might communicate with them and fashioning messages that might someday reach them... unless we get to them first!

These messages also raise the question of whether ETCs might be doing the same: could advanced civilizations be sending probes with their own messages, ones that share what life is like on their respective homeworlds? The fact that we have sent out four MIABs to date has motivated some scientists to consider the possibility that space is littered with derelict spacecraft, some of which could be messenger probes. Perhaps some of them are even here in our Solar System, lingering near Earth or in the far expanse of the Kuiper Belt.

Matt Williams is a space journalist, science communicator, and author with several published titles and studies. His work is featured in The Ross 248 Project and Interstellar Travel edited by NASA alumni Les Johnson and Ken Roy. He also hosts the podcast series Stories from Space on Patreon. He lives in beautiful British Columbia with his wife and family. For more information, check out his website.

#6361. Highly Specific Observations While Scouting for the 2026 Eater Awards

The great dishes, gorgeous restaurants, and quirky cocktails that commanded our attention, even if they didn’t make the big list

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

The past year has been one of “Great Chickenings” and fine dining flips, British food invasions and restaurants whose dining rooms feel like living rooms, vibrant global steakhouses and unserious Y2K food. Among the slate of our 2026 Eater Award winners — which also brought undeniable new chef talent, core-memory-forming dishes, and groundbreaking bakeries and bars — are the places we could not stop thinking about for highly specific reasons. While this crop of restaurants and bars did not make the ultimate cut for the 2026 Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, they commanded enough attention during our expansive scouting and research months to deserve acknowledgment. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager

Cabbage is having its moment. From a star turn on the Sandy Liang runway as a ruffled bag to a hand-painted Bordallo Pinheiro dinner set and a declaration from Vogue that the leafy green has gone “chic,” the cruciferous vegetable is 2026’s “it” girl. The cult of the cabbage has made its way to Monte’s in Montecito, a cozy Korean American bistro where cone cabbage gets coal-roasted and kissed with salty smoked shiitake XO, an umami-heavy spin on the Hong Kong-born sauce. The fall-apart-tender cabbage beds on creamy tofu puree, the whole thing studded with hazelnuts that bring out the vegetable’s innate sweetness. Preparations like the one at Monte’s make it feel as though cabbage isn’t just this year’s distinguished vegetable — its dominance is here to stay. — Rebecca Roland, deputy editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest

Maybe it was the Negroni, the Old Fashioned, and the gingery mezcal-laced Missed Opportunity. Perhaps it was the jetlag (who can say for sure?), but the bathroom at Bobo — the Filipino bar attached to Muhajir in Chicago’s Lincoln Park — left a lasting impression on me. In a world that’s fully embraced the bathroom selfie, Bobo has answered the call with refractory horizontal-mirrored panel walls and colored light that shifts from reds to greens, turning this lavatory into a mesmerizing disco ball. It’s a fitting touch that matches chef Jacob Dela Cruz’s vision for a red-light district-esque tropical hideaway. — Brenna Houck, Eater editorial manager

In a world of outrageous martinis, the one at Greenpoint Malaysian restaurant Kelang earns its playful name. The Dirty Fish riffs on a Vesper with gin, vodka, dry vermouth, and, saliently, fish sauce, which levels up the drink’s savoriness in every way. The pungent condiment mimics olive brine, delivering a salty taste of the sea to the already strong drink, which then gets garnished with wavy scallions and a long sliver of aromatic ginger. The cocktail showcases owner Chris Low’s background as a Malaysian kid who grew up in New York. It’s simply presented — a cloudy drink in a stemmed coupe glass with those gloating garnishes — and pairs best with that fluffy paratha served over creamy and spicy dal. — Nadia Chaudhury, deputy editor, Eater New York

Gone may be the days of business power lunches at Wolfgang Puck’s Spago or Grill on the Alley that required a suit and tie. In their place, a new arrangement has emerged — the low-key power lunch. There may be no better place for the midday meal masquerading as a meeting right now than at Little Fish in Melrose Hill, the first full-service restaurant from the former pop-up-turned-fish sandwich window. The light-filled dining room hums during daytime with flexibly scheduled creatives and well-dressed parents toting young children, all adults in the room sipping wine picked by sommelier Kae Whalen. On the menu, a tuna melt from maverick chefs and owners Anna Sonenshein and Niki Vahle will convert even nonbelievers, especially when paired with peppery fries dunked in horseradish aioli. Of course, there is the calling card fried fish sandwich, but smarter diners go for the beach sandwich layered with guindilla peppers and soy-cured mussels and a bay leaf chip stracciatella flecked with chocolate chips. Melrose Hill and its confluence of independent restaurants has morphed into a miniature walkable neighborhood — the perfect place to see and be seen. And what’s more low-key power lunch than that? — RR

Historically, California is a gold mine of kitsch restaurants, from Clifton’s Republic to the pillowy pink dining room at the Madonna Inn. Night Hawk is the next jewel in that camp crown; the Greek-influenced San Diego restaurant is an anchor of Coronado Island’s hypermaximalist new Baby Grand hotel and beckons diners into a lush, faux-rock-filled outdoor dining room with pink clamshell chairs, waterfalls, and cocktails that have names like the Adonis in Bloom and Spanakopita Punch. In short: Tony Duquette by way of an acid tab. — Francky Knapp, staff writer

British food hit a fever pitch nationally this year as Americans awakened to the allure of meat pies and mushy peas. But if any restaurant truly dispelled notions of the country’s cuisine as dull or bland, it was Ambassadors Clubhouse, with its extensive menu of Punjabi showstoppers such as seven-layer, aloo-filed, Amritsari-style samosas; butter chicken in the form of lollipop-like chops with a heady char; and matka Beliram lamb, its crimson oil heralding intense flavor. In opulent, velvet-adorned surroundings that feel like a hideaway from the city, this luxe London import deliciously makes the case that Indian food is as essential to British cuisine as fish and chips. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter

The most beautiful new restaurant in California is tucked into a shopping center in Montecito’s tony upper village. Little Mountain, which opened in November 2025 under chef Diego Moya, gives more to the scene than just a locavore menu that leans into live-fire cooking — it brings a bona fide, Architectural Digest-worthy destination that I would get married (and remarried) in. It may be hard to decide which room to sit in should you land a reservation in time: the comfortable dining room with gold-veil natural lighting and plush caramel booths and banquettes; the larger-party table that foregrounds an open kitchen and its centerpiece hearth; the dim, dark bar that may be the sexiest sliver of drinking den on the Central Coast; the covered patio that leads into a monarchial private dining area; or the outdoor patio that evokes dining in a home garden. Anywhere you sit, you can’t go wrong, especially as the food starts landing in front of you. — NF

Chef Theo Adley opened Heretík last spring, and it has brought a breath of fresh, San Sebastián-esque sea breeze air into the Denver dining scene. The French- and Basque-leaning restaurant serves an endless summer menu of dishes like Santa Barbara uni, a playful pan con tomate martini, and scallops à la plancha with bearnaise and seaweed. The menu’s coastal Euro allure gets amplified by its interior design choices, which sprinkle in vintage furniture and tapered, wax drip-laden candles — but with a name like Heretík, you know that all of that romance is going to come with a healthy dose of cheek. — FK

Chickens, you can’t take credit for this one: The British-inspired pub Dean’s proved that bigger is not always better with its take on a Scotch egg, which employs quail eggs instead of the typical chicken ones. In larger Scotch eggs, what appears in each bite can be inconsistent. But the result of the shrunken-down approach here is a reliably favorable ratio of meat to egg, in which each bite at once encompasses crunchy breading, tender meat filling, runny yolk, and just enough still-bouncy egg white. It’s as nonnegotiable at Dean’s as a pint of Guinness. — BM

Ladyfish in Portland, Maine, has been clear about one thing since the beginning: “A summer fling,” the restaurant declared when it announced its May 2026 arrival. Jordan and Marisa Rubin of Portland sushi spot Mr. Tuna convinced chef Christine Lau to relocate from New York City to helm the seasonal seafood pop-up. Lau, whose resume includes Japanese-Italian and Chino Latino restaurants, brings her distinctive flair to classic Maine ingredients for dishes like scallops in a blanket with fried milk bread and the showstopping twin lobster mountain served with fries, rice cakes, and dan dan au poivre sauce. True to its word, the restaurant closed at the end of October. Here’s hoping the return of next year’s summertime crowds also brings back this match made in seafood heaven. — Stephanie Wu, editor in chief

Los Angeles-born chef Ray Garcia opened Broken Spanish Comedor in Culver City in late 2025, years after his groundbreaking Mexican fine dining restaurant, Broken Spanish, and more casual B.S. Taqueria closed in Downtown Los Angeles. Garcia’s contribution to Alta California cuisine, rooted in Mexican cooking told through a California lens, remains one of the most distinct of this generation of restaurants. Still, he manages to surprise both longtime fans and newcomers to his work: The Comedor, whose name nods to the Indigenous homestyle restaurant tradition in Mexico, feels fresh in its A-frame home. It’s not uncommon for locals and those working in Los Angeles hospitality to stop in for a meal of crispy, crown-whorled chicharron or quesillo-threaded refried lentils; a classics-leaning drinks menu (cócteles, cervezas, vino) keeps the room humming happily. In a year brimming with big restaurant comebacks (see also: Venice’s resurrected Tasting Kitchen and Keith Corbin’s reframed Alta Adams), it feels good to have an Angeleno chef like Ray Garcia capture our collective imagination again. — Mona Holmes, editor, Eater Southern California/Southwest

If ever there was a destination in need of effective hangover cures, it’s New Orleans. While I was totally ready to rally after a two-bar, two-restaurant evening the night before (I am, of course, a professional), I also wasn’t mad about consuming something fortifying at Casimiro, the charming all-day cafe from award-winning Acamaya chef Ana Castro, the next morning. The restaurant delivered: textbook chilaquiles, impossibly fluffy conchas, crispy pescaditos, and one of the best tortas I’ve ever had. If hair of the dog is in your future in the City That Always Drinks, go with the well-balanced Cynar daiquiri to finish. — Missy Frederick, dining editorial director

The weirdest thing I ate on a pastry this year was “lettuce cream” lacquered onto the BLT Danish at Dahlia in Minneapolis. The chartreuse-colored cream anchored a slice of late-August tomato and dollops of bacon jam atop persistently crisp laminated dough. One bite was enough to make me think, This should be more of a thing. You wouldn’t know at first glance that this bakery, tucked into an office complex, turns out treats of this caliber: jam-filled croissants with speculoos crumble, unassumingly perfect English muffins, plush milk bread and fluffy focaccia for sandwiches. This kind of out-of-the-box baking makes eating pastries right now so fun. — BM

#6360. Scientists Warn: The World Has Less Than Four Years of Carbon Budget Left

Solar power, wind energy, and electric vehicles are reshaping global emissions trends, but a new scientific assessment reveals that the world’s remaining carbon budget is shrinking at an alarming rate.

Global fossil fuel emissions are expected to fall slightly in 2026, but the world’s total carbon dioxide output is still projected to rise. A new assessment by the Global Carbon Project estimates that fossil CO2 emissions will decline by 0.4% to 38.2 billion metric tons (42.1 billion U.S. tons), partly because of expanding clean energy and disruptions linked to the Iran conflict.

However, increasing emissions from deforestation and other changes in land use are expected to push total global CO2 emissions to 43.3 billion metric tons (47.7 billion U.S. tons), up from 42.8 billion metric tons in 2025. The findings show that renewable energy is beginning to reshape global emissions trends, but its growth has not yet produced a sustained worldwide decline.

Oil is expected to account for much of the projected reduction in fossil fuel emissions. Global CO2 emissions from oil are forecast to drop by 1.9%, largely reflecting the energy shock associated with the Iran conflict, which has increased prices and constrained supplies. Natural gas emissions are expected to decrease by 0.3%, while coal emissions could rise by 0.6%. Emissions from international aviation and shipping are each projected to fall by 1%, with reduced activity in the Middle East contributing to the aviation decline.

“A decline in fossil CO2 emissions is encouraging, but a reduction driven partly by geopolitical shocks is not a sustainable climate solution,” said Professor Pierre Friedlingstein, director of the Global Carbon Budget Office at the University of Exeter, who led the study. “The long-term answer remains the rapid deployment of clean energy technologies. While renewables and electric vehicles are increasingly offsetting growth in energy demand, further acceleration is needed if global emissions are to peak and enter a sustained decline.”

Glen Peters, Research Professor at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research, emphasized that temporary reductions should not be confused with lasting progress. “A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak unless it is driven by structural change. Accelerated deployment of solar, wind, batteries, and electric vehicles are pushing emissions down in dozens of countries, and slowing emissions growth in many more, but the changes are not sufficient to lock in a peak in global emissions.”

Solar and wind power, together with electric vehicles, are increasingly limiting emissions despite rising energy demand. According to the assessment, these technologies are meeting or avoiding roughly two-thirds of the increase in global energy demand. Solar and wind generation alone are projected to prevent 4.6 billion metric tons (5.1 billion U.S. tons) of CO2 emissions in 2026, compared with 4.1 billion metric tons in 2025 and just 0.28 billion metric tons in 2010.

China is central to this transformation. Although it produces approximately 32% of global fossil fuel emissions, it also accounts for half of the emissions avoided worldwide through renewable energy and electric vehicles. China’s emissions are projected to decline by 0.9% in 2026, helped by lower oil consumption and continued renewable electricity expansion. Coal emissions, however, are expected to increase slightly by 0.3%. China also leads the world in carbon uptake from reforestation and afforestation (new forests).

“Clean technologies are making a real difference in reducing global emissions. Solar and wind power and electric vehicles are expanding rapidly, led by China. Countries on every continent are decreasing their emissions while growing their economies. A further acceleration could turn the tide on global emissions within a few years,” said Professor Corinne Le Quéré, Royal Society Research Professor at the University of East Anglia’s School of Environmental Sciences.

Emissions are projected to decline by 1.3% in the United States, primarily because coal consumption is falling after increasing in 2025 amid high natural gas prices and cold weather. The European Union is expected to record a 1.5% reduction, while Japan’s emissions could decrease by 1%. India is moving in the opposite direction, with emissions projected to rise by 4.4%, exceeding its average annual growth rate of 3.5% over the past decade. Emissions across the rest of the world are expected to decrease by 0.7%, largely because of reduced oil consumption.

An accompanying analysis, currently in press in a separate peer-reviewed journal, identifies a broader shift in the relationship between economic growth and carbon emissions. In 59 countries, emissions were lower in 2025 than in 2019, before the COVID-19 pandemic, even as their economies expanded. Emissions growth has also slowed in regions where total emissions continue to rise, including China, India, and other emerging economies.

The decline in fossil fuel emissions is being offset by increasing carbon releases from land-use change (such as deforestation). These emissions are projected to reach 5.1 billion metric tons (5.6 billion U.S. tons) in 2026. The increase is linked partly to peat fires and forest degradation in Southeast Asia, where drier conditions associated with El Niño have heightened fire risks. Nearly all peat fires are ignited by human activities.

Natural ecosystems also influence how much CO2 remains in the atmosphere. Forests, soils, and oceans absorb substantial amounts of carbon, acting as natural carbon sinks. The Global Carbon Budget reports that land-based carbon absorption has recovered after weakening sharply during the 2023 and 2024 El Niño event. However, the powerful El Niño developing in 2026 is expected to affect this natural carbon uptake over the coming year.

The latest assessment estimates that only 150 billion metric tons (165 billion U.S. tons) of CO2 can be emitted before cumulative emissions reach the level associated with 1.5°C (2.7°F) of global warming above preindustrial levels. At current emission rates, that remaining carbon budget amounts to less than four years. Meanwhile, atmospheric CO2 concentrations are projected to reach 427.7 parts per million in 2026, approximately 54% above preindustrial levels.

Removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere is another part of the challenge. Permanent deforestation released an average of approximately 3.8 billion metric tons (4.2 billion U.S. tons) of CO2 annually between 2016 and 2025. Reforestation and afforestation offset roughly half of those emissions. China, the European Union, and the United States account for the largest combined removals through forest restoration and expansion, while deforestation outweighs these gains in countries including Brazil, Russia, and Indonesia. Technologies designed to remove atmospheric CO2 remain limited, currently capturing less than the amount released by fossil fuels in just 30 minutes.

“Alongside reducing emissions, we need to scale up CO2 removal to reach greenhouse gas neutrality. Afforestation and reforestation already remove substantial amounts of CO2, but these gains are still more than offset by emissions from deforestation, and novel carbon removal remains very limited. We need to act on all these fronts now,” said Professor Julia Pongratz of Ludwig-Maximilian-University Munich.

Despite continued increases in total emissions, their long-term growth rate has slowed substantially. Global CO2 emissions rose by an average of 0.3% annually over the past decade, compared with 1.7% annually during the preceding decade. The accompanying analysis projects that between now and the end of 2028, additional solar and wind generation and electric vehicles could prevent emissions equivalent to 64% to 79% of those associated with rising energy demand. Electric vehicles are becoming increasingly influential, although only about 10% of the global passenger car fleet was electrified in 2025 (or 6% excluding hybrids).

The researchers conclude that continued deployment of clean technologies could bring the first sustained global decline in CO2 emissions within reach. However, achieving that outcome depends on maintaining and accelerating their expansion rather than relying on temporary reductions caused by economic or geopolitical disruptions. As the authors write, “If further acceleration of clean technology deployment can be supported through time, a sustained peak and decline in global CO2 emissions could be a few years away.”

Reference: “Global Carbon Budget 2026” by Pierre Friedlingstein, Michael O’Sullivan, Robbie M. Andrew, Judith Hauck, Matthew W. Jones, Peter Landschützer, Corinne Le Quéré, Hongmei Li, Ingrid T. I wish liberals had not pushed unsustainable population growth mainly through immigration the last few decades. The planet was already far over capacity. That really put us in a bad situation that won’t peak now for decades.

What has pushed growth of population is quite simple; the invention of antibiotics in 1944 and their widespread use since. Global population growth accompanied by assorted increased uses of energy went exponential after 1945, as did CO2 production. World-wide vaccination programmes such as that which wiped out smallpox, would have helped.

Immigration is the result of population growth, not its cause!

The expansion in death control, without an off-setting expansion in birth control, is responsible for population growth. Immigration is merely a change in where the people live. It may be responsible for a slight increase in population if people are able to move to a country that provides them with improved nutrition and health care that they can afford. However, immigration is not responsible for the world growth of population.

a-n-d the only figure that means anything is the we keep above 0.04% atmospheric carbon because falling further to 0.02% (half present levels) sees the worldwide death of plant-life from being starved of what it breathes: CARBON. And then it will not be there to supply all the little (gullible) kiddies with the Oxygen they need. Al – as in 100% – of the talk is propaganda – designed to chip money into climate causes and, importantly, those the run the scam. Facts hurt.

The problem is that nobody really gives a damn. Oh sure, people would like to save the planet, but only if someone else is making the sacrifice, not them personally. I am disgusted by my generation (Boomers) who rant and rage about saving the environment, but then jump in their SUV every weekend and drive a couple hundred miles to their second or third home in the country. Those second and third homes are kept heated and lit all year round regardless of occupancy. After arriving at their second homes these same city dwellers spend all weekend driving around looking for God knows what, skiing on manmade snow, or driving boats and off road vehicles. Personal carbon output be damned. Like I said, nobody really gives a damn about climate change.

A second home that is only lived in part-time does not result in the same consumption of resources as a primary home. Unless they want to throw away money, they change the thermostat setting when they aren’t there, only leave security lights on when unoccupied, and therefore aren’t using as much electricity/gas when absent; water consumption is similarly related to the amount of time spent in a particular residence and therefore goes down in the primary residence when visiting the secondary residence.

“Clean technologies are making a real difference in reducing global emissions.”

The unstated assumption is that global warming is being driven by human emissions, especially fossil fuels. While wildly popular with arm-waving alarmists, the correlation argument is not supported strongly by temperatures. There is no agreement on the climate sensitivity, or the change in temperature with a doubling of CO2. During the 2020 shutdowns during the COVID10 pandemic, the reductions in anthropogenic emissions were as great as 18% during one month of the seasonal increase in ramp-up in CO2 concentration, with an annual average decrease of about 10%. Yet, there was no obvious decrease in the rate of the annual CO2 increase (~2.5 PPMv/yr) and the peak and average temperatures were about the same for 2019 through 2021. [ https://wattsupwiththat.com/2022/03/22/anthropogenic-co2-and-the-expected-results-from-eliminating-it/ ] The one thing that is notable is that that ramp-up phase of CO2 during El Nino years is steeper and reaches a higher peak than in other years. That is, the CO2 increase seems more sensitive to the temperature than the other way around. Perhaps the claimed cause and effect are backwards? At the very least, the temperature situation is more complex than just being controlled by CO2.

#6359. Euclid's First Data Release: A Stepping Stone to its 3D Map of the Sky

The ESA's Euclid has already teased us with some early results. In the past it's given us a small, 60 square degree of the sky created with a few days of observations. Those images showed individual targets from the Horsehead Nebula to the Perseus cluster of galaxies.

But now we have data from more than one year of the telescope's observations, named DR1-Foundation. DR-1 Foundation covers a sky area as large as about 9,500 full moons, and captures light from more than one billion objects. It took about 13 months to gather all this data.

Understanding dark energy and dark matter means studying as much of the Universe as possible. The effects of dark energy and dark matter are felt at large scales, and by constructing an image of galaxy superclusters and the filaments they exist on, as well as the voids between those filaments, Euclid will lead to new understandings of both dark energy and dark matter.

There are other efforts to map this structure, some dating back decades. DESI, the Dark Energy Survey Instrument, has created the largest 3D map so far, but Euclid's will be larger. Euclid's will have more depth and volume, and since it's space-based while DESI is ground-based, it won't have to deal with atmospheric interference and will have a higher resolution.

This data release is from the Euclid's Wide and Deep Surveys, two surveys that will form the backbone of its 3D map. Even though the data covers 1900 square degrees of the sky, they only represent about 14% of the sky the space telescope will cover in its six-year mission.

This image shows Euclid's Wide Survey in light yellow and its Deep Survey in darker yellow. The Deep Survey are targeted regions within the Wide Survey. They're overlain on a star map from Gaia and a dust map from Planck. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA; ESA/Gaia/DPAC; ESA/Planck Collaboration. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence

The Wide Survey is Euclid's primary campaign and will cover almost half of the galactic sky. It's an imaging and spectrographic survey in visible and near-infrared. It's the telescope's main cosmology survey and will cover a large volume to constrain dark energy and dark matter.

The Deep Survey serves a different purpose. It'll find fainter objects like dwarf galaxies, low-mass galaxies, and tidal tails, as well as high redshift galaxies and quasars. It will serve to calibrate the Wide Survey, and will provide its own, separate science based on its higher density of sources.

Basically, the Wide Durvey provides the greater volume, and the Deep Survey looks more closely and gives more depth. The two combined are needed for a cosmological survey.

Part of the release includes Euclid's image of the core of the Messier 81 galaxy group. This image shows part of that, centered on the Messier 81 galaxy, the group's largest member. The smaller NGC 3077 is on the left, which is also a member, as are many other small members spread across the image. Wispy blue clouds, sometimes called 'galactic cirrus clouds' are also visible. An irregular dwarf galaxy is also visible in diffuse blue to the left. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre and E. Bertin. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence

Euclid also delivered an image of NGC 1291, a stunning ring galaxy about 33 million light years away. It's also called the Golden Eye galaxy, and it has an inner ring and an outer ring, as well as an inner bar. It's inner and outer rings may be because of a merger with a gas-rich galaxy in the past.

This is Euclid's image of NGC 1291, a ring galaxy that faces us head-on. It's about 33 million light years away, and highlights Euclid's power. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre and E. Bertin. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence

Euclid also captured images of Abell 3128. It's 800 million light years away and contains hundreds of individual galaxies. Massive clusters like this one are important probes for dark energy and dark matter, but especially for dark matter. They serve as important gravitational lenses and reveal a lot about where dark matter is concentrated. They can help cosmologists test Lambda-Cold Dark Matter, which is the standard Big Bang theory of the Universe. They also help Euclid calibrate itself.

This is the Abell 3128 cluster, part of the Horologium supercluster. Horologium is home to more than 30 smaller clusters, and Abell 3128 is one of its richest members. Abell holds spirals and ellipticals, and a gravitational lens is in the middle, warping and magnifying the light from a distant background galaxy. The image shows only a fraction of Abell 3128, and also part of another galaxy cluster named ACT-CL J0330-5227; while in reality the two clusters are separated by a huge distance of around 5 billion light-years, they overlap here in our line of sight. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre and E. Bertin. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence

We're only at the appetizer of the visual and scientific feast that Euclid will deliver. By the time it's completed, its 3D map of the sky will be visually entrancing and full of science. It's already discovered a new comet, the most ancient quasar in the Universe, and new images of the Milky Way's over-populated center.

It's off to a strong start and will only get better.

You can explore previous images from Euclid's 2024 Early Release Observations (ERO) and its Quick Euclid data release 1 (Q1) from 2025 at ESA Sky.
