A common antibiotic may be linked to a higher risk of miscarriage and stillbirth when used early in pregnancy, a new study suggests.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Taking doxycycline, a commonly prescribed antibiotic, during the first trimester of pregnancy may increase the risk of pregnancy loss, a new study suggests.

The antibiotic is broad-spectrum, meaning it targets a wide range of bacteria. It's often used to treat acne, respiratory infections and sexually transmitted infections, such as chlamydia and syphilis. Doctors generally avoid prescribing the drug during the second and third trimesters because it belongs to a class of antibiotics that can bind to calcium in developing bones. Animal studies suggest that this may disrupt fetal bone development.

However, evidence on doxycycline's safety during early pregnancy has been mixed and limited. The new study, published Tuesday (Nov. 10) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, provides clearer evidence of a link between doxycycline use in the first trimester and pregnancy loss.

"I would advise physicians to carefully consider the benefit-risk balance when prescribing doxycycline to women who are pregnant or planning a pregnancy," study first author Almut Winterstein, a pharmacist and drug-safety researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science in an email.

Using information from two U.S. insurance databases, the researchers analyzed 224,870 pregnancies in people ages 12 to 55. More than 218,230 of these patients were treated for respiratory tract infections, and over 6,630 were treated for acne, between conception and the end of the first trimester. About 4,385 of the women filled a prescription for doxycycline during that time frame, while the others received an alternative antibiotic.

Among women with respiratory infections, those prescribed doxycycline had a 40% to 54% higher risk of pregnancy loss, compared with those prescribed amoxicillin, another broad-spectrum antibiotic in a different class. The exact level of risk varied between the two databases.

The researchers also compared the doxycycline users against women prescribed macrolides, the class of antibiotics that includes azithromycin (or "Z-Pak"). Again, the doxycycline users saw a higher risk — 39% and 36% higher, respectively.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Among the patients treated for acne, doxycycline users had a 49% higher risk of pregnancy loss in one database than those given the antibiotic clindamycin. In the second database, though, the difference wasn't statistically significant. Winterstein said that may be because there were fewer patients included in that analysis.

Overall, doxycycline was associated with seven to 11 additional pregnancy losses per 100 pregnancies, compared with the other antibiotic options assessed, the researchers reported.

The researchers examined the risk associated with taking various antibiotics in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.

It is not yet clear how the drug might contribute to pregnancy loss. Because the study was observational, it cannot prove that the antibiotic itself caused those losses, which included miscarriages and stillbirths. (Miscarriage is pregnancy loss before 20 weeks of pregnancy, whereas stillbirth refers to pregnancy loss after the 20th week.)

Animal studies hint that doxycycline could interfere with early placental development, potentially making it harder for the placenta to support a growing pregnancy, Luke Grzeskowiak, an associate professor and clinical pharmacist at Flinders University in Australia who was not involved in the study, said in an email.

The study authors also noted in their report that the drug may have direct effects on the developing embryo. But these explanations remain hypothetical; the researchers have not established that either mechanism occurs in humans.

"Pregnancy loss affects around one in four pregnancies and can happen for many reasons," Grzeskowiak noted. Although doxycycline exposure may add to that risk, taking the antibiotic does not necessarily mean pregnancy loss will occur. The available data suggests that it is just one risk factor among many.

Because doxycycline may be prescribed before a pregnancy is recognized, doctors should consider the possibility of pregnancy when prescribing this drug to women of reproductive age, particularly those who are sexually active, Grzeskowiak suggested. That does not mean doctors should avoid prescribing the antibiotic to these women, he emphasized; rather, clinicians should consider pregnancy plans and medical history when choosing a treatment.

In some cases, doxycycline may still be the best option for a severe infection, Winterstein told Live Science, and that infection could itself put a pregnancy at risk. But for less-serious infections, safer alternatives may be available, she said.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Doxycycline and risk for pregnancy loss: A multi-database, multi-indication cohort study. Annals of Internal Medicine. https://doi.org/10.7326/annals-26-01647

#6296. Rock shelter full of old charcoal suggests that Neanderthals burned 24 pounds of wood per day and had a cleaning system

Researchers mapped 640 charcoal fragments from a Neanderthal camp and found two distinct zones of burned wood.

From 2019 to 2022, excavators at Abric Romaní in Capellades, Spain, picked 640 charcoal fragments out of one layer of sediment by hand. They logged the position of every piece.

The largest measured about half an inch (13 millimeters). Together the pieces show where Neanderthals burned wood about 60,000 years ago, and where some of the waste may have gone.

Most of the charcoal lay around hearths near the shelter wall. Smaller patches lay to the south, and the study’s authors say those could be cleared hearth waste, though charcoal alone cannot prove it.

The layer is known as Level Ra. IPHES-CERCA, the Catalan institute that works at the site, calls it a Neanderthal camp specialized in deer hunting.

Amador Romaní discovered the shelter in 1909. The current project began in 1983, and more than 200 hearths have been identified. A wooden club with no clear parallel also came from this site.

Sediment built up fast here, at up to 31 inches (80 centimeters) per thousand years in Level Ra. The team did not sieve it, because sieving could have broken the charcoal. The authors note that hand-picking can bias the sample.

Crews took three-dimensional coordinates for each fragment by hand and with a total station, a surveying instrument. The 2022 season aimed to finish the whole surface of Level Ra.

On Aug. 19 of that year, the crew working in Level Rb lifted bone pieces coated in mineral crust. Specialists identified them as part of a Neanderthal skull.

Irene Cazalla, a restoration technician at IPHES-CERCA, then conserved them. The institute said no Neanderthal remains had turned up in more than 40 years of research at the site.

Tomás Fernández-Iriarte of IPHES-CERCA analyzed the charcoal and wrote the first draft, the paper’s author statement says. The work ran on an Olympus BX41 microscope at up to 500 times magnification.

The team checked its identifications against a collection of modern charred wood kept at the institute. A total of 484 fragments, about 76 percent, came from the Pinus sylvestris type. That group covers three mountain pines with very similar wood.

Those pines live today above about 1,970 feet (600 meters). The authors think their range was probably wider during the Ice Age.

Compression wood showed up in 501 fragments. It is a growth trait tied to stress and is common in branches. The authors say the occupants most likely burned branches, but more tree-ring work is needed to separate them from trunks.

A test on 100 fragments gave an alteration score of 0.55, within the range for rotten wood. The authors read this as a sign that the fuel was deadwood in varying states, moderately rotten, though the test covered only that subsample and not every wood type separately.

The paper cites ethnographic reports on small groups of five or six people in temperate climates. Those groups used up to 24 pounds (11 kilograms) of wood per day.

With that much to haul, the authors think the wood did not travel far. Mountain pines drop a lot of dead wood, so the people in the shelter probably took what lay nearby.

Squares R60 and S59 of the excavation grid held something different. The team found a group of Prunus charcoal there, from a genus represented by only 17 fragments in the whole sample.

The authors listed kindling or the extraction of a specific resource as possible reasons. They also raised fruit gathering, but no fruit or seeds have turned up in this level.

The northern sector held 495 fragments and the southern sector 145. The team mapped them with Kernel Density Estimation, a method that turns scattered points into a density surface.

Squares U53, T57, T54 and U56 were the densest, at 68 to 87 fragments per grid unit. They sit inside a larger spread from U51 to U59, beside the wall and on top of the hearths.

Southern patches reached 51 to 68 fragments per grid unit and overlapped less with hearths. The authors wrote that this pattern “could be explained by discrete hearth-cleaning events.”

Excavators have proposed a dump with burned bones in Level M and drop-and-toss areas in Level O. At Hohle Fels Cave in Germany, analyses found dumped residues from hearths, including some tied to Neanderthal occupations.

Other research has compared Neanderthal and Homo sapiens living spaces and explored early Neanderthal ideas of home.

Water flowed out of the rock walls here and carried minerals over the floor. Mineral inclusions marked 47.6 percent of the fragments.

The team first logged small reddish dots on the charcoal as “spores.” An electron microscope at Rovira i Virgili University showed they were iron deposits that formed later.

Fungal threads called hyphae appeared in 15.7 percent of the pieces. The southern sector had proportionally more of them, along with more mineral alteration.

The authors call the southern patches compatible with displacement or maintenance of hearths, but say their position alone “is insufficient to demonstrate such processes.” Weathering and water could also have shaped them.

Charcoal also cannot show if the fires belonged to one stay or several. One group may have cleared its own hearths. A later group may have come back after a gap and reused old fire spots.

Bones, stone tools and a geoarchaeological study of the hearths still have to be mapped across the same floor. The authors say they are working to upload the data, which is available on request for now.

Level Ra is fully excavated, and its 640 pieces of burned wood now exist as points on a grid.

The full study was published in the Journal of Paleolithic Archaeology.

#6295. Experts who study AI in classrooms ranked what matters most, and it isn’t the technology

Seventy experts from 18 countries rated 15 trends in AI in education, and teaching AI skills to both students and teachers came out at the top of the list.

Most conversations around integrating AI in classrooms focus on flashy new tech, like AI tutors for every student or programs that grade homework overnight.

But according to 70 specialists from 18 different countries, the most critical AI trend for the next three years has nothing to do with buying new software.

Their number one priority is basic AI literacy. Both students and teachers need to be taught what these tools are actually doing and when to question their answers.

Rwitajit Majumdar of Kumamoto University in Japan led the study. Colleagues at Dublin City University, Griffith University, the University of Twente, and universities in Germany and Finland joined him.

It’s an expert survey, not a trial in classrooms, so its answers are the panel’s judgment rather than measured results.

The team used a Delphi process, which is a way of drawing a consensus out of experts in rounds. First, 17 researchers submitted 56 trends in AI and education. The team grouped those into 15 themes, from virtual teaching assistants to automated grading to equal access.

Then 70 people rated each theme from 1 to 10 on three questions. How important will it be for learning and teaching within three years? How much impact will it have? And how hard will it be to get right?

Twenty-six of the raters came from academia and 23 from research. Eight worked in policy, eight were teachers, and five came from industry. Germany and Ireland between them supplied 31 of the 70.

The ratings were then argued over in person. About 130 researchers, policymakers, and practitioners met in Dublin in June 2025 at EDUsummIT, a gathering endorsed by UNESCO.

In small groups, each participant took on the role of a teacher, a developer, a researcher, or a policymaker and argued from that seat.

AI-related competences for learners and educators scored highest on both impact, at 8.57 out of 10, and importance, at 8.64.

The panel rated it moderately hard to achieve, at 7.49. That left it with a positive balance of payoff to difficulty, which the authors read as strong consensus that competence comes first.

Two themes tied for second on impact, at 8.13 each. One was automated assessment and feedback, the AI tutor that marks work and responds to each student. The other was the changing role of the teacher who works alongside such tools.

The two parted ways on difficulty. The experts rated automated feedback a moderate challenge, at 7.13. They rated the teacher’s new role one of the hardest things on the list, at 8.40, which the authors read as high impact and high complexity at once.

Two more themes rounded out the top five. One was whether an AI system can explain itself and be trusted, with an impact score of 7.84. The other was whether every student gets equal access to it, at 7.81.

Both drew challenge scores above 8. The authors read those as barriers in ethics, infrastructure, and policy rather than in the technology itself.

Two cheaper wins also stood out in the panel’s arithmetic. AI-assisted content creation and AI for administrative paperwork both paired high importance with lower difficulty, which the authors flagged as candidates for near-term action.

The themes at the bottom were the most technical ones and were also rated as hard. This made them the least urgent.

Linking AI to classroom devices such as virtual reality headsets scored 5.39 on impact. Software that connects AI to a school’s older data systems scored 5.60, and AI-built maps linking subjects across the curriculum scored 5.90.

Across all 15 themes, the panel’s average importance score was 7.31. That sat slightly above its average impact and challenge scores, but the three didn’t differ in any reliable way.

The experts saw AI in education as roughly as hard as it is promising.

A consensus method can narrow the range of views it reports, the authors wrote. The 70 experts were also a convenience sample rather than a representative one.

Furthermore, no students and no parents took part, though they are the people for whom the systems are built.

The ratings forecast three years ahead. Whether the themes the panel ranked highest turn out to be the ones that matter in real classrooms hasn’t been checked.

The authors called for larger panels in each region, with students and parents included, and for work that goes beyond ranking priorities to testing them.

The full study was published in the journal Computers and Education Open.

Scientists on China's Tiangong space station used a laser trap to cool a clump of atoms to just above absolute zero, setting a new record.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have cooled atoms to the coldest temperature ever recorded, using a laser trap aboard China's Tiangong space station.

Tiangong included an experiment in which atoms were cooled to 10 picokelvins, which is barely above absolute zero, the coldest theoretical temperature possible in physics. Absolute zero is minus 459.67 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 273.15 degrees Celsius) and the threshold at which all particles in an object are believed to stop moving.

Scientists hit the mark using "optical tweezers," known more formally as an optical-dipole trap (ODT), which hold atoms in a laser beam," the scientists reported Nov. 5 in the journal Science.

The team placed 20,000 rubidium atoms in the trap in order to restrict their motion. This reduced motion, along with the weightlessness induced by the low-gravity environment aboard the space station, caused the cloud of atoms to cool to much lower temperatures than are possible on Earth.

The experiment's results could help improve future space-based research, the team said.

"This record-low temperature could stimulate a new generation of ODT-based experiments in quantum simulation and precision measurements in space," the researchers wrote in the paper.

Despite this achievement, it's doubtful that scientists could ever hit absolute zero. One interpretation of the third law of thermodynamics, which looks at how systems behave when they approach absolute zero, is that the particles would always have a bit of entropy (disorder) associated with them, making absolute zero unachievable.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"One version of the third law states that it would require an infinite number of steps to reach absolute zero, which means you will never get there," Saibal Mitra, a professor of physics at Missouri State University, told Live Science in a 2024 interview.

The second law of thermodynamics, which states that entropy always increases, would also be violated if scientists could reach absolute zero, he added. "If you had a heat sink at absolute zero, then you could build a machine that was 100% efficient," Mitra said.

That said, space makes it easier to get close to absolute zero because microgravity allows atoms to "float" and become more efficient at cooling, Science News reported. The researchers took their weightless collection of atoms and created a quantum state of matter known as a Bose-Einstein condensate, in which very cold atoms clump and create a "fifth state" of matter as they behave akin to a single atom.

Tiangong's very cold clump follows similar experiments on the International Space Station that reached 52 picokelvins and from a weightless fall induced by a drop from a tall tower, in which atoms hit 38 picokelvins, Science News added.

#6293. Science to restore speech is moving fast. Here’s what’s next

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Michigan woman uses a brain implant to speak with her neurosurgeon. Efforts to restore speech highlight what’s at stake when we lose opportunities to talk.

Scientists are racing to restore people’s ability to communicate. Powerful AI-based methods to decode speech signals and predict words, along with advances in technology, promise success.

This episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me takes listeners through the breadth of scientific efforts to restore words, emotions and even gestures to people who can’t move or talk.

We’ll hear from Casey Harrell, a man with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis who can no longer talk. A user of today’s technology, Harrell has a unique perspective on what he’d like to see improved for the technology of tomorrow.

And as season two wraps up, listeners will be left with a reminder of the power of a voice: a piece of comedy from Jules Rodriguez, performed with his voice clone in front of a live crowd.

“Being backstage and then seeing him come out, like, roll out his wheelchair, and everybody goes nuts because they’re like, ‘What is going on here? This doesn’t make sense,’” says Jules’ wife, Maria Aleandra Fernandez. “And every time I was like, ‘This is life. This is love. This is passion. What else is there?’ I don’t know that there’s anything else more powerful than what this guy is doing here.”

Laura Sanders: OK, I want to ask who your favorite comedians are and why. Who makes you all laugh?

Jules Rodriguez: Pete Holmes and Mike Birbiglia are some of my favorites.

[Audio] He was just like, I’m a bear, et cetera.

[Audio] The best part of sleep is falling asleep. That’s the only part you’re there for.Jules: Their styles are different, but I have always gravitated towards their authenticity.

Sanders: There’s another comedian who is extra meaningful for Jules: Conan O’Brien.

[Audio] Today is a bit of a different sort of episode. I’ll be talking to Jules and Maria.

Sanders: After MA had reached out, Conan invited the couple onto his podcast, where they connected about comedy. Conan still checks in on Jules every so often.

[Audio] It’s incredible to me that in our conversations, you’re very frank about the pain that you go through, and how intense it is. But you’re also always so positive and funny and, frankly, you give me a lot of [beep]. Which I find to be, well I hate it, by the way, first of all. Oh, get over it, Conan.

Jules: Conan is very special to me. Watching and listening to him helped me disconnect from the harsh reality of my life. And when I got to meet him and chat with him, it meant the world to me.

Maria Aleandra Fernandez: Having the most normal conversation with Conan O’Brien is something I will never get over.

[Audio] So he has a bunch of banked phrases. He’s going to play a few of our favorites. OK. I’m fine. I’m perfectly [beep] fine. [laughter] Come on man, are we doing this or not? Oh my God, oh my God. I’m destroying this marriage. MA: He really is so genuine and like, not only willing to talk to us, but really looks forward to talking. Like, I love talking to you guys. I’m not just doing it to be a nice person, which feels, you know, feels wonderful.

[Audio] You have my love, my respect and we’re thinking about you guys all the time.

Sanders: As you were talking earlier, it made me think about what it means to make somebody laugh and to entertain them, and like how actually very, very special that must be. Just kind of, at its heart, it’s, it is joy and humans connecting. And so, extra special.

MA: That’s the other thing I’ve learned mainly through Jules, about humor and comedy. And who were we watching yesterday? The NPR interview with Dave Chappelle. [Audio] Dave Chappelle says he is very clear about his role as a comedian.

MA: And Dave Chappelle said something that is so spot-on. He said that comedians are how people metabolize things.

[Audio] We’re like the nation’s kidney. We help everyone metabolize not just facts, but feelings around facts, or ideas. And jokes are just a shorthand for all of that.

MA: And I’m also a nerd and I’ve been reading some Greek tragedies and studying about how, you know, that’s also like the artists that help people metabolize feelings and emotions. And when he said that, I was like, that’s exactly it. And that’s what Jules has done.

It’s something that heals. And it’s not even like it’s self-deprecating. It’s not like, oh, let’s make fun. And the way he does it is so smart and genuine, but also not taking himself seriously. It just disarms everything. You’re just like, oh, OK. And that idea of metabolizing the really hard feelings that come around grief, mortality, losing a person, seeing how he’s trapped in his body, but he chooses not to be trapped in that really big way is so profound.

Sanders: Science is iterative. It builds. It may take a wrong turn or two, but overall, it’s moving toward a deeper understanding of our world and of ourselves.

By using their voices, by telling their stories, by telling their jokes, Jules and MA are helping me, and maybe you too, metabolize the pain – and the joy – of living. Welcome to The Deep End, Talk to Me.

[Voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? Hi. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi.

Stavisky: Ultimately, we want people to be in full control of what they’re communicating. This should come from their intent. We haven’t talked much about them, but these implants have their own very successful research history. They’ve allowed people to control a robotic arm, for instance.

Brosler: Most of these devices so far have been designed to restore one function at a time, whereas in reality, frequently people who are paralyzed are missing both the ability to speak and perform body movements. And so in this study, we asked whether a single brain implant could be used to decode both speech and movement at the same time.

Sanders: It turns out, it could. She and her colleagues were able to decode gestures for communication — things like thumbs up, or a head nodding yes — and words. This combo approach is a more natural way of getting a point across.

Brosler: We naturally use gestures alongside our speech. So for example, some gestures can substitute for speech entirely, like nodding yes, shaking your head no, waving, shrugging, giving a thumbs up. But they can also add or change the meaning of what we’re saying. So for example, if you say maybe combined with nod head yes, that has a very different, you know, meaning than if you say maybe and shrug or shake your head no.

Sanders: My kids know that a slow maybe with a skeptical eyebrow raise is much closer to a no than my fast upbeat maybe with a little head nod. There is so much subtext in our body language.

Brosler: So I think of, you know, gestures and body movements as an additional communication channel that can work together with speech to add expressivity to what we’re trying to say.

Sanders: In the study, the output was a digital avatar who looked like the person. Success looked like the avatar moving and getting the word right.

Brosler: And the idea is that we enable the participants to use speech and gestures alone or together. So in theory, someone could say hello while waving.

Sanders: The researchers started simple, with just a few phrases — hello, bye, good idea, how’s it going, let’s go — and just a few gestures, like a shrug or a point, a fist pump, thumbs up.

Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

Sanders: The sheer number of different approaches to restoring communication is a sign that this neurotechnology is coming fast. Here’s Willsey.

Willsey: I think it’s good. There’s a lot of players that are entering into the field that have a variety of different ideas where they can run the clinical trials and see how these different devices stack up.

Sanders: There are lots of reasons to be optimistic about the future here, and it’s a future that isn’t even that far off. Here’s David Brandman, one of the researchers at UC Davis who works with Casey. He’s also the neurosurgeon who implanted Casey’s device.

Brandman: I think I’m about five years away from being able to meet a patient with ALS and having the following conversation, and saying, you know, Ms. Smith, I’m sorry you’ve been diagnosed with ALS. I don’t have a cure for you, but I do have a device that I can implant that can help you communicate despite facing a future of paralysis. It’s a device that would be implanted. It’s fully wirelessly. It’s cosmetically invisible, and you’d be able to use it to communicate your needs and have a meaningful conversation with friends and family. So I think that kind of conversation is about five to 10 years away.

Sanders: It’s a beautiful vision. When you’ve been a reporter as long as I have, you’re skeptical when scientists say something big is just five to 10 years away. But in this case, I see it.

It’s easy to get drawn into the technical details here. Different types of implants, the decoding processes, AI-powered voice clones and what they can do and can’t do — what they should do and shouldn’t do. But if you step back and really look, you’ll see that this research is all propelled by a very simple and powerful fact: The human voice is too important to lose.

Casey: What does my voice mean to me? It means so much. I think it is the most important thing that I have lost in this whole disease.

Sanders: So now we are here, in this moment, as Jules would say, right here, right now. And right now, the human voice is shifting and changing, expanding in ways that were completely unthinkable even just a few years ago. The future of the human voice and its many replicas is anybody’s guess.

Sanders: In one of Jules’ comedy sets, the one he did in November of 2024, he wheels out onto the stage as the song “Walking on Sunshine” plays.

As the crowd settles and finishes their clapping and woo-ing, Jules pauses. You can’t see this, but he wiggles his eyebrows — a lot. The crowd goes crazy every time. He hasn’t said a single word yet. After another pause, he deadpans with his voice clone: “That is all the time I have. My Make-A-Wish covered only a few minutes. Goodnight, everybody.”

And with that, Jules takes control and he’s off on a tear, ripping through stories of a weatherman who seems too happy about standing out in hurricanes, the exquisite guilt trips lovingly crafted by his Cuban parents, and the indignities of having body parts shaved with his sister right there in the room. Jules has the audience laughing so hard. It’s magnificent.

MA: And being backstage and then seeing him come out, like roll out in his wheelchair and everybody go nuts because they’re like, what is going on here? Like, this doesn’t make sense. And every time I was like, this is like life. This is love. This is passion. This is like, what else is there? Like, I don’t know that there’s anything else more powerful than what this guy is doing here and what I can help him do.

Sanders: I get what MA meant when she said that comedy is something that heals. When his set actually does come to a close, he tells the audience. [Audio] Now you have to watch me slowly get off this stage. Goodnight, everybody.

Sanders: It’s hilarious. It’s happy. It’s sad. It’s perfect.

This is The Deep End, Talk to Me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast, tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot. Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org.

#6292. Scientists learn why a sensitive part of our DNA is actually a built-in shield against the sun

Under early-Earth ultraviolet light, thymine broke faster than uracil but steered the damage toward lesions that can be undone.

Before Earth had an ozone layer to block the sun, early life was constantly blasted by intense ultraviolet light. Because of this, scientists were puzzled by why DNA evolved using a chemical building block called thymine. It takes significantly more UV damage than similar molecules.

Thymine initially looked like a big evolutionary mistake. But new measurements reveal a clever survival trick.

The specific damage thymine takes from UV light is incredibly easy to undo. Instead of being a weak point, thymine actually takes the hit so the rest of the DNA stays safe.

Peter Rentzepis and two members of his lab at Texas A&M University, Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar, exposed both letters to the same ultraviolet light and tracked what broke.

Thymine fell apart faster overall, but it formed the permanent kind of lesion more slowly than uracil did.

“We found that thymine tends to direct UV damage into a more reversible form,” said Khosh Abady, a research assistant in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering.

He added that this suggests early genetic molecules may have survived intense sunlight by controlling the damage and making it easier to repair, not by avoiding the damage.

RNA and DNA each spell their code with four letters, and three are shared. RNA uses uracil. DNA uses thymine, which is uracil with one small carbon group attached.

Thymine absorbs ultraviolet light most strongly at 265 nanometers, and uracil at 259. A six-nanometer shift matters on a planet with no ozone layer.

Models of the early Sun suggest the light reaching the surface was about 2.5 times more intense at thymine’s peak than at uracil’s. Thymine’s absorption band is also about 9 percent wider.

On paper, life swapped in the letter that catches more of the most damaging light.

The team dissolved each letter in water and froze the solutions at 5°F (-15°C) in quartz cells. Then they shone a narrow ultraviolet LED on them at 265 nanometers.

Freezing pushes the molecules out of the growing ice into crowded pockets, which mimics how letters sit side by side in a strand, where the main lesions form between neighbors.

Over an hour of exposure, the team tracked three things. They measured how much light the molecules absorbed and how much they glowed.

They also recorded each sample’s Raman spectrum, a fingerprint of chemical bonds that shifts as bonds break and form.

Judged by how fast its absorption faded, thymine degraded in ultraviolet light nearly three times as fast as uracil. It also glowed about 4.5 times more brightly.

The team reads the glow as a sign that excited thymine lingers longer before settling down, which leaves more time for reactions.

Ultraviolet light produces two main lesions between neighboring letters. In one, two letters lock together in a small ring. The team classifies this lesion as reversible, since it can come apart again without enzymes.

In the other, the letters bond in a way that rearranges them for good.

Thymine formed the permanent kind at a rate of 1.56 per minute in the team’s fitted curves, against 2.04 for uracil. So thymine took more damage but steered it toward the repairable kind.

The authors wrote that the letters appear to have been selected to keep damage confined and reversible, not to avoid it. Repair enzymes did not yet exist.

“In that sense, thymine may have acted as a molecular sunscreen, absorbing harmful UV energy and keeping the damage confined to the genetic bases rather than allowing it to harm more vulnerable parts of the molecule,” Khosh Abady said.

The experiment used single letters packed in ice, not strands of DNA or RNA in water. The authors wrote that the frozen setup does not capture the full chemistry of real genetic molecules.

The 2.5-fold difference in early sunlight is a modeled figure that depends on the atmosphere assumed.

A separate test, published this month, found that life’s letters were not consistently tougher under ultraviolet light than alternatives that life does not use. So the sunscreen idea is one explanation among several.

There is also a later, better-known reason for thymine. Cytosine, another DNA letter, slowly decays into uracil on its own, and a cell that used uracil as a normal letter could not tell that mistake from the real thing.

That defense needs repair enzymes, so the authors place it after the sunlight pressure, as a reinforcement rather than the origin.

The measured signatures of thymine and uracil, before and after damage, have a second use.

The team wrote that the data could help read ultraviolet damage in whole cells, which would show whether a water-treatment lamp has actually inactivated microbes.

Next, the lab plans to look earlier in the story. The open question is what brought the letters together in the first place, and whether some arrived on meteorites rather than forming on Earth.

The full study was published in the journal PNAS.

#6291. New study shows that a home video game using brain stimulation electrodes can help depression, but a fake version worked just as well, confusing scientists

People with depression used a brain stimulation kit at home for six weeks, but a switched-off sham with a decoy game worked just as well.

Strap on a cap wired to a small box, play a video game on a tablet for half an hour, and repeat every weekday for six weeks. Adults with major depression who applied that brain stimulation at home got better.

So did the adults whose cap switched itself off after a few seconds and whose game was a look-alike with the training taken out.

The cap carried a weak electric current through the scalp, a low-cost form of brain stimulation that researchers are testing for home use. The video game was built to exercise attention, memory and self-control.

Together they were no more effective than the fake pair, and the authors wrote that the combination isn’t ready for clinics in its current form.

What the trial did show is that people with depression can run a treatment like this at home, which was the question the trial was built to answer first.

Mor Nahum of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem led the trial, called DiSCoVeR. In an interview with Earth.com, she said the improvement on both sides was the first of two surprises.

“Substantial improvement in control groups is in fact well known in depression research, including in medication trials, but it is still striking to see it so clearly in a carefully matched control condition,” Nahum said.

The 109 people in the final analysis were between 18 and 65 years, and had major depression that had lasted between a month and five years.

They were recruited at Hadassah Medical Center in Jerusalem, LMU Munich and Riga Stradins University. Most were already taking antidepressants on a steady dose, and about four in ten were in talk therapy, which the trial allowed.

Each person had up to five sessions in the clinic to learn the kit, then took it home. Software guided the placement of the electrodes on the scalp before each session. The target was 30 sessions of 30 minutes, on weekdays, over six weeks.

Half the group, chosen at random, got the real current and a game that got harder as players got better. The other half got a sham: a cap that ramped up and then stopped, plus a slower game with the same look and none of the training exercises.

Neither the participants nor the doctors scoring their symptoms knew who had which.

Of the 109, 86 finished at least 20 sessions, which cleared the bar the researchers had set in advance: a majority finishing at least 20. Participants completed nearly 2,500 sessions across the three countries.

Side effects were about as common in both groups. Two people in the active group were hospitalized, one with suicidal thoughts and one with worsening depression, and both cases were judged unlikely to be related to the treatment.

Symptoms were scored on a scale from 0 to 60, and the average at the start was about 25. After six weeks, the active group had dropped 7.3 points and the sham group 8.2. A gap that small could easily be chance, and it was no different a month later.

On one well-being questionnaire, the sham group improved more. People in the active group also reported feeling more pressure during their sessions in the last two weeks, and less confident in their own performance.

Researchers asked participants at week one and week six which group they thought they were in. In the first week, 57 percent of the active group guessed right and 35 percent of the sham group did.

By the end, the two groups guessed about equally well, at 59 and 65 percent respectively. Those who believed they were in the sham group improved less than the others, whichever group they were really in.

Nahum told Earth.com that about a quarter of participants consistently held that belief, and that the gap in their scores appeared early.

She called it an exploratory finding. Nahum said the team cannot yet tell whether low expectations held people back or whether people who were not improving concluded they must be on the sham.

“But it suggests that what patients believe about their treatment may matter a great deal,” she said.

Because the team always paired the real current and the real game, the trial can’t say what either one does alone. Nahum said the two may even have interfered with each other, given the extra pressure the active group reported.

The paper advises a four-way design next time: current alone, game alone, both, and neither.

Other recent trials found the same. Pairing this kind of brain stimulation with psychotherapy or with a digital program added no benefit either. A 2025 review concluded that its effects on depression are small and inconsistent.

Follow-up here stopped at ten weeks, so lasting effects are unknown. And the researchers can’t rule out that playing a game every day had effects of its own, such as relaxation.

Nahum and several co-authors have applied for a patent for the game used in the active arm.

Asked by Earth.com what someone curious about home brain stimulation should take from the trial, Nahum drew a line between the home setup and the shop shelf.

“I would strongly advise against buying devices online and self-treating,” she said. Trial participants were trained in the clinic and monitored remotely, she said, and anyone struggling with depression should first talk to a mental health professional.

What drove the improvement in both groups is the open question. Nahum listed the candidates: the stimulation, the training, expectations, engagement, ongoing care, or simply the structure of returning to a treatment every day.

Next, she wants to measure expectations before treatment starts and test whether they predict who improves. The bigger problem, in her view, is the average itself.

“Depression is very heterogeneous, and an average result can hide people who respond well alongside others who don’t,” she said.

The markers that would sort patients that way, clinical, cognitive or brain-based, are what she plans to look for next.

The full study was published in the journal JAMA Network Open.

Over 300 Live Science readers responded to a recent poll about whether they'd train themselves to lucid dream if they could.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Lucid dreaming describes when you realize you're in a dream as it's unfolding. Sometimes, people can control the content of their dreams from this state of awareness.

Recently, researchers claimed that they found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they were awake. Following the release of that study, Live Science asked its readers whether they would learn to lucid dream if they could.

Over 300 readers weighed in, with 77% saying "Yes, I'd want to try to control my dreams." Additionally, 17% of respondents said "No, I already lucid dream enough without training," 3% said "No, I don't see the point," and the final 3% said they weren't sure.

In the comments, one reader shared that they'd once experimented with hypnagogic napping, a technique famously used by Thomas Edison and Salvador Dalí in which the famous luminaries would wake themselves up just as they were drifting to sleep. Edison claimed that this helped him access a creative sweet spot at the edge of sleep and wakefulness.

"When I was experimenting with the hypnagogic state (using the Edison method) I started having spontaneous lucid dreams," the reader wrote. "I can confidently say, that there were some of the most profound experiences of my life, so the answer is definitely yes."

Another reader reported having lucid dreams "about once or twice a year," adding that they typically wake up shortly after realizing it's a dream. "My most recent one was of my recently deceased wife. I became very sad when I realized she wasn't supposed to be there," the reader wrote. "I hugged her and told her I don't want to be without her. She replied that I could live a long life if I took care of myself (This was a very typical response from her...lol). I feel very blessed to have had that dream."

Other readers chimed in on Facebook. "Already have it [lucid dreaming], but if I didn't I would certainly practice to do so," one wrote. "Hell yes," another said, in response to the idea of training themselves to lucid dream.

Other readers noted that they already lucid dream quite often or that they can consistently control their dreams, with one even saying that all of their dreams are lucid. Another said, "Some nights I interrupt it [my dream] like Monty Python — 'Too silly!' and start over."

But while one person compared lucid dreaming to "writing and directing your own movie," another noted that "lucid dreams can be boring, repetitive, annoying." So while many people would practice lucid dreaming if they could, not everyone sees the appeal.

#6289. Light is hard to block from every direction. This physicist found a way

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Mandana Tadayon, Anna Mattson and Emily Conover

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Physicist Stefano Martiniani has designed an entirely new class of materials that blurs the line between order and chaos. Called gyromorphs, these metamaterials rely on crystal-like geometric structure and liquidlike randomness to block light from penetrating at any angle.

Physicists thought, structurally speaking, that they could not create such hybrid materials. “But this is evidence that you can, under certain constraints,” says Martiniani, of New York University. He likens the gyromorphs’ disorderliness to a crowd of people. You could see through the crowd if individuals stood still in straight lines, but not if they are clustered together in random groups. But there’s order too: From anywhere you stand in a gyromorph crowd, you’ll see a ring of people at a given distance.

Gyromorphs are a type of metamaterial, a substance with a structure designed to give it properties not found in naturally occurring materials. Metamaterials can control light, sound or other waves, and are often used in smartphones, medical imaging and computers. Martiniani says gyromorphs could be used to make more energy-efficient optical computers, which use light to process and store data.

To design a gyromorph, Martiniani needed to find a way to achieve the perfect structural balance. He turned to FReSCo, a program his lab created that designs molecular structures to meet researchers’ specifications, for help. “We had an algorithm, we gave it an objective, and then it was able to solve that objective, finding a solution that we were not expecting,” he says. “That is the best kind of discovery.”

#6288. An Apollo astronaut flew tree seeds around the Moon, but no one kept track of where the trees were planted when they returned to Earth

Apollo 14 carried tree seeds around the Moon in 1971, creating Moon Trees across America. Artemis I launched a new generation of seeds in 2022.

In 1971, Apollo 14 command module pilot Stuart Roosa carried tree seeds in his personal kit while he orbited the Moon. The seeds came from five species: loblolly pine, sycamore, sweetgum, redwood and Douglas fir.

Back on Earth, the seeds grew into seedlings that were later planted across the United States. Yet no list was ever kept of where the trees ended up.

Since 1996, a NASA scientist has kept a list of the surviving trees, built from reports sent in by the public. In 2022, a new batch of tree seeds flew around the Moon on Artemis I.

Roosa was born in Durango, Colorado, in 1933. In the early 1950s, he worked for the Forest Service as a smokejumper, a firefighter who parachutes in to fight forest fires.

Ed Cliff, then chief of the Forest Service, knew Roosa from his smokejumping days and contacted him about bringing seeds into space. Stan Krugman of the Forest Service was put in charge of the project and selected the seeds.

Roosa carried “possibly 2,000 or more seeds” in a canister, according to NASA’s history office.

After the return to Earth, the seed bags burst open during decontamination. The seeds were scattered around the chamber and exposed to vacuum, and it was thought they might not survive.

A first attempt to germinate some of the seeds in Houston worked, but the seedlings did not survive long because the facilities there were inadequate.

A year later, the remaining seeds went to Forest Service stations in Gulfport, Mississippi, and Placerville, California, which received the redwoods and Douglas firs. Many of the seeds, and later cuttings, grew into viable seedlings.

Most of the seedlings were given to state forestry organizations in 1975 and 1976, to be planted as part of the nation’s bicentennial celebration. They went to sites reportedly in 40 different states.

A loblolly pine was planted at the White House on January 19, 1977. That tree is no longer alive.

A sycamore was planted at the visitor center of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland on June 9, 1977. It is still growing there.

Others went to the International Forest of Friendship and to Washington Square in Philadelphia, where the tree has since died. A few were planted abroad, including in Brazil and Switzerland.

After more than 40 years, NASA reports, there is “no discernable difference” between Moon trees and trees grown from seeds that stayed on Earth.

The list began after Joan Goble, a third-grade teacher in Indiana, asked NASA for information about the trees in 1996.

Her request led Dr. David R. Williams, now a retired curator at NASA’s National Space Science Data Center, to start a list of Moon trees. Dozens of people have since sent in information about others.

The list sorts the trees into living, status unknown and no longer alive. Survivors include trees at the Indiana Statehouse, the Alabama State Capitol in Montgomery and Capitol Park in Sacramento.

Second-generation trees, grown from seeds or cuttings of mature Moon trees, are also growing around the world. Roosa’s daughter, Rosemary Roosa, has promoted planting them.

Artemis I launched on November 16, 2022, and its Orion spacecraft splashed down on December 11. Nearly 2,000 tree seeds flew on board, according to a 2023 NASA announcement.

The seeds traveled about 40,000 miles (64,000 kilometers) beyond the Moon and about 270,000 miles (435,000 kilometers) from Earth. They came from sycamores, sweetgums, Douglas firs, loblolly pines and giant sequoias.

Kasten Dumroese is a research plant physiologist and national nursery specialist with the Forest Service’s Rocky Mountain Research Station.

“Four of the five species flown on the original Moon Trees mission were onboard again,” Dumroese said.

Before the flight, the Forest Service X-rayed the seeds to check their internal tissue. The scans were repeated after the flight to look for any changes caused by spaceflight.

“We made sure the seeds were filled with good tissue before we sent them up,” said Kayla Herriman, a seed extractory manager with the Forest Service in Bend, Oregon.

NASA’s call for applications, which closed on October 6, 2023, drew more than 1,000 submissions from organizations. NASA scheduled distribution in four planting cycles, from spring 2024 through fall 2025.

The first batch went to almost 50 institutions across the contiguous United States, NASA said when it announced the first recipients in April 2024.

On June 4, 2024, a sweetgum seedling was planted on the U.S. Capitol grounds, with the crew of Artemis II in attendance.

The seedling had left the Forest Service’s Moscow Forest Science Laboratory while dormant and spent three months at the U.S. Botanic Garden before the ceremony.

“I actually feel a little jealous, because that little sweetgum has been to the moon, and it has come back,” said Reid Wiseman, the Artemis II commander.

#6287. The Beachy Bungalow in La Jolla That Let Me Cosplay as a California Surfer

As a travel editor, people are always shocked when I tell them I’ve only been to California once. Especially when I tell them that my one trip was to Napa—a blur of rolling hills and full-bodied Cabernets. There are so many sunny cities I’ve dreamed of visiting in the Golden State, but the world is big, and the flights from NYC are long. This fall, I finally got the push I needed to see more of America's most populous state: One of my dearest friends decided to get married in San Diego. My husband and I booked our plane tickets without blinking an eye, eager to see two fabulous people tie the knot and experience some excellent beaches, sunsets, and burritos along the way.

While deciding where to hunker down during our visit, I couldn’t get La Jolla out of my mind. A vibey little surf town about 14 miles north of downtown San Diego, it seemed like the perfect base—just a short drive from the wedding venue in Rancho Santa Fe, and boasting plenty of iconic restaurants (the Marine Room!) and attractions (the sea lions!). When I found Hamilton I, an adorable bungalow just three blocks from the beach, available for rent through Homes & Villas by Marriott Bonvoy, it sealed the deal. I nabbed it for three nights.

Check Availability at Homes & Villas by Marriott Bonvoy

Tucked into a long, quiet side street off of one of La Jolla’s main roads, I knew Hamilton I would do us just fine from the moment our Uber dropped us off. We had spent the first two days of our trip in downtown San Diego, getting our fill of the city; the energy in this neighborhood was just different. Imagine the shaka sign, but as a feeling. We walked past Hamilton II, the bungalow’s sister property, before reaching our home's front door, where a keypad granted us entrance. The first thing I noticed upon stepping inside was the sun-dappled living room, with its massive TV and walls bursting with beachy-cool art. The next was the basket of snacks in the kitchen left by the hosts—a huge green flag in my book.

Happy to have some space to spread out, my husband and I dropped our suitcases and toured the rest of the home, which has three small bedrooms (two kings, one queen), two bathrooms, a washer and dryer (huge news for us city folk), and a dining nook with a long oval table and eight rattan chairs. We chose to sleep in the largest of the three bedrooms, the only one with an en suite bathroom, and used the other two bedrooms as our closets. As I mentioned, the bedrooms aren’t huge and share walls at the back of the bungalow, so the property is probably best suited to close groups of friends or families with kids.

The biggest draw of the home is the backyard, accessible via a sliding door in the living room. You come to California for the sunshine, and the compact but well-designed outdoor space allows guests plenty of opportunities to soak up every last ray. Depending on the time of day, you can bounce between a smattering of adjustable lounge chairs, a small dipping pool, an outdoor dining table next to a barbecue, and a lounge area with a firepit. Despite backing onto a busy street, the backyard feels like a little oasis, thanks in part to the walls of greenery bordering the space.

Over the course of our three days at Hamilton I, my husband and I hit most of La Jolla’s most popular attractions, either by foot or via a quick Uber ride. We managed to dip our toes in the salty sea, kayak over to La Jolla Cove, wander through nearby Coronado, peruse the shops in La Jolla Village, eat a shocking amount of Mexican food, attend a magazine-worthy wedding, and so much more in so little time, returning to the bungalow to sleep peacefully each night. Every amenity we could have needed had already been thought of by the host, from extra blankets and fans to strong Wi-Fi and water pressure. We also had 24/7 access to a dedicated hospitality manager, who sent a couple of check-in texts throughout our stay to make sure everything was hunky-dory (it was).

Every morning, we’d make coffee in the kitchen or pick it up from a nearby café, passing longboarders and surfboard-toters along the way, then sit out in the backyard to wake ourselves up with the ultimate duo: caffeine and vitamin D. Having an entire home to call our own was such a treat, and cosplaying as a laid-back surfer couple, if only for a few days, was a welcome salve for our New York City–dwelling souls. I mean, who can be mad when you have the beach a few blocks away and laundry in-unit?

By the end of our stay, it was clear to us why our friends decided to get married in San Diego, and why it has become an increasingly popular travel destination as of late: Good vibes go a long way, and this part of California has them in spades. Also, the burritos are as good as people say. I’ll be back for more adventures in the Golden State—and I’ll be looking for a home away from home just like Hamilton I when that time comes.

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

A new AI model, called Brain-IT, can transform brain scans into images and reverse the process, turning images into what they'd look like as brain activity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An artificial intelligence (AI) tool can use brain scans to recreate the images people looked at with eerie accuracy.

The system, called Brain-IT, uses data from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to measure activity in the visual cortex, the part of the brain that processes visual input. A computer model then predicts both the broad layout of an image and high-level information about its content. It then passes those predictions to an AI image generator, researchers explained in a study uploaded to the preprint database arXiv. The research was presented at the ICLR 2026 conference, held April 23-25, and publicized by its authors in September.

Brain-IT builds on an approach called the Universal Brain Encoder. That model begins with an image and then predicts the fMRI response that would be expected in individual "voxels" ‪—‬ small 3D units ‪—‬ in a brain scan.

"The key idea is that every voxel, a tiny cube of brain tissue, gets its own learned vector that captures what it cares about in images," said study first author Roman Beliy, a doctoral candidate in the Department of Computer Science and Applied Mathematics at the Weizmann Institute of Science in Israel.

Some voxels may be tuned to relatively simple elements of an image, such as edges, textures or locations. Others might be responding to higher-level abstract categories, like faces, bodies or scenes.

Traditional image-to-fMRI systems have generally been custom trained for each participant and dataset. The Universal Brain Encoder is more flexible. It learns from data from multiple people and can transfer information across participants, datasets or different MRI systems with varying magnetic-field strengths, according to the study.

A voxel can determine which parts of an image are relevant to it based on its learned profile, essentially saying, "I recognize edges. Which parts of this image are edges?"

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The Universal Brain Encoder starts with an image and predicts brain activity; Brain-IT starts with measured brain activity and reconstructs the image the person saw. In other words,it asks "based on this brain activity, what was the subject looking at?". It sorts thousands of tiny brain-scan measurements from the visual cortex into 128 groups based on the kinds of visual information they tend to carry.

The system then lets those groups share clues with one another, allowing it to combine, for example, information about a scene's shape, color and possible objects, to build a more complete picture of the image, Beliy explained.

The decoder produces two types of visual predictions. One captures semantic information ‪—‬ the features associated with what is likely in a scene; for an image of a dog standing in grass, for instance, this would include things like the features of a dog and an outdoor, grassy setting. The other captures structural information, like the broad visual layout or how forms are arranged.

In the above example, this would be aspects like the outline of the dog or where it was positioned in the frame. The structural prediction gives the generator a starting point for the image, rather than beginning from pure noise, while the semantic info guides an image generator that removes the remaining static until the image emerges.

Although the new tool can recreate what people see, it can't reproduce memories or imagined scenes.

"We're not reading people's thoughts," study co-author Michal Irani, a computer scientist at the Weizmann Institute of Science, told Live Science. "The images we do manage to recover from fMRI require people's cooperation and full intended collaboration."

The original image of a baseball game (left) and the reconstruction (right) generated by the Brain-IT AI model based on the brain activity of a person viewing the image.

Brain-IT's synthetic images were compared with the images that participants saw. Brain-IT surpassed prior leading methods on standard objective reconstruction metrics and produced more faithful results, the study authors wrote. The system shined when limited fMRI data from a new participant was available, with just one hour of data from a new participant producing results as accurately as earlier approaches that had been trained on 40 hours of recordings.

A high-scoring or realistic-looking output should not be mistaken for a perfect copy of what someone saw, however.

In the final stage of processing, the system uses an off-the-shelf diffusion generator trained on massive numbers of images. Models like this generate plausible images and can smooth textures, sharpen facial features or fill in missing details.

Beliy said this "beautification" can make reconstructions more polished and convincing and introduce details that don't necessarily come from the brain data itself. In other words, the scan constrains the generated picture, but the AI model supplies some of its realism from learned patterns in photographs.

While the new system produces impressive results for seen images, it can't be used to reconstruct an imagined or remembered image.

"Brain-IT relies on how the brain processes a seen image," Irani said. "Information flows from the eyes to the primary visual cortex and onward through a series of visual areas that recognize objects and scenes."

In a controlled experiment, researchers also know precisely which image was shown, giving the model a target during training and evaluation. In contrast, memories and imagined images do not offer the same clean reference. They can be vague and shaped by brain networks involved in memory and thought, with only partial and weaker reactivation of visual regions, Irani said. One limitation that would prevent this technology from being widely deployed is that the only way to get reliable results is from fMRI scanning, which is cumbersome and expensive. The team is currently experimenting with using easier-to-collect electroencephalogram (EEG) data, which is obtained via electrodes on the head, but that work is in the very preliminary stages, according to Irani.

The new system could help brain researchers better understand which visual information is represented in different brain regions, how those regions interact and how individuals’ patterns differ. Such tools could eventually reveal differences in visual processing that could help clinicians spot neurological, neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions.

"There are numerous useful medical applications which we are currently striving toward," Irani said. "These include using our brain encoder/decoder to detect and analyze brain disorders such as MS, PTSD, autism and psychiatric disorders."

Beliy, R., Zalcher, A., Kogman, J., Wasserman, N., & Irani, M. (2025, October 29). Brain-IT: Image Reconstruction from fMRI via Brain-Interaction Transformer. arXiv.org. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.25976

#6285. This magic mushroom can kill

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hallucinogens and poisons have never been found in the same mushroom — until now

Meet the dark magic mushroom, Galerina indica. The tiny fungus makes both a hallucinogen and a deadly toxin.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

People who eat this tiny magic mushroom may hit a lethal low instead of getting high.

The fungus makes hallucinogenic psilocybin and deadly amatoxin, researchers report November 11 in Current Biology. Dubbed “dark magic mushrooms,” it is the first species of fungus discovered to make both types of compounds.

Chemist and fungal biologist Andrew Kunik found the dark magic mushroom in 2025 growing on a decaying moss-covered palm trunk in a central Florida wetland. Kunik, who was then doing post-baccalaureate research in the lab of fungal biologist Matthew Smith at the University of Florida in Gainesville, identified the mini mushroom as Galerina indica.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

That species had not been reported in Florida before, Kunik says. “It’s quite rare and unusual.” He also found two other new related species, tagged with the placeholder names Galerina species 1 and Galerina species 2.

Other researchers had previously described G. indica’s appearance and found DNA signatures that distinguish the fungus from related species. But no one had cataloged the mushroom’s complete chemical or genetic makeup.

Related Galerina species make amatoxins, deadly chemicals that can kill in even tiny amounts and are found in death cap mushrooms and other species. Kunik and colleagues looked for those toxins in G. indica and the two other new Galerina species. G. indica makes a previously undiscovered form of amatoxin the team is calling alpha-proamanitin, the chemical analysis revealed.

The small mushroom also had blue bruises, a clue that it might make psilocybin, a psychedelic chemical being tested as a treatment for mental health disorders. Fungi usually make either amatoxin or psilocybin. Not both. Galerina species 1 also makes psilocybin but doesn’t make amatoxin, and species 2 makes neither.

“This finding shows that there’s a lot more diversity in [fungal] chemistry and the ways that they’re combined than we had really thought about,” says Anne Pringle, a mycologist at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who was not involved in the work.

Discovering these dual compounds in one mushroom was both exciting and required further analysis to confirm, Kunik says. “Surprising discoveries require great depth of evidence,” he says.

A complete workup of the mushroom’s DNA revealed genes for producing both types of chemicals. Ancestors of these dark magic mushrooms probably picked up those genes by swapping DNA with other species. Such DNA swapping, called horizontal gene transfer, is one way that organisms can quickly evolve new traits, like when bacteria exchange antibiotic resistance genes with unrelated species.

Ancestors of G. indica and its relatives probably acquired amatoxin genes early on. Those toxins are made by many of G. indica’s cousins, which indicates that amatoxins are probably heirlooms passed down from common ancestors. Ancestors of species 1 and species 2 seem to have dropped the amatoxin genes at some point since they no longer make the compounds.

The two psilocybin-producing species may have independently obtained the psychedelic genes in separate DNA swap meets, or a common ancestor may have picked up the genes and then passed them down to G. indica and species 1. There’s not enough known about the fungi’s family tree to sort out which scenario is correct.

And there’s another unsolved evolutionary mystery, Pringle says. “We still don’t know why mushrooms are poisonous.” Many scientists think it is for defending against predators, but hard evidence is lacking, she says.

“Can I eat it?” is often the first question people ask when finding a new mushroom, Pringle says. “I’m always so uncomfortable with that question and that conversation. And this paper confirms that, in fact, you should be uncomfortable.” After all, eating these dark magic mushrooms could send people tripping into the grave.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

A.R. Kunik, et al. The ‘‘dark magic mushroom’’ co-produces amatoxins and psilocybin. Current Biology. 2026. doi: 10.1016/j.cub.2026.10.041

Tina Hesman Saey is the senior staff writer and reports on molecular biology. She has a Ph.D. in molecular genetics from Washington University in St. Louis and a master’s degree in science journalism from Boston University.

A tiny asteroid entered Earth's orbit in April and is expected to leave in January. Meet the minimoon 2026 QQ8.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Earth and its moon will have company this holiday season. In April, our planet picked up a passing "minimoon," pulling the space rock into a temporary orbit, astronomers have confirmed.

The object, dubbed 2026 QQ8, was first observed by Hungarian researcher Krisztián Sárneczky in August. It was officially reported by the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Minor Planet Center — the body that logs and confirms new solar system objects — on Oct. 29. This extraterrestrial traveler is expected to stick around until January 2027, extending its stay through the holidays before breaking free of our planet's influence.

2026 QQ8 is tiny — only about 6 feet (2 meters) across, according to the IAU. If it got too close to Earth, it would likely burn up in our planet's atmosphere. However, researchers don't think there is much chance of that happening, since 2026 QQ8 is currently orbiting at around 1.5 times the average distance of the moon.

2026 QQ8 takes 359 days — almost a full Earth year — to orbit the sun. It comes close to our planet every 10 years or so. This minimoon is classified as an Aten asteroid; this population of space rocks occasionally cross into Earth's orbit and have semimajor axes smaller than Earth's, meaning they typically orbit closer to the sun than our planet does. Large Aten asteroids are considered the most dangerous type of asteroid, as they can easily get lost in the sun's glare before speeding toward Earth — but, again, our new mini companion is far too small to pose a threat.

2026 QQ8 is not the first minimoon discovered circling Earth. That distinction belongs to 1991 VG, which was around 30 feet (10 meters) in diameter when it was detected in November 1991. Astronomers now think Earth grabs minimoons pretty frequently; we are likely to have at least one at any given time. Most of the space rocks stay around for less than a year, although a handful may remain in Earth's gravitational pull for decades.

New telescopes ‪are expected to help researchers spot more minimoons as they enter and leave Earth's orbit. These include the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which began operation earlier this year. The Rubin observatory, which takes a full scan of the entire Southern Hemisphere sky every few days, has already spotted what may be a new dwarf planet lurking in the outer solar system, as well as a new satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. Over its planned 10-year mission, the observatory is expected to detect millions of previously unknown moving objects in space.
