#6260. 25 Best Travel Apps for 2026: The Apps We Actually Use

We reviewed every recommendation and added new apps for AI trip planning, eSIMs, flight tracking, budgeting, and travel safety.

After travelling to more than 130 countries, we have used travel apps for everything from finding a last-minute room and navigating a city offline to translating menus, tracking flights and staying connected without paying ridiculous roaming charges. Some apps have earned a permanent place on our phones. Others have become outdated, overpriced or unnecessary.

For this 2026 guide, we cut through the clutter and chose the travel apps that solve real problems before and during a trip. You do not need to download every app on this list. Choose the ones that match your destination, travel style and the problems you are most likely to face.

The best travel apps for 2026 are Google Maps for navigation, Google Translate for language help, WhatsApp for communication, TripIt for organizing reservations, Google Flights for comparing airfare, Booking.com for hotels, Airalo or another destination-appropriate eSIM for mobile data, Uber for rides and AllTrails for hiking. Most travellers need only one or two apps from each category.

The Best Travel Apps for 2026 at a Glance

Our picks are based on usefulness, ease of use, geographic coverage and whether the app solves a genuine travel problem. We have also included alternatives where the best choice depends on your destination.

Before getting into specialized apps, these are the five we would start with. They cover navigation, translation, communication, flight updates and trip organization.

Google Maps is still the app we use most often while travelling. It handles driving, walking and public-transit directions, lets us save hotels and restaurants, and shows opening hours, recent reviews and nearby services.

Before leaving reliable Wi-Fi, download the map for your destination. Offline maps are especially useful when you land without mobile data or drive through an area with poor reception. Keep in mind that live traffic, some transit information and certain search features may not work offline.

What we like: It combines navigation, trip planning and local research in one place.

What to know: Directions, opening hours and business listings are not always accurate. Double-check important information directly with the business.

Our verdict: Download it before almost any trip.

Google Translate has helped us order food, read signs and have simple conversations in places where we did not speak the language. You can type a phrase, speak into the phone or point the camera at text for an instant translation.

Download the languages you expect to use before your trip. That gives you a useful backup when you do not have data, although online translations can be more complete.

What we like: The camera function is incredibly useful for menus, ticket machines and signs.

What to know: Translations can be awkward or wrong, especially with slang, regional phrases and complicated instructions.

Our verdict: It is one of the most useful free international travel apps.

WhatsApp is the default communication tool in many parts of the world. Hotels, tour companies, drivers and local contacts often use it instead of standard text messages.

It supports individual and group chats, voice calls, video calls, photos, documents and live-location sharing over an internet connection. That makes it useful for keeping a travel group together or confirming a pickup without paying international texting charges.

What we like: It is widely used and keeps trip communication in one place.

What to know: It needs mobile data or Wi-Fi. Check the phone number carefully before sharing personal information or sending money.

Our verdict: Install it before leaving home and verify your number while you can still receive regular text messages.

This may not be the most exciting recommendation, but it is one of the most practical. Download your airline’s official app before departure and sign in to your booking.

Airline apps can provide mobile check-in, boarding passes, gate notifications, delay information and rebooking options. During a disruption, the app may update before airport screens or email notifications do.

What we like: It gives you a direct line to the airline’s current information about your flight.

What to know: Push notifications are useful, but do not rely on them alone. Keep checking the departure board and listen for airport announcements.

Our verdict: Download it for every flight, even if you delete it after the trip.

TripIt turns confirmation emails into one organized itinerary. Forward your flight, hotel, rental-car and activity confirmations, and the app puts the details in chronological order.

This is particularly useful on complicated trips with several flights, hotel changes or train journeys. Instead of searching through your inbox at a check-in desk, you can pull up the reservation in one place.

What we like: It reduces the chaos of juggling confirmation emails.

What to know: Review imported details because automatic parsing is not infallible. Real-time alerts are generally part of the paid plan.

Our verdict: Best for multi-stop trips, business travel and anyone who likes everything organized.

AI can be helpful for brainstorming routes, comparing neighbourhoods, creating packing lists and turning scattered ideas into a first-draft itinerary. It should not be treated as the final authority on visa rules, border requirements, prices, opening hours, transit schedules or safety alerts. Verify anything that could cost you money or prevent you from entering a country.

ChatGPT is most useful when you give it real constraints: your travel dates, budget, interests, pace, mobility needs and where you are staying. It can then help turn those details into a practical first draft rather than a generic list of attractions.

We also use AI to compare neighbourhoods, create checklists and identify questions we still need to research. The trick is to treat the result as a planning assistant, not a booking engine or government authority.

What we like: It is flexible and can quickly reorganize a complicated trip.

What to know: AI can produce outdated or invented information. Always confirm bookings, travel rules, prices and operating hours through official sources.

Our verdict: Excellent for planning and editing; unreliable as the sole source of truth.

Wanderlog combines itinerary planning, maps, reservations, notes and collaboration. It is useful for road trips and group travel because several people can add places and adjust the plan.

The visual map helps reveal when an itinerary makes no geographic sense. That sounds obvious, but it is remarkably easy to plan breakfast on one side of a city, lunch on the other and dinner back where you started.

What we like: The shared planning and map view make group trips easier.

What to know: A detailed itinerary can become cluttered. Keep some flexibility rather than scheduling every hour.

Our verdict: A strong choice for collaborative planning and road trips.

Finding a cheap flight is only part of the job. These apps help us compare dates, monitor prices and track disruptions once the trip begins.

Google Flights is not a conventional downloadable app, but it remains one of the fastest ways to compare airfare. The calendar and price graph make it easy to see whether leaving a day earlier or using a nearby airport could reduce the fare.

Set a price alert when you are not ready to book. Google Flights sends updates when fares change, but you will usually complete the purchase with the airline or another booking provider.

What we like: It is fast, flexible and excellent for comparing dates.

What to know: It does not show every airline or every possible fare. Compare the final price, baggage allowance and change rules before booking.

Our verdict: Our first stop for airfare research. Before pressing confirm, read our guide to airline booking traps that can make a cheap flight cost more

Skyscanner is useful when you know you want to travel but have not settled on a destination. Its flexible search tools can surface options by month, country or broad destination.

It also compares hotels and rental cars, although we mainly use it for flight discovery. Once you find a fare, pay close attention to whether the booking is through the airline or an online travel agency.

What we like: Flexible searches are ideal for travellers who can follow the deal.

What to know: The cheapest result is not automatically the best one. Customer service and change policies vary by booking provider.

Our verdict: Best for inspiration and flexible travel dates.

Available on: iOS and supported Apple devices

Flighty turns a flight number into a detailed timeline with schedule changes, aircraft information and disruption updates. Frequent flyers appreciate how quickly it presents complicated flight information.

It is most useful on travel days, especially when weather or airport congestion starts knocking schedules sideways. The free version is enough for occasional travellers, while frequent flyers may value the paid alerts.

What we like: It presents flight changes clearly and can reduce airport uncertainty.

What to know: Some of its best features require a subscription, and platform availability may not suit every traveller.

Our verdict: A specialist app worth considering if you fly often.

Finding the right place to stay is about more than price. We look at location, recent reviews, cancellation policies, hidden fees, and whether the property actually suits the way we travel. These accommodation apps make it easier to compare hotels, apartments, hostels, and vacation rentals without bouncing between a dozen websites.

Booking.com remains one of the easiest places to compare a wide range of accommodation, from simple guesthouses to luxury hotels. The filters are especially useful when we need parking, a specific neighbourhood, breakfast, air conditioning or a refundable rate.

Read recent reviews rather than relying only on the overall score. We pay particular attention to comments about noise, cleanliness, construction and whether the room matches the photos.

What we like: Huge inventory and practical search filters.

What to know: Cancellation and payment rules vary by property. Confirm whether taxes and resort fees are included before booking.

Our verdict: Our top general-purpose hotel app.

Airbnb is most useful when we want a kitchen, laundry, a living area or enough bedrooms for a group. It can also provide options in neighbourhoods with few conventional hotels.

Compare the total price rather than the nightly rate. Cleaning charges, service fees and local taxes can change the value quickly. Read the house rules and cancellation policy before paying, and check whether the host has a substantial history of recent reviews.

What we like: It can provide more space and practical amenities than a hotel.

What to know: Quality is inconsistent, and fees can make a seemingly cheap stay expensive.

Our verdict: Best for longer stays and groups, not automatically the cheapest option.

Best for: Hostels, dorms, private rooms and social accommodation

Price: Free to search; booking deposit or fees may apply

Hostelworld makes it easy to compare hostels by location, room type, atmosphere and recent guest reviews. It is particularly useful for solo travellers who care about communal spaces and meeting other people.

Do not assume every hostel is a party hostel—or that every quiet-looking property will actually be quiet. Read recent reviews for comments about security, lockers, bathrooms, noise and the surrounding area.

What we like: It provides hostel-specific details that general hotel sites often miss.

What to know: A low bed price can rise after taxes, linen fees or deposits. Check whether lockers require your own padlock.

Our verdict: The most useful specialist app for hostel travellers.

There is no single eSIM provider that is cheapest or fastest in every country. Compare the local network, amount of high-speed data, hotspot rules, validity period and whether the plan is data-only before buying.

Airalo makes it straightforward to buy and install an eSIM before a trip. You choose the destination, select a data package and follow the installation instructions on a compatible phone.

We like that it removes the need to find a physical SIM card immediately after landing. Regional plans can also be convenient on multi-country trips, although a country-specific plan may offer better value.

What we like: Easy setup and broad destination coverage.

What to know: Most plans are data-only, and the local network or speed can vary. Check phone compatibility before purchasing.

Our verdict: A convenient starting point for travellers new to eSIMs.

Ubigi is worth comparing with Airalo because eSIM value changes by country. In some destinations, one provider may offer a better local carrier, more data or a longer validity period.

Install the app and eSIM before departure whenever possible. Take screenshots of the setup instructions in case your connection disappears halfway through activation.

What we like: It gives travellers another established option instead of assuming one provider always wins.

What to know: Coverage and value depend on the specific plan. Read the plan details rather than buying based only on the headline price.

Our verdict: Compare it destination by destination.

Getting around an unfamiliar city can be one of the most confusing parts of travel. These apps help us compare public transit, plan longer connections, and arrange rides when trains or buses are not practical.

Citymapper can be easier to understand than a standard map when a city has several transit systems layered on top of one another. It compares routes, shows transfers and often gives useful instructions about which station exit to use.

We find it particularly useful in large cities where choosing the wrong train direction or exit can add a surprising amount of time.

What we like: Clear transit directions and route comparisons.

What to know: Coverage is limited to supported cities, and live information depends on local transit data.

Our verdict: Excellent in cities where it is available.

Rome2Rio is useful during the early planning stage when you know where you want to go but not how to get there. Enter two places and it outlines possible combinations of flights, trains, buses, ferries and driving routes.

We use it as a starting point rather than the final booking authority. Once we understand the route, we verify schedules and buy tickets directly from the transport operator whenever practical.

What we like: It makes complicated overland connections easier to visualize.

What to know: Estimated times and prices can change. Confirm every important connection with the operator.

Our verdict: One of the best tools for answering, ‘How do we actually get there?’

Uber can remove the uncertainty of explaining a destination, handling cash and negotiating a fare in an unfamiliar city. The app shows the route, vehicle and driver details before the ride begins.

Availability and regulations vary widely. In some destinations, another local app is more common, and airports may require pickup from a designated ride-hailing area.

What we like: Upfront trip details and cashless payment are convenient.

What to know: Surge pricing can be expensive. Always confirm the licence plate and driver before getting into a vehicle.

Our verdict: Useful where it operates, but check the dominant local alternative.

Managing money abroad can get complicated quickly. Exchange rates, foreign transaction fees, ATM charges, and shared expenses all add up, especially on longer trips or when travelling with other people. These apps help us understand what things really cost, manage different currencies, and keep track of who paid for what without turning dinner into an accounting meeting.

Wise lets eligible customers hold and exchange several currencies and spend with a linked card. It can be useful for frequent travellers, remote workers and anyone receiving money in more than one currency.

Always compare the total conversion cost with your regular bank or credit card. The best option depends on your country, card benefits and the type of transaction.

What we like: Transparent conversion information and multi-currency tools.

What to know: Availability, card features and fees vary by country. It is a financial service, so protect the account with strong security.

Our verdict: A useful tool for frequent international travellers.

XE is the app we open when a price full of unfamiliar zeros makes our brains quietly leave the room. It converts currencies quickly and helps you understand what a meal, taxi or hotel actually costs in your home currency.

Remember that the rate shown in a converter is not necessarily the rate your bank, ATM or exchange desk will give you after fees.

What to know: It shows a reference rate, not a guaranteed retail exchange rate.

Our verdict: Keep it on your phone for quick price checks.

Splitwise prevents the end-of-trip ritual where everyone stares at a pile of receipts and suddenly forgets who paid for the rental car. Add shared expenses as you go, assign who owes what and let the app calculate the running balance.

It is particularly helpful for groups using different payment methods or taking turns covering major expenses.

What we like: It reduces awkward money conversations and messy arithmetic.

What to know: It records debts but does not automatically settle every balance. Agree on currencies and exchange rates at the beginning of the trip.

Booking tours and activities in advance can save time, especially when popular attractions have timed entry or limited availability. We use these apps to compare tours, skip-the-line tickets, day trips, and local experiences, but we always check the operator, recent reviews, cancellation policy, and exactly what is included before booking.

GetYourGuide is useful when timed-entry tickets sell out or when a guided visit adds real context. It covers major attractions, walking tours, food tours, day trips and airport transfers in many popular destinations.

Read the cancellation policy and identify the actual tour operator before booking. A marketplace can list several versions of what looks like the same experience.

What we like: Strong inventory in major tourism destinations.

What to know: Quality depends on the local operator, not only the booking platform.

Our verdict: A good place to compare organized experiences.

Viator has a broad inventory of tours and activities around the world. We use it to see what is available, compare departure times and identify experiences that may be difficult to organize independently.

As with any marketplace, read the newest reviews and check exactly what is included. A low starting price may refer to a basic option without transport, admission or the advertised upgrade.

What we like: It covers an enormous range of destinations and activities.

What to know: Listings from different operators can look very similar. Check inclusions, pickup details and cancellation terms.

Our verdict: Best for comparing a wide range of tours.

Finding the right trail or campsite takes more than choosing the prettiest photo. We look at distance, difficulty, recent trail conditions, offline map access, weather, and whether the route matches our experience level. These hiking, camping, and outdoor apps help us plan more confidently, but they should always be used alongside proper preparation and local safety information.

AllTrails is an easy starting point for finding hikes by location, distance, difficulty and user rating. Recent reviews can reveal muddy sections, closures, parking problems and trail conditions that a static guidebook cannot.

Download the route before leaving reception and carry a backup. A phone app is useful, but it does not replace proper preparation, weather awareness or a dedicated navigation tool in remote terrain.

What we like: It makes trail discovery accessible and provides recent user feedback.

What to know: Crowdsourced routes can be inaccurate. Do not rely on a single phone app for serious backcountry navigation.

Our verdict: Best for day hikes and casual outdoor planning.

Gaia GPS is aimed at travellers who need more detail than a simple trail list. It supports topographic maps, route planning and map layers useful for hiking, camping and remote travel.

Learn how to use it before heading into the backcountry. Download the required maps, carry power and tell someone your route. Technology is helpful right up until the battery dies.

What we like: Detailed mapping and route-planning tools.

What to know: It has a learning curve, and important map features may require a subscription.

Our verdict: Better suited to experienced outdoor travellers than casual city walkers.

The following apps can be excellent, but they are more specialized or depend heavily on your destination:

Hidden-city ticketing involves booking a connecting itinerary and intentionally leaving at the connection instead of taking the final flight. It can violate airline conditions, makes checked baggage impractical and can cause the rest of an itinerary to be cancelled. We would not build a trip around it.

Price forecasts can be useful signals, but airfare and hotel prices remain unpredictable. Treat predictions as estimates, not promises. Book when the price, schedule and cancellation terms work for your trip.

Use apps to organize information, not to replace official immigration sources. Entry requirements can depend on nationality, residency, passport type, trip purpose and even transit airports.

Google Maps can provide offline driving navigation for downloaded areas, and Google Translate supports downloaded language packs. Outdoor apps such as AllTrails and Gaia GPS can offer offline maps depending on the plan. Save boarding passes, hotel addresses and reservation numbers before leaving Wi-Fi.

AI can build a useful first draft, but it should not be allowed to quietly invent your holiday. Use it to organize ideas, compare possible routes and identify questions. Then verify flights, hotels, opening hours, ticket rules, visa requirements and safety information through official or first-party sources.

An eSIM can be useful when your regular carrier charges high roaming fees. Compare the local network, data allowance, hotspot rules and validity period before purchasing.

Google Maps and Google Translate support downloaded offline content. Some hiking apps provide offline maps through paid plans. Download everything before leaving reliable Wi-Fi.

The best travel app is not the one with the longest feature list. It is the one that solves a problem at the moment you need it. For us, Google Maps, Google Translate, WhatsApp, an airline app and an itinerary organizer cover the basics. From there, we add an eSIM, flight tracker, budgeting app or hiking map depending on the trip.

Download your essentials before leaving home, test that you can sign in and save critical information offline. Then put the phone away once in a while. The app is supposed to help you experience the trip—not become the trip.

#6259. The Best Stocking Stuffer for Jet-Setters Is This Viral Handbag Accessory

If there’s one thing I love almost as much as planning a trip, it’s having a cute lineup of travel gear to help me get there. The perfect carry-on, a reliable travel tote, a passport holder that doesn’t look like everyone else’s—and, as of late, a bag charm (or three). The accessory du jour has officially made its way from our handbags to our airport ensembles, and I can’t think of a more delightful stocking stuffer for the traveler in your life.

Commerce writer Jessica Chapel is showing off Coach's signature cherry bag charm

Bag charms have a longer fashion history than their current moment suggests: Jane Birkin famously adorned her namesake Hermès with personal keepsakes. Hermès then introduced its Rodeo charm in 2005, and Fendi sent its furry Monster charms down the runway in 2013. After a runway revival at Miu Miu and Balenciaga shows in 2024, the look made its way back to stylish travelers everywhere.

It makes sense, really: We put so much thought into what we pack and what we carry, so why not have a little fun with the bags that get us there? A bag charm is an easy way to give a well-loved weekender a fresh look, or make that familiar canvas tote feel a bit more like your own. There are colorful beads, mini leather accessories, nostalgic trinkets, whimsy characters, and even designs with a practical purpose. Some bag charms are simply there to look good; others offer a clever place to tuck away small essentials. And when your suitcase is circling the baggage carousel among a sea of lookalikes, a fun, personal detail is hardly a bad thing.

Beyond the styling, I like to think of bag charms as a new kind of travel keepsake. We’re always bringing pieces of our trips home: a street market find, a knickknack from a beach town, some wonderfully impractical souvenir that means everything to us and very little to anyone else. Rather than tucking them away on a shelf, clip these charms onto a tote or suitcase, and they’ll join you for the next adventure. The same goes for a charm gifted by a friend or one that reminds you of home. Nothing says, “think of me on the road,” quite like this.

Bag charms add a pop of color to a neutral bag or suitcase

And there’s no shortage of ways to make the look your own. Layer a few bag charms together, mixing colors, textures, and shapes, or keep things more understated with a single leather accent or jewelry-like detail. Think of it as accessorizing your luggage with the same consideration you give the rest of your travel outfit. Whether you’re shopping for the friend who’s always planning a weekend away, the family member with an enviable vintage luggage collection, or the frequent flier who appreciates thoughtful detail, there’s something in the mix for just about every kind of traveler.

Bag charms are small, they’re personal, they’re wonderfully extra, and truthfully, a whole lot more exciting to unwrap than another pair of compression socks. (Sorry, compression socks). Ahead, I’ve rounded up the best bag charms to gift this season, from playful fashion finds and colorful conversation starters to travel-friendly designs that do a little more than just look pretty.

A little cherry on top, quite literally. Made from glittery resin and metal, this bright red pick brings a playful pop of color to a tote, backpack, or set of keys. It’s a particularly good choice for the friend whose wardrobe could always use one more fun thing.

For the person who prefers their accessories a little more understated—but still appreciates a good detail—this bad boy pairs deep green beads with gold-tone hardware and a lobster clasp, offering their favorite bag a subtle hit of color and texture.

For the New Yorker in your life, here's some Big Apple nostalgia to take on the road. Kate Spade pays homage to its hometown with this mini MetroCard-inspired design—and for those who remember the ol’ swipe of a subway card, it's a fun yet tasteful piece of the city to carry along.

I’m adding this gold boot gem to my cart. For a little Western flair—minus the need to break in a new pair of boots—the iconic brand Tecovas has turned its Loretta boot into a mini accessory crafted from solid brass with an antique finish. It comes with both a key ring and a D-ring, so it can go wherever its owner does—whether that’s a road trip, a dude ranch weekend, or simply the daily commute.

Talk about chic! Sézane’s Juliette keychain has a caramel-color resin exterior with delicate white lace detailing, but the real treat is inside: a pocket mirror that opens with a pivoting mechanism. It’s ideal for a quick lipstick check before stepping off the train or heading out to dinner.

For the friend who has approximately 1,000 photos of their dog on their phone—and would happily add one more to the rotation. This little Jack Russell is embroidered onto supple full-grain leather, with a debossed Lauren Ralph Lauren logo on the back. A rather handsome stand-in for a four-legged travel buddy.

A handbag for your handbag? I’m listening. This mini zippered pouch is styled like a classic carryall, with leather construction and gold-tone hardware, and clips onto a larger bag to keep small essentials close. It’s available in red, cobalt blue, and silver, and can be personalized with a foil-debossed monogram—making it an especially sweet gift for a loved one.

A little luck for the road never hurts! This Madewell design brings together a wishbone, stone, and moon motif in a red-and-gold-toned cluster, and is finished with a dog-clip closure. It’s a playful pick for the friend who loves a meaningful trinket—or could use a little good fortune on their next big adventure.

For the friend who's always planning their next trip, this miniature version of Away’s signature hard-shell carry-on is made from the same durable polycarbonate shell and opens into two little compartments for small essentials like a spare key or folded cash. It clips onto a bag or backpack, and the Coast Blue shade is a nice nod to the real thing.

Meet the mini-me of one of our editors' favorite travel bags. Calpak's best-selling Luka duffel—this compact zip pouch comes in a pearlescent finish and clips onto a larger bag with a carabiner-ready loop. Better yet, it actually earns its keep: There’s room for keys, earbuds, cash, or whatever small essentials you’d rather not fish around for at the bottom of your tote.

A flower that doesn’t need watering—or a vase. Inspired by the marigolds of Diwali, this three-dimensional design is made from layered Italian leather petals and comes in yellow or orange. The leather leaf can also be monogrammed, making it a thoughtful gift with a personal touch. It’s a lovely way to bring a little color to someone’s everyday bag.

The Pan American Health Organization has determined that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, meaning domestic spread of the virus is now significant and sustained.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Measles is officially back in the United States after the disease had been eliminated from the country for more than 25 years.

The U.S. officially eliminated measles in 2000, meaning that at that time, the country had gone over a year without continuous domestic spread of the disease. Travelers would occasionally bring measles into the country, sometimes sparking significant local outbreaks, but these didn't tip enough dominoes to lead to ongoing domestic transmission.

That status has now changed, the Wall Street Journal reported Friday (Nov. 13). The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which is the regional office of the World Health Organization for the Americas, has reevaluated the United States' measles elimination status and determined that it should be revoked. With this decision, the U.S. joins several other nations that have seen a local return of measles, including the U.K. and Canada.

The decision follows a series of major measles outbreaks that kicked off in January 2025. Nearly 2,300 cases were reported nationwide in 2025, and so far in 2026, almost 5,412 confirmed cases have been confirmed, although both tallies are likely undercounts.

"When January 2025 picked up, I felt like this might be the point of no return," Maimuna Majumder, a distinguished scholar in the Computational Health Informatics Program at Boston Children's Hospital, previously told Live Science. "I do want to just stress that measles elimination has always been a tenuous prospect, and it is, by design, tenuous," she added.

It takes work to keep an eliminated disease from resurging. The effort rests largely on keeping vaccination rates above a critical threshold — because the measles virus spreads so easily, at least 95% of the population needs immunity via either vaccination or past infection to prevent large outbreaks from occurring and fueling uncontrolled spread. National measles vaccination rates have been falling in recent years, with just 10 states reporting rates above the immunity threshold among kindergarteners for 2025-2026.

Experts point to several factors to explain the trend, including declining funds and staff for public health efforts and wavering public trust in vaccines and scientific expertise. The appointment of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary and the loss of long-standing federal health leadership further fueled the trend, they say, as vaccine guidance has been changed in ways that likely sow confusion and the federal rhetoric around vaccines now frames their safety and effectiveness as open questions when they are actually well-established.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Measles infections can have serious consequences, including long-term disability and death.

The nation's first measles-related deaths this year were reported in Pennsylvania in August, and five more have followed, according to state health officials. (Some of these deaths have not been confirmed by the federal government.) A death reported in Wisconsin and another in New York have brought the current total to eight, per states' counts.

In the U.S., about 1 to 3 out of every 1,000 measles cases results in death. Pennsylvania has recorded just over 1,500 cases, so its number of reported deaths is higher than expected, hinting that the state's true case rate has not been fully captured in the data.

In survivors, measles can cause long-term health problems, including brain damage and immune amnesia, in which the immune cells tasked with remembering past infections have their "memories" wiped.

The PAHO's meeting to reevaluate the United States' status was originally scheduled for April but was pushed to November.

To regain its measles elimination status, the U.S. must go 12 months without continuous spread of the virus.

#6257. In National Geographic’s “Expedition: Saving Our Seas,” it’s all hands on deck

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Narrated by Auli’i Cravalho, the documentary dives into how oceanographers are racing to understand the world’s changing waters

Aerial imagery of research vessel Star Keys safe harboring in Abel Tasman, New Zealand.

As documentaries about Earth’s accelerating climate crisis go, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is surprisingly buoyant.

The ocean covers more than two-thirds of Earth’s surface. And “as the climate heats up, our seas are under pressure like never before,” narrator Auli’i Cravalho, the voice of the title character in Disney’s Moana, says at the opening of The National Geographic Society’s new documentary. The film documents how oceanographers are racing to document and mitigate climate change’s impacts on ocean and coastal habitats.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas premieres November 13 on the National Geographic Channel at 9pm EST and streams the next day on Disney+ and Hulu.

Despite that solemn mission, Expedition: Saving Our Seas is full of hope — and stunning visuals. The documentary offers a window into the scientists’ wonder and joy in their work as they discover new life forms in the depths of the Southern Ocean, or successfully nurture young corals threatened by warming in the Pacific Ocean.

The film opens with a twist on the usual world map: At the center is one great ocean, surrounded by land. Trivia buffs know Earth has five oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. But geographic names aside, these five oceans are just one, linked by a global system of currents known as the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt.

“It’s this giant connected ocean that ignores all of the political boundaries, ignores all of the names we call them,” says Andrew Thurber, a biological oceanographer at the University of California, Santa Barbara, whose research is among those featured in the film.

The documentary loosely follows the current’s path as it zips around the world from project to project.

The first project in the documentary is Thurber’s. He’s on board a research vessel in the frigid Southern Ocean, which rings Antarctica. Using a remotely-operated vehicle dubbed SuBastian, Thurber and his colleagues are scanning the seafloor, hunting for the world’s southernmost hydrothermal vent.

Hydrothermal vents spew superhot, chemically-enriched seawater. In the generally nutrient-poor Southern Ocean, that makes these vents a potential food oasis to support deep sea life.

Throughout the night, as the ROV scans the seafloor, Thurber and his colleagues stay glued to the video it sends back, oohing and aahing as never-before-seen life-forms come into view. “It was a marathon of excitement,” he says now.

Then they see it: A large black smoker, the southernmost hydrothermal vent ever found. And all around it: swarms of pregnant female krill.

“That blew all of our minds,” Thurber says. Krill are the keystone species of the entire Southern Ocean food web, a crucial food source for baleen whales, seals, penguins and fish. But krill are threatened by both industrial fishing and climate change. This discovery, Thurber says, helps make the case for a marine protected area, a region where fishing and other human activities should be restricted.

From the Southern Ocean, the Great Ocean Conveyor Belt flows thousands of kilometers to the north, where marine ecologist Maiyai Taal Hocheimy is tracking how the rising waters of the Atlantic Ocean are encroaching on Banjul, the capital of The Gambia in West Africa. Her hope is that salt-tolerant mangrove trees along the coast, with their dense network of soil-retaining roots, might help hold back the sea in the coming decades — provided that the community can be enlisted to help maintain the mangroves.

I found Hocheimy’s work especially inspiring because she is working to shape the future of oceanography. In 2017, she founded the GREAT (Gaining Research Experience in Africa for Tomorrow) Institute, the first aquatic and coastal science research institute in The Gambia. The mangrove project recruited young local scientists to help conduct the research.

“The goal is to train the next generation of environmental stewards,” Hocheimy says. “We have to show that mangroves have value, so they’ll understand and want to protect them. It is their future at stake.”

That sentiment is echoed many times in the film — the importance not only of enlisting young scientists but also centering local scientists who pose new questions that oceanographers who parachute in from other places may not think to ask, says marine biogeochemist Kristina Brown.

In the documentary, Brown, of the University of Manitoba in Canada, co-leads an expedition to explore the waters of Sherman Basin, a large bay north of the Arctic Circle in Nunavut, Canada. This region has been hunted and fished by Inuit people for centuries.

But it might change beyond all recognition in the next few decades, Brown says. So, the local Inuit community invited her to help create the first catalog of what species are present in the waters and on the seafloor. “[It’s] the first project I’ve been involved in where the local community both defined the research questions and have brought their own unique expertise to the research project.”

Watching how communities around the world are increasingly taking ownership of studies in their own waters was, for me, the most exciting takeaway of this documentary.

“We want to democratize access to the deep sea, to enable people who haven’t had access to these kinds of tools to ask more and new questions,” says Katy Croff Bell, the founder and president of the Ocean Discovery League, a nonprofit ocean exploration group based in Saunderstown, Rhode Island.

As a result of inaccessibility, little of Earth’s vast ocean has been mapped, particularly the deep sea. Bell’s organization is developing inexpensive technologies such as a hardy little camera and sensor system dubbed DORIS, for Deep Ocean Research and Imaging System. It can descend to 6,000 meters and costs less than $10,000.

Expedition: Saving Our Seas offers just a few scant minutes to each project before moving on around the globe to the next, so there’s no time to learn about each project in depth. But the overall takeaway of watching these vignettes, back to back, is that there is a young, energetic community of scientists taking on the challenge.

Mitigating climate change’s impacts on the oceans is, after all, a race against time. So it’s nice to think we might have all hands on deck.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

This story was updated on November 13, 2026, to correct the spelling of Katy Croff Bell's name, and to correct the location of the corals mentioned in the story from the Indian to the Pacific Ocean.

Carolyn Gramling is the earth & climate writer. She has bachelor’s degrees in geology and European history and a Ph.D. in marine geochemistry from MIT and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

#6256. 13 Travel Slippers That Are Comfier Than the Ones From Your Favorite Hotel

After a full day of sightseeing—or an even longer one spent in and out of airports—few things feel better than kicking off your shoes and sliding on a cozy pair of slippers. The complimentary slippers at a luxury hotel are always tempting to take home, but if we're honest, they rarely last beyond a few wears. Fortunately, plenty of more durable—and more comfortable—options exist, from plush, shearling slides and classic wool slip-ons to lightweight travel slippers that barely take up any room in your suitcase. Some have cushioned footbeds and rubber soles sturdy enough for a quick trip outside; others feature soft, suede soles better suited to padding around the house.

Whether you want a warm, fluffy pair by your bed or a foldable option for your next long-haul flight, there’s a slipper for everyone on this list. Read on for the very best pairs to pick up this season from Bombas, Cozy Earth, Ugg, and more.

⁠These lightweight, fuzzy slippers feature a soft, wool-like polyester upper, a breathable lining, and a memory foam footbed for a cushy feel underfoot. The nonslip soles are sturdy enough for quick trips outside to grab the mail or take out the trash, but they're best suited for indoor wear. Even better, they're machine washable, so you can easily keep them in pristine condition all season long. Available in five colors and backed by more than 10,000 Amazon reviews, they're an affordable option for wearing around the house or packing for a weekend away.

It's easy to see why this under-$25 Amazon find has racked up more than 23,000 five-star ratings. Not only are these slippers ridiculously soft (and just the right amount of over-the-top), but they're also pretty practical, thanks to the thick memory foam insole that retains its shape even after daily wear.

While your winter wardrobe likely contains a cashmere sweater or two, don’t sleep on these cashmere slides from Garnet Hill. Thanks to the slip-on slides’ sumptuous cashmere construction and breathable, thermal-insulating fibers, they’ll keep your feet warm and toasty—but not sweaty—all winter long. The padded footbed provides an extra layer of pillowy-soft comfort.

After a long day on your feet, you'll be glad to have these Quince slippers waiting by your bed. They have a soft suede leather upper and thick Australian shearling lining that feels plush against bare feet. And unlike some fuzzy slippers that leave your feet sweaty, the shearling material naturally wicks away moisture and regulates temperature, so you can wear them year-round.

The soft, moisture-wicking sheepskin wool lining of this classic shoe has made it an all-time favorite from the nostalgic Australian brand. The Scuff comes with a thin rubber sole that has just the right amount of support and stability for being on your feet in the kitchen or just puttering around the house on the weekend. Colors include the popular chestnut (shown above), dark gray, and black.

This luxury slide keeps your feet dry and cool, thanks to its moisture-wicking and temperature-regulating design. They're fluffy and warm, and so easy to slip on when you first wake up in the morning. Plus, they feature a slip-resistant sole, making them one of the sturdiest picks on the list.

One of the little luxuries of a hotel stay is slipping into the plush robes and slippers hanging in the closet. Now you can capture that vacation-level comfort at home with The Ritz-Carlton Frette slippers. Crafted from ultra-soft microfiber, they feel cozy and spa-like, while the nonslip soles make them practical for everyday wear around the house. The embroidered hotel logo adds a touch of opulence, and when they need a refresh, simply toss them in the wash.

These striped slippers from Parachute look like something you'd find at a cool boutique hotel. Made in Turkey from thick, absorbent cotton terry, they're soft underfoot and comfortable to slip on after a shower or while lounging at home. The stripes add a little more personality than your typical spa slippers, and the rubber soles grip slippery floors effortlessly. They're durable enough for everyday wear, too, though you may want to size up for a roomier fit.

Made with ultra-soft sheep fur and a plush shearling lining, these chic slippers provide plenty of warmth on chilly fall and winter mornings. As warm as they are, they're also naturally odor-resistant and breathable, so you don't have to worry about your feet getting too hot. They offer a grippy, durable outsole, so while they're best suited for lounging indoors, they can also be worn outside if necessary; you'll feel a little more secure wearing them out on the Airbnb's deck or down to the hotel lobby than in other pairs. They come recommended by commerce editor Meaghan Kenny, who regularly turns to them for extra warmth on cold weekend mornings at home.

Bombas has quite a few solid slippers from which to choose—including the Gripper Slipper that really blurs the line between sock and shoe. But the Sunday Slipper, with its super-soft faux fur and slip-on, slip-off capability, sits at the top of the heap when it comes to versatility. If you're stumped on what to gift someone for the holidays, the best-selling style is foolproof.

Birkenstock manufactures footwear of fabulous durability and quality, from the popular sandals and clogs that you can wear here, there, and everywhere to the more indoor-friendly Zermatt shearling slipper. Despite being supremely soft, the latex sole offers a boost of support, which is why they make such a great house shoe. They come in men's and women’s sizes, and you can pick between wide or narrow fits for optimal comfort.

The Ugg Tasman slipper might be the most recognizable slipper on this list, and it's popular for good reason: The closed-back design makes it a more practical alternative to the brand's classic Scuff slipper; the plush sheepskin lining and durable suede upper ensure coziness and durability; and the Fair Isle–inspired Tasman braid around the trim adds a hint of character.

L.L.Bean fans rave about these clog-like slippers for their arch support, heel cushioning, and playful patterns, featuring designs ranging from turtles to moose to ombré forest trees. They have a fleece lining and rubber anti-slip sole, and are roomy enough to wear your thickest socks underneath in colder months, making them our top pick for cold feet.

What are the best brands for travel slippers?

Bombas and EverFoams design lightweight slippers that are conveniently packable, while Ugg and Quince offer cozy shearling options that take up a bit more suitcase space. If you love the slippers you usually find at luxury hotels, The Ritz-Carlton also sells its signature Frette spa slippers online, so you can bring five-star comfort right to your home.

Slippers can be a welcome change from sneakers or boots on a long-haul flight, especially if you’re hoping to get some sleep. Choose a lightweight, packable pair with nonslip soles, but switch back to shoes when walking around the cabin or using the bathroom.

What should you look for in the best indoor slippers?

When shopping for indoor slippers, fit and material matter most: Wool and shearling provide warmth without trapping too much heat, while memory foam adds cushioning. Look for a soft, flexible sole with enough grip to keep you from slipping on hardwood or tile floors.

#6255. The Sky Today on Saturday, November 14: Venus and Mercury in Virgo

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Following inferior conjunction early this month, Mercury has reappeared in the morning sky. Now magnitude 0.3, you can find the small planet some 5° above the eastern horizon an hour before sunrise. It lies to the lower left of brighter Venus (magnitude –4.8), which sits alongside Virgo’s luminary Spica, about 12° to Mercury’s west.

This morning, Mercury is less than 1° south of 4th-magnitude Kappa (κ) Virginis, which should be visible until the sky brightens enough to wash out the star. You can capture both in the same field of view in either binoculars or a telescope. Mercury now appears as a 32%-lit disk that is 8” across. Compare that with Venus, which features a narrower phase just 13% lit but stretches 51” by comparison. The brighter planet lies just 1.4° northwest of Spica, the brightest star in Virgo.

Both Spica and Kappa can act as guideposts to help you spot Venus’ and Mercury’s motion, respectively, over the next few days. Mercury is moving east and will pull away from Kappa to the lower left. Venus, which just recently reached a stationary point, is also moving east, but will swing slightly northeast (to the upper left) of Spica for a few days before tracking more directly east.

Mars passes 1.2° north of Jupiter at 10 P.M. EST — we’ll focus on this pair in the early-morning sky tomorrow.

Sunrise: 6:44 A.M.Sunset: 4:44 P.M.Moonrise: 11:33 A.M.Moonset: 8:56 P.M.Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (29%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Jupiter and Mars are approaching opposition in February next year. They are now rising late in the evening and dominate the early-morning sky. By 3 A.M. local time on the 15th, the two planets are 40° high in the east. Mars sits just to the upper left (north) of Jupiter, having passed 1.2° due north of the gas giant late last night, shortly before rising. Both planets sit to the upper right (west) of Regulus, the brightest star in Leo the Lion.

In addition to spotting the pair of planets together in a telescope, you’ll want to zoom in on Jupiter in particular, as its Galilean moons are showing off this morning. Around 3 A.M. EST, Callisto stands alone west of the planet, with Io (closest) and Ganymede to the east. Twenty-two minutes later (at 3:22 A.M. EST), Io’s shadow appears at the eastern limb and begins to transit. Just over an hour later, with Io closing in on the same limb, Europa pops into view as it reappears from an occultation at 4:27 A.M. EST. It is just south of Io, which passes due north of Europa at 4:34 A.M. EST. Io then begins a transit two minutes later, slowly following its shadow. Io’s shadow reaches the western limb and disappears at 5:38 A.M. EST, while the moon takes a little over an hour to reach the same point, ending its transit at 5:52 A.M. CST (now daylight in the Eastern time zone).

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#6254. 12 Airline Booking Traps That Could Cost You Money in 2026

Airline websites are not necessarily badly designed, even though they often feel that way. In many cases, the booking process is doing exactly what it was designed to do: get you focused on the lowest advertised fare before revealing the cost of everything else.

You start with a flight that looks like it costs $400. By the time you add a carry-on bag, choose a seat, and work through the final checkout screens, the total is suddenly $650.

After more than 18 years of travel to over 130 countries, we still catch ourselves slowing down to double-check airline bookings. The difference now is that we know where the expensive mistakes are usually hiding. We also use flight-search and tracking tools to compare routes and monitor changes. See our guide to the best travel apps for 2026.

The lowest price on the first screen is rarely enough information to tell you which flight is actually cheapest. You need to compare the complete journey, including baggage, seats, fare restrictions, connections, operating airlines, and the risk involved if something goes wrong.

To avoid costly airline booking mistakes, compare the total price of the journey rather than the advertised base fare. Check the conditions of the exact fare, baggage allowances, operating airline, cabin on every segment, connection times, and whether the flights are issued on one protected ticket.Before paying, compare the flight as a round trip, two one-way tickets, and a multi-city itinerary. Before leaving home, verify your passport, visas or travel authorizations, transit requirements, check-in deadline, and gate-closing time.

These airline booking traps—also common flight-booking mistakes—can turn an apparently cheap ticket into the most expensive option.

One of the first mistakes travellers make is comparing flights by airline logo.

You see the airline you normally use, remember the points sitting in your account, and stop comparing. But loyalty should not convince you to pay hundreds of dollars more for a worse schedule, a more restrictive ticket, or a fare that excludes everything you need.

Airline points can still be valuable, especially when you are close to earning useful status or have benefits such as complimentary baggage. But loyalty should be one part of the calculation, not the starting point.

The days of automatically paying more because “this is our airline” are over. Loyalty should follow value, not the other way around.

Basic Economy can be a perfectly reasonable fare. The trap is buying it without understanding what has been removed.

It may work well when you are taking a short flight, travelling with only a small personal item, do not care where you sit, and are confident your plans will not change.

The problem is that airline websites normally display the lowest available fare first. Once you are in booking mode, it is easy to select that number and move forward without reading the restrictions.

You may save $40 on the ticket and then spend $85 adding the carry-on bag you needed from the beginning.

Before booking Basic Economy, price the next fare category. A Standard Economy ticket may cost more initially but include a carry-on bag, checked luggage, seat selection, or greater flexibility.

Also consider whether seat selection genuinely matters. Travellers with children, mobility considerations, medical needs, or a strong need for an aisle or window seat should include that cost when comparing fares.

Do not buy the lowest number. Buy the fare that includes what you actually need.

Airlines do not necessarily sell every Economy Class seat at the same price. Seats are divided into fare classes or pricing tiers, often called fare buckets.

When the cheapest tier sells out, the price can jump even when the aircraft still has many empty seats.

That is one reason a flight might appear at $480 in the morning and $620 later that day. It does not always mean the plane suddenly filled up. It may mean the least expensive fare class is no longer available.

When you see a noticeable price increase, do not assume you must either pay it immediately or lose the trip.

A competitor may now be cheaper. In other cases, the next fare level may include baggage, seat selection, or flexibility that makes it better value than the stripped-down ticket you were originally considering. A fare jump is a signal to widen the search, not automatically accept the new price.

For the tools we use to compare dates, airports, and fare changes, see our guide to the best travel apps for finding flights.

The standard airline search box encourages travellers to enter a departure city, destination, outbound date, and return date.

That does not mean a traditional round trip is always the cheapest or most efficient way to book.

Before purchasing an expensive international itinerary, compare it three ways:

An open-jaw ticket means flying into one city and returning home from another.

For example, if you are travelling through Europe, you might fly into Paris and return from Rome. Even if the airfare is similar to a return ticket from Paris, you could avoid paying for a train or flight back to your starting point. You may also save a hotel night and an entire day of backtracking.

Different airlines can also be used in each direction. One carrier may offer the best outbound flight, while another has a much better return schedule.

When comparing separate tickets, check baggage fees, fare restrictions, connection risks, and cancellation policies. The goal is not to find the cleverest itinerary. It is to determine which option gives you the best total trip.

With a codeshare flight, the airline selling the ticket may not be the airline flying the plane.

You might purchase the journey through one airline’s website and then arrive at the airport to discover that a partner carrier operates the flight.

Before buying, look for the words “operated by” in the flight details.

Then check the itinerary on both airline websites. Confirm the aircraft, seat map, baggage allowance, terminal, and check-in instructions.

After booking, make sure you have the operating carrier’s reservation number. The confirmation number issued by the airline selling the ticket may not work on the partner airline’s website.

Codeshares are not automatically bad. They can provide more destinations and useful connections. The problem is that they create a handoff between companies, and that handoff can become confusing when you need assistance.

As we have learned, one of the most expensive sentences in travel can be: “You need to contact the other airline.”

Mixed-cabin fares are one of the easiest airline traps to miss.

The search result may display a large Premium Economy or Business Class label, making it appear that the entire journey is in the upgraded cabin.

Then you expand the flight details and discover that the 40-minute connection is in Premium Economy while the eight-hour overnight flight is in regular Economy.

We have come close to booking this type of itinerary several times.

Before paying, check the cabin listed beside every individual segment. Make sure the premium seat is on the flight where you will actually benefit from it.

Do not assume one premium segment provides premium benefits throughout the trip.

Screenshot the cabin shown for each flight and confirm that it appears correctly in the final reservation. A mixed-cabin fare is only a deal when the upgraded cabin is on the part of the journey that matters.

There is rarely one simple baggage policy that applies to every passenger flying with an airline.

Do not check only the airline’s general baggage page. Open the conditions attached to the specific fare and route you are considering.

This is especially important when connecting from a transatlantic flight to a smaller airline or low-cost carrier within Europe. A bag accepted on the first flight may be too large, too heavy, or not included on the next one.

A bag fitting inside the overhead compartment does not automatically mean it meets the airline’s rules. Wheels, handles, and outside pockets are normally included when the bag is measured.

Price your luggage before buying the flight. A ticket that appears $30 cheaper can quickly become more expensive once the necessary baggage is added.

Paying for bags online in advance is also frequently less expensive than waiting until the airport, although the difference varies by airline.

Finally, weigh your suitcase at home using a real scale. Picking it up and declaring that it “feels about 20 kilos” is not a reliable baggage strategy.

Once you know your allowance, follow our two-minute checked-bag routine before handing your suitcase over at the airport.

A self-transfer may be the most expensive mistake in this guide.

Some search and booking sites combine two separate tickets and display them as one journey. Look for warnings such as:

The critical detail is that the airlines may not recognize the flights as one protected itinerary.

If the first flight is delayed and you miss the second one, the second airline may consider you a no-show. You could lose the remaining flights on that reservation and be forced to purchase a new last-minute ticket.

The first airline may not be responsible for helping because it transported you to the destination shown on its ticket.

Leaving the international transit area can also trigger entry or transit requirements that would not apply during a normal airside connection.

Self-transfers can work when you have a long buffer, carry-on luggage, an airport you understand, and enough flexibility to absorb a disruption.

We would not use one when connecting to a cruise, wedding, organized tour, or once-daily long-haul flight.

Always compare the self-transfer price with a protected itinerary. The higher fare may not simply be buying convenience. It may be buying the airline’s responsibility to get you to your final destination.

Airlines can sell a connection that technically meets the airport’s minimum requirements.

That does not necessarily mean it is comfortable, sensible, or suitable for you.

A 45-minute connection at a large international airport might involve:

If a connection makes you nervous while sitting at home, it will not feel better when you are waiting for the aircraft door to open. Choose connection time based on the consequences of missing the next flight.

A long layover can be inconvenient. A missed connection can cost a full day or derail the entire trip.

We use third-party flight sites for research. They are useful for comparing airlines, dates, and routing options.

Buying through one is a separate decision.

A third-party fare may be genuinely cheaper, but make sure you are comparing the same product. It could involve:

The biggest issue normally appears when the schedule changes or the flight is cancelled.

The airline may tell you to contact the company that issued the ticket. The booking company may then tell you that only the airline can resolve the flight.

Before buying, find the itinerary through the search site and compare it directly with the airline. When the price difference is small, booking with the airline may be worth it for easier communication during disruptions.

Also check the payment currency. Some booking sites offer to convert the total into your home currency. This feels convenient but may include a less favourable exchange rate.

When your credit card does not charge a foreign transaction fee, paying in the original currency may be less expensive. Compare the final converted amount and check your card’s fees rather than choosing a currency based on familiarity.

Some of the most expensive travel problems do not happen during booking. They happen at the airport after your hotel, tour, rental car, or cruise has already been paid for.

A valid passport may not be enough to enter your destination or transit through a connecting country.

Depending on your nationality, route, and destination, you may need:

A passport can be valid on your departure date and still fail to meet the destination’s entry requirements. Complicated connections are also a good reason to review our international travel safety tips before departure.

Names matter too. The name on your airline ticket should match your passport and any visa or travel authorization. Do not assume that a nickname or commonly used name will be accepted.

Before an international trip, take five minutes to verify:

Canadian travellers should verify current destination-specific requirements using official government travel advisories and the relevant embassy or immigration authority, since entry and transit rules can change.

Five minutes at home can save the entire trip at the airport. For our complete pre-departure routine, read our travel safety checklist for 2026.

Departure time is when the aircraft is scheduled to leave. It is not the time you should arrive at the gate.

Boarding begins earlier, and the gate closes before departure. The exact cutoff depends on the airport, airline, route, and destination.

Once the gate is closed, seeing the aircraft through the terminal window will not save your seat.

If you miss the flight, the cost may extend far beyond a replacement ticket. You might also lose:

Build your airport schedule backward from the airline’s check-in, baggage-drop, boarding, and gate-closing deadlines.

Check current security conditions using the airport’s official app or website, but do not treat an estimated wait time as a guarantee. Add time for airport parking, shuttle transportation, baggage drop, security, passport control, terminal changes, and finding the gate.

It is better to have extra time near the gate than to spend the start of your trip running through an airport while your name is being called over the loudspeaker. Arriving early does not help much if your carry-on slows you down at screening. Read our airport security tips and common mistakes before packing.

Before confirming a flight, we recommend checking the entire itinerary one final time.

The best defence against airline booking traps is not a secret search setting or complicated flight hack. It is slowing down long enough to compare the complete journey.

All 12 of these traps work best when travellers are rushing.

We see a low fare, get excited about the trip, and want to finish before the number changes. The booking process then reveals the bags, seats, restrictions, connections, and other costs after we have already become emotionally committed to the flight.

The cheapest flight is not necessarily the one with the lowest number on the first screen. It is the flight that gets you to your destination without surprise charges, unrealistic connections, or an expensive problem at the airport.

After more than 18 years of travelling, experience has not made us immune to booking mistakes. It has simply taught us when to stop, reopen the details, and check everything one more time.

Take five minutes before pressing confirm. Those five minutes could save hundreds of dollars—or save the entire trip.

In this excerpt from "The Secrets of our DNA," geneticist Turi King examines how DNA was used to reveal the ultimate fate of the last members of the House of Romanov.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In 1917, the Russian Revolution was in full swing. Tsar Nicholas II had abdicated, and he and his family were exiled to a remote Siberian town. There were plans to get the family to the U.K., but King George V (Nicholas' first cousin) and the British government withdrew their offer of asylum over concerns of the ramifications.

After the Russian Provisional Government was overthrown by the more extreme Bolsheviks in October 1917, Nicholas, his wife, their children and several members of the family's staff were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, where, in July 1918, they were executed. Their bodies were hidden and remained lost to time ‪for nearly a century —‬ until modern technology, with some help from the British royal family, unraveled the fascinating story of their disappearance.

In this excerpt from "The Secrets of Our DNA: How Genetics Has Changed the World" (Pegasus Books, 2026), author Turi King, director of the Center for Evolution at the University of Bath, looks back at the incredible story of how DNA was used to solve a major mystery of modern history: What happened to the last members of the House of Romanov?

I was sitting in a lecture theatre at Cambridge University in 1994 when one of my lecturers, Erika Hagelberg, spoke about a new study she had just been involved in. It was the first major case to combine both mitochondrial DNA and DNA fingerprinting to identify human remains: those of the Russian imperial family.

But first I need to take you back to Russia in 1917 and the abdication of the tsar following the Russian Revolution.

The Russian royal family, the Romanovs, had been the reigning imperial dynasty since 1617, and three centuries later, Tsar Nicholas II was on the throne. Nicholas was the cousin of George V, king of the United Kingdom, their mothers being sisters, and had married George's cousin Princess Alix (Alexandra) of Hesse, who was apparently Queen Victoria's favourite grandchild. Nicholas and Alix had five children, four daughters (Olga, Tatiana, Maria and Anastasia) and a son, Alexei.

The tsar and his wife were not well liked by the Russian population and political unrest culminated in the revolution of 1917, when Nicholas was forced to abdicate. The family were kept under house arrest and in 1918 they were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg with the royal physician, Dr Botkin, and three of their staff. On the night of 16 July, the family, their doctor and staff were herded into the cellar together and executed. Their bodies were then taken to a secret location and placed in a hastily dug communal grave, doused in sulphuric acid in an attempt to disfigure them and hinder identification, and then covered over, the location of the grave being lost for more than 70 years.

The Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, 1919.

Ironically, the new Russian government had wanted to get the Romanovs out of Russia due to the risk of their becoming a rallying point, but a plan to grant asylum to the Romanovs in the U.K. because of their links with the British royal family fell through, owing to a reluctance on the part of George V to grant it. Yet those links with the British royal family would eventually prove crucial in their identification.

Fast-forward to 1991, when several skeletons were found in a shallow grave some 20 miles from Yekaterinburg. Many of the bones were badly damaged but it was possible to determine, based on examination of the skeletal remains, that there were nine individuals — two short of the 11 killed that night. The faces of the skulls were badly damaged in all of the skeletons, all of them showing evidence of violence either in the form of bullet holes or bayonet wounds or both. Before the genetic study, Russian forensic scientists had used numerous techniques alongside historical data to tentatively identify the remains as some of the members of the Russian royal family, their doctor and servants.

These included examining the bones, to determine approximate age and sex, and some of the teeth, the expensive dental work, incorporating gold, platinum and porcelain, indicating that certain remains must belong to members of an aristocratic family. The team worked out that the two missing individuals would have been two of the children, one of the daughters (while it was hard to determine which one it would be, given how close in age they were, it was thought that it was either Maria or Anastasia) and the son, Prince Alexei.

The Russian chief forensic medical examiner then contacted a team in the U.K., which included Erika, to see if genetic evidence could be used to confirm the identification. The U.K. team used the amelogenin genetic sex test, now part of standard forensic DNA testing, which confirmed the sex of the skeletons (four male and five female bodies), while an early form of DNA profiling showed that there was a family group here — two parents and three children — and four unrelated individuals. So far, so good.

Next, they needed to prove that this was the Russian royal family, and they did this using mitochondrial DNA analysis. As you'll remember, mitochondrial DNA is passed down by a mother to all her children, male and female, but only daughters can pass it on — so if female-line family members of Tsar Nicholas and Tsarina Alexandra could be found and would agree to give a DNA test, their mitochondrial DNA should match that of their royal ancestors. It just so happened that the late Prince Philip, husband of the late Queen Elizabeth, was related to the tsarina through the female line: she was his great-aunt, his maternal grandmother being the sister of the tsarina. He kindly gave a DNA sample.

The testing that they did was standard for the time in that they looked at two regions known as hypervariable regions 1 and 2 (HVR1 and HVR2). You'll remember that mitochondrial DNA has 37 rather crucial genes on it where any "typo" that occurs as the DNA is being copied could have serious consequences if the mutation is deleterious. By contrast, in those parts of the mitochondrial genome that don't code for anything, such as these two hypervariable regions, mutations can occur more freely without necessarily causing issues, meaning that these regions contain much more genetic variation. These are the sections of mitochondrial DNA that scientists began analysing for identification purposes. While it's not as precise as DNA profiling because many thousands of people will all have the same mitochondrial DNA type, it can be very helpful in a case such as this.

Prince Philip's DNA was eventually used to confirm the identities of the lost Romanov family.

When the team sequenced these two regions, Prince Philip's mitochondrial DNA was found to match that of the putative remains of the tsarina and her daughters. Next they found two living female-line relatives of the tsar, descended from his maternal grandmother: a great-great-niece, Princess Xenia Cheremeteff Sfiris, and a first cousin twice removed, James Carnegie, 3rd Duke of Fife. The mitochondrial DNA from these two matched each other perfectly, and they, in turn, matched that of the tsar, except at one base where there was both a match and a mismatch.

This is because the tsar had what's known as a heteroplasmy at this position: some of the mitochondrial DNA sequences showed a T and others showed a C, his maternal relatives showing a T. Heteroplasmy is known to take place primarily through mutations occurring when the DNA is copied to make new cells in a person's lifetime, but it can be inherited from a maternal ancestor with heteroplasmy. Extremely rarely, it can come from paternal mitochondrial DNA making it into the cell. So the fact that heteroplasmy existed in the DNA sample didn't negate the match, and the probability that these were the Romanovs was still between 70 to 1 through to 840,000 to 1 in favour. But, it did sow some seeds of doubt. Incidentally, we now know that heteroplasmy is fairly common, with potentially over half of the human population having at least one heteroplasmy, albeit at a low percentage in terms of their mitochondrial DNA carrying it.

So, to be doubly sure, in 1996 the remains of the tsar's brother, Georgij, who had died in 1899, were exhumed and he was found to have exactly the same mitochondrial heteroplasmy. Given the very low chance of two people having this particular heteroplasmy if they weren't related, this pointed to the mitochondrial DNA data the researchers obtained being 130,000,000 times more likely if these were the Romanovs than if they were an unrelated family.

The case was solved in terms of identifying the tsar, tsarina and three of their daughters, but the mystery still remained as to what had happened to the two other children. In the scientific paper reporting the results, the authors conjectured that possibly the two children had been buried separately, or that they could have survived the massacre. Incidentally, there was a woman living in the U.S. who claimed to be Anastasia, saying she had managed to escape being executed, and so the fact that two of the children were missing from the Romanov family group only fuelled the idea that maybe she truly was the missing princess.

Then, in 2007, a group of amateur archaeologists, digging a mere 70 metres away from the previously discovered mass grave, came across more human remains. Skeletal evidence showed that they were the remains of two bodies, a young woman aged 15-19 and a probable male aged 12-15. DNA analysis was brought to bear and again showed that the two individuals were siblings and related to the Romanovs already identified. As an extra DNA test, Y-chromosome testing was carried out, the Y chromosome being passed from father to son, to confirm that the Y chromosome of the newly found male skeleton was indeed male and that it matched the Y chromosome of the tsar. This also then matched male-line relatives — a second cousin once removed of the tsar (third cousin of Alexei) through Tsar Nicholas I. The missing Romanov children had been found.

Help us improve Live Science Pro: We're always trying to make our content better. Leave us feedback about Pro here.

From an award-winning expert on DNA, discover the myth-busting book that opens a dazzling window into the world of modern genetics.

Fascinating, compassionate, and entirely captivating, The Secrets of Our DNA is the essential book that explains how genetics has changed and transformed the world around us.

Turi King is renowned for presenting complex findings on DNA and genetic science in an accessible and compelling way and she has won awards for her public engagement in science. Turi is the director of the Milner Centre for Evolution at the University of Bath. She is an honorary fellow of the British Science Association, a fellow of the Society of Antiquaries of London, a member of the Chartered Society of Forensic Sciences, and a member of the International Society of Forensic Geneticists. She is well known for her academic work leading the identification of Richard III; advising on the case of Mary Jane Kelly (the last victim of Jack the Ripper); leading the project on sequencing Hitler’s genome; as well as her media work co-presenting BBC’s DNA Family Secrets.
